title: Bills might have re-unlocked Josh Allen, and that makes Buffalo's offense all the more dangerous
summary: Allen had five completions of 30-plus yards, his most in a game in his career
full_text:
For years, Reliant Stadium had been a house of horrors for Josh Allen and the Bills . Last year, he took eight sacks and threw two picks in a 23-19 loss in Houston. The year before, he completed 9 of 30 pass attempts. Yes, nine. In the 2020 wild card round, Buffalo blew a 16-0 lead, and in 2018, as a rookie, Allen suffered an elbow injury in his first visit to H-town.
But what did Allen and Buffalo unleash on the Texans on Sunday? Well, that could be scary for the rest of the league.
Allen went 20 for 29 for 334 yards and two touchdowns — and added two touchdowns on the ground — in the Bills' 36-31 Week 1 win over the Texans . His 34-yard dart to Joshua Palmer proved to be the game-winner.
WHAT A THROW. WHAT A CATCH. 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/8tOhQ17O3h
"We do like Reliant Stadium," Allen said as he entered his press conference. "Woohoo!"
He also must have liked how the Bills' offense looked, both in personnel and game plan. Allen found DJ Moore , making his Bills debut, five times for 100 yards and a touchdown (plus a 46-yard gain via pass interference). He found Dalton Kincaid five times for 130 yards.
The numbers are nice, but look under the hood, and you'll see a different approach than any in recent memory. Allen's average pass traveled 13.2 yards downfield — a number higher than any of his games in 2025. Or 2024. Or 2023. He had a career-high five completions of 30-plus yards.
"Hell — heck yeah!" Allen beamed when asked if he liked the return of the big play, so excited he broke his own rule of not cursing.
"Sorry, heck yeah! We love chunk plays. That's how you score 36 points. You give yourself the opportunity to go score in four or five plays on a drive instead of the long, methodical, 13, 14, 15 plays. That's also a way to win football games, so we don't wanna just try to live off the chunk plays. We wanna be smart, and we wanna take our opportunities when they're there, but we just wanna be smart with the football, which we were tonight."
He's exactly right. Last year, the Bills, lacking a true downfield threat, became a conservative passing offense. Allen, largely limited to screens and quick passing, finished 25th (out of 33) in air yards per attempt and 18th in deep throw rate.
Allen won't revert to the early-career, chuck-it-deep youngster he once was — he has become a far better, more well-rounded quarterback — but he reminded everyone Sunday his arm can unlock truly special moments.
Sometimes it's players, and sometimes it's plays. The Bills have both, and that's a statement. That they have both and can do it against one of the NFL's best defenses makes the statement even louder.
Consider late in the first half, with the Bills pinned at their own four-yard line. Play conservatively, pick up a few yards and not try anything too dangerous against Houston's nightmare-fuel defense, right? Forget that. How about this beautiful 38-yarder to Kincaid?
Josh Allen with the throw and Dalton Kincaid with the catch 🔥 BUFvsHOU on CBS/Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/fj7tVqbYlg
Then, on the other side of the two-minute warning, a 15-yarder to Moore followed by this:
MOORE OF THIS PLZ‼️ @JoshAllenQB x @idjmoore 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/SHEQkBZHs1
Three plays, 96 yards, 41 seconds.
Allen called the Moore touchdown a "horseshoe throw" — a throw that goes where it's not supposed to based on the play call. He said the same thing about the Palmer touchdown. But Allen has the arm to throw a ball through a tornado and have it come out the other side, spiral intact — basically what he did on the Moore touchdown pass — and the downfield weapons to make the not-supposed-to-happen completions. On the game-winner to Palmer, Allen said he saw the safety cheating Moore's way.
"There's a reason we brought him here — the ability that he can make plays downfield," coach Joe Brady said of Moore. "He opens it up for everybody."
Imagine what a healthy Kincaid can do, too. Ideally for Buffalo, Sunday was just a taste. The tight end has flashed clear talent as a big-play producer, but constant injury woes have prevented him from playing full-time or at full effectiveness. Last season, he led all tight ends in yards per route run. The problem? His 202 routes ranked only 48th among tight ends.
But he was healthy all offseason and added strength, boosting not only his ability but also his availability. Brady explained Kincaid can be used in more looks and more alignments because he's become a more effective blocker.
"When he's on the field, we're a better team, and we're a better offense," Brady said. "So proud of Dalton."
"He's a stud," Allen said, smiling. "Absolute stud."
On a day when the normally excellent run game wasn't as effective as usual — just 86 yards on 4.1 yards per tote — the big-play passing was a game-changing change-up.
Or maybe the big-play passing was the fastball.
Maybe, with Moore, a healthy Kincaid and, of course, Allen (whose howitzer-level arm strength was too rarely on display recently), the Bills can have different fastballs. Want to try to take away the run and tackle on short passes? Allen now has the guys to beat you deep. Want to make sure nothing gets behind you? The run game, led by 2025 NFL rushing yards leader James Cook , can control the game and provide explosiveness on the ground. Plus, Allen has grown leaps and bounds in the quick passing game since his career began.
And even when the defense seems to have the right play, Allen can still beat you.
This is only Week 1, when there's as much foreshadowing as there is fool's gold across the league. Perhaps there's even more of the latter. The Bills had all offseason to develop an excellent plan against an excellent defense, and they did. There were still stops and starts offensively, and the defense has a long way to go, too. September's successes mean nothing in January and February.
But for one week, the Bills' offense not only showed some of its patented efficiency, but its long-overdue return to downfield explosiveness. It's arguably the most impressive performance from a single unit across the sport on the opening weekend
author: Zachary Pereles

title: Cover 32: Bengals see early returns from big offseason investment, plus game balls, biggest gaffes from Week 1
summary: Tyler Sullivan dives into all the biggest items from Week 1 in the NFL, including Josh Allen ending his road woes against the Texans
full_text:
A good rule of thumb in life is this: You get what you pay for.
The Cincinnati Bengals are starting to realize that firsthand after seeing immediate returns from a defense where they deployed an unprecedented amount of resources over the offseason. In all, Cincinnati spent roughly $138.7 million in free agency, with the bulk of that spending going toward the defensive side of the ball.
Most notably, edge rusher Boye Mafe received a $60 million deal, safety Bryan Cook got $40.25 million, and defensive tackle Jonathan Allen signed a contract worth a total of $25 million. And that was just what they did on the open market. The Bengals also shipped out the No. 10 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft to New York to land All-Pro defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence , who they promptly signed to a one-year, $28 million extension.
This investment, while admittedly hefty, was necessary for Cincinnati.
While Joe Burrow (when healthy) has spearheaded a high-octane offense over his tenure, the organization's ceiling has been battered down because of poor play on the defense. Last season proved to be rock bottom, allowing the third-most points per game (28.9) in the league and allowing the most yards per play (6.2). Their points-per-game-allowed metric had decreased in each of the previous four seasons. That was the cause of the action we saw this offseason.
While you may look at 27 points allowed in a Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to begin 2026 as the Bengals' offense simply bailing the defense out once again with 33 points scored, you'd be mistaken. Cincinnati's defense appears to have turned a corner, and this new cast of characters was at the center of the winning effort.
In the opener, the Bengals' defense generated four total turnovers (all fumbles). Three came on consecutive drives from the middle of the first quarter to the beginning of the second. The first put points on the board with linebacker Demetrius Knight Jr. recovering a loose ball after Baker Mayfield was sacked by Myles Murphy and Barrett Carter and returned it 27 yards for the score.
BENGALS WITH THE SCOOP AND SCORE!!! TBvsCIN on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XV5FjYppBP
Just three plays after that scoop-and-score, Cook took down Bucs running back Bucky Irving , popped the ball free, and Mafe recovered. Those were three key pillars of this offseason defensive makeover contributing to an early turnover.
BENGALS WITH THE SCOOP AND SCORE!!! TBvsCIN on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XV5FjYppBP
Meanwhile, the third fumble was recovered by Cook, and Mafe forced the fourth, so this new group made significant waves in their debuts.
6 tackles, 1 forced fumble, 1 fumble recovery
3 pressures, 1 sack, 1 fumble recovery
2 pressures, 1 sack, 3 tackles
On top of the turnovers, Cincinnati finished the opener with four sacks, holding Tampa Bay to converting 5 of 10 third-down opportunities, and allowed a touchdown on just two of their four red zone trips. Meanwhile, a touchdown in this game wasn't the defense's fault, with Burrow tossing a pick six in the third quarter. So, they really surrendered 20 points in the win.
While that doesn't sound like much, for a defense that ranked at or near the bottom of the NFL in most meaningful categories last year, this is a substantial step forward.
A common talking point about the Bengals entering 2026 has been getting these defensive figures up. They don't need to be a top 10 defense in the NFL, but can they be near league average? If so, the firepower on offense gives them a Super Bowl-caliber ceiling. From what we saw in Week 1, they might be well on their way to spending their way out of the basement and thrusting themselves into serious title contention.
How Game Balls work: Six are awarded to standout players from the slate on teams who won their contests, and only one player on a team can get a game ball.
Lawrence picked up right where he left off at the end of the 2025 season where he led the NFL in total touchdowns over his final eight games. In the opening win against Cleveland, Lawrence was superb, leading scoring drives on his first four possessions. This was his third career game with four or more passing touchdowns and his 12th career game with three or more passing touchdowns (which tied the most in franchise history).
His final touchdown of the day was arguably his best. Lawrence evaded pressure, rolled out to his left, and somehow uncorked a dart 32 yards down the field to connect with Jakobi Meyers in the back of the end zone.
Trevor Lawrence with his 4TH TD pass of the game 🔥 PUTTING ON A SHOW CLEvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/77IDTz3gOw
This was MVP-caliber play from Lawrence, who is entering Year 2 under Liam Coen.
Gibbs was the top pick in most fantasy football drafts for a reason. With David Montgomery traded to Houston this offseason, there was a promise for an increased workload, and we saw that in Week 1. Gibbs registered 34 touches in the overtime win over New Orleans and piled up 186 yards from scrimmage. This was Gibbs' 12th career game with two or more rushing touchdowns, which is tied for the second-most since entering the NFL in 2023. He also tallied his 50th career touchdown in this game, making Gibbs just the sixth player in NFL history to have this many scores in his first 50 career games.
Jahmyr Gibbs doing what Jahmyr Gibbs does! TD Lions 👀 NOvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/q0dJZhPU9F
It was another Herculean effort by Josh Allen as the Bills quarterback willed his team to a 36-31 win against the Texans . Allen carved up what has been widely considered to be one of the top defenses in the league, with Buffalo averaging 7.9 yards per play. This was Allen's first career road win against the Texans, entering this matchup with a 0-4 mark. Allen recorded his seventh career game with 300-plus passing yards, two-plus passing touchdowns, and two-plus rushing touchdowns, which extends his NFL record. This was also his 26th career game with four or more total touchdowns, which ties Brett Favre for fifth all time.
Josh Allen takes it in himself for the TD 💪 BUFvsHOU on CBS/Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/ihfkBNmfeS
Henry continues to be the ageless wonder. The 32-year-old demolished the Colts ' run defense in Baltimore's 41-23 win in Indy. This was his seventh-career game with 140-plus rushing yards and three-plus rushing touchdowns, which ties him with Jim Brown for the most in NFL history. His rushing touchdowns also helped him surpass Marcus Allen for the third-most in NFL history (126).
KING HENRY RUMBLES IN FOR ANOTHER TD!! BALvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/4h8WpRsLW5
FIFTY-NINE! The Chicago Bears dropped 59 points in the Week 1 win over Carolina, and Williams was a man possessed in Charlotte. He became the first player in Bears history with 250-plus passing yards, two-plus passing touchdowns, 50-plus rushing yards, and two-plus rushing touchdowns in a game. These 59 points scored were the third-most in a game in Bears history.
CALEB TO KMET FOR 6 CHIvsCAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/KedXXw4da5
Even amid quarterback turnover with Kyler Murray going down in the first quarter and Carson Wentz coming in under durress, Justin Jefferson reminded folks why he's considered one of the top receivers in the NFL. He caught eight of his nine targets on the day for two receiving touchdowns. Remember, Jefferson had two receiving touchdowns in ALL of last season.
JUSTIN JEFFERSON FULL SEND Vikings are POURING it on pic.twitter.com/Ekm93GH9Mw
We'll go back to the NFL opener for our first gaffe, with Patriots quarterback Drake Maye's inexplicable game-losing interception. Trailing 13-10 in the fourth quarter, New England got the ball to the Seattle 16-yard line with less than 30 seconds to play in regulation. While the Patriots could take a shot to the end zone, Maye needed to be smart with a game-tying field goal (and forcing overtime) in…

summary: A former Arizona Cardinals running back was sentenced to five years in federal prison for a dogfighting ring operation in Oklahoma. He was tried and convicted on six felony counts: […]
full_text: A former Arizona Cardinals running back was sentenced to five years in federal prison for a dogfighting ring operation in Oklahoma. LeShon Johnson operated a large-scale endeavor that involved hundreds of pit bulls. In August, he went on trial in Oklahoma federal court for the operation. He was tried and convicted on six felony counts: one count of sale, transport, and delivery of a dog for use in an animal fighting venture, two counts of selling a dog for use in an animal fighting venture, and three counts of possessing a dog for use in an animal fighting venture. RELATED: KYLER MURRAY POSTS A PHOTO WEARING A VICK JERSEY WITH A PIT BULL Johnson played for the Cardinals for a portion of 1995 and then in the 1996 and 1997 seasons. He was a waiver claim for Arizona. Ex-NFL RB LeShon Johnson sentenced to 5 years for dog fighting https://t.co/IANoLJpepx #NFLDraft #NFL #Football pic.twitter.com/AwraZaxNM4 — Draft Diamonds ™️ (@DraftDiamonds) September 10, 2026 In addition to the five years in prison, Johnson was sentenced to three years of supervised release and a $30,000 fine. He was acquitted of 17 other similar counts. As part of the investigation in 2024, authorities seized 190 dogs. It will go down as the most canines seized in a federal dogfighting investigation by the Department of Justice. Back in 2004, Johnson entered a guilty plea to state animal fighting charges and received a five-year deferred sentence connected to those charges. Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. stated in a news release regarding Johnson’s sentence this time around: “LeShon Johnson will face justice for building another particularly egregious and violent dog fighting scheme. As Johnson was well aware, dog fighting is a felony in all 50 states. To anyone attempting to build violent and illicit business schemes: you can run, but you can’t hide from the Department of Justice.” Despite his conviction in 2004, Johnson continued to traffic dogs for illegal fighting. He should lose his @NFLPA pension. Clearly he is ungrateful he has it in the first place and this reflect poorly on the perception of fans for people who played in the @NFL . — Counterpoint (@cntrpntnews) September 10, 2026 Johnson was self-employed with “Mal Kant Kennels.” It advertised that they bred “champion and grand champion” pit bulls. By word of mouth, their adult dogs were said to “create offspring with fighting traits.” The distinction is that “champion” dogs have already won three fights while “grand champion” dogs have won five. Through his kennel, Johnson would sell stud rights to other dog owners as well as puppies from either champion or grand champion animals. Dog fighting is a felony in all 50 states. He grew up in Oklahoma and was a bull rider on the junior rodeo circuit. Is it possible that this is where Johnson began his infatuation with violence coupled with an animal? Johnson was drafted by the Green Bay Packers in Round 3 of the 1994 NFL draft out of Northern Illinois, where he rushed for 1,976 yards in his senior year. In his year in the league, the Packers released him, and the Cardinals claimed him. In his first year with Arizona, he suffered an injury in training camp in 1996 that lingered until the Week 4 game against the New Orleans Saints, when he rushed for 214 yards, which remains the franchise’s second-best single-game effort. After that, Johnson never rushed for 100 yards in a game for the remainder of his career. In 1998, he had a bout with lymphoma cancer. He made a comeback with the New York Football Giants and played the 1999 season, and started four games. While with the Cardinals, Johnson played in 32 games with 8 starts, had 164 carries for 715 yards, scored 3 touchdowns, converted 25 first downs, and averaged 4.4 yards per attempt.

title: Cooper Rush seems likely to start at QB for Falcons vs. Panthers in Week 2
summary: We’ll know for certain on Wednesday. But there was a change to the Falcons media availability schedule for this week that hit my inbox Tuesday morning, and the “starting QB” press conference scheduled for Wednesday now has Cooper Rush’s name in that slot. It’s not an announcement, it hasn’t been confirmed by the team — […]
full_text: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We’ll know for certain on Wednesday. But there was a change to the Falcons media availability schedule for this week that hit my inbox Tuesday morning, and the “starting QB” press conference scheduled for Wednesday now has Cooper Rush’s name in that slot. It’s not an announcement, it hasn’t been confirmed by the team — but it seems pretty obvious that’s the direction we’re heading. We should also get updates on Wednesday from Stefanski on Michael Penix’s status and Tua Tagovailoa’s back, as well as the back issues Rush seemed to still be dealing with during Sunday’s loss to the Steelers. Could the plan at starting quarterback change over the course of the week? The quarterback depth chart has been such a wild ride since the beginning of camp, so nothing would surprise me at this point. For those of you on the Jack Strand-wagon, I’m sure we’ll hear more from Stefanski Wednesday on how the rookie UDFA fits into the team’s plans, now and into the future. They seem high on him, but any UDFA out of a small program is going to need significant development. Strand is athletically gifted, and he’s also brilliant. His learning curve should be shorter as a result, but it still exists. As our fearless leader Dave Choate likes to say, it’s time to gird our loins and start preparing for whatever surprises the Atlanta Falcons quarterback depth chart has in store for us this week. Hopefully one of those surprises will be a divisional win over the Panthers on Sunday.

(Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Looking for some good news? Well, too bad. The Falcons lost Tyler Goodson, who was a productive runner and receiver this summer and was the team’s de facto third running back, to the Dallas Cowboys. Because Goodson was on the practice squad, Dallas was free to pluck him and did so to help out their thin running back corps. The Cowboys are signing RB Tyler Goodson off the #Falcons practice squad, per @AaronWilson_NFL . Risk you take with just 2 RBs on the active roster. — Miles Garrett (@MilesGarrettTV) September 15, 2026 The Falcons knew they were taking a chance with their roster construction, which saw them only keep Bijan and Brian Robinson Jr., but probably didn’t expect to lose their veteran insurance this quickly. The team will almost certainly be calling up Zacch Pickens or Zach Harrison off the practice squad to replace Da’Shawn Hand, who may be lost for the season , and will therefore be able to easily add a player. The problem is that the player they add is unlikely to be as well-rounded as Goodson, who did a nice job this summer and offers you plenty as a runner, receiver, and returner. Look for former Brown Jerome Ford, who overlapped with Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees in Cleveland, and special teamer/capable receiving back Travis Homer as potential free agent additions. I doubt the Falcons will go very long without adding to the room. We wish Goodson well, but it sure is a bummer to lose him.

title: Falcons vs. Panthers, Week 2: Kevin Stefanski declines to name starting QB Monday
summary: There’s a specific question on the mind of pretty much every Falcons fan: Who’s the starting quarterback for Week 2? Kevin Stefanski spoke to the media Monday afternoon (I was in a meeting and couldn’t join the Zoom call, but I caught part of it on NFL Network), and confirmed he will not have an […]
full_text: Aug 28, 2026; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Atlanta Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski gestures from the sideline during the first quarter of a pre season game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rich Storry-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There’s a specific question on the mind of pretty much every Falcons fan: Who’s the starting quarterback for Week 2? Kevin Stefanski spoke to the media Monday afternoon (I was in a meeting and couldn’t join the Zoom call, but I caught part of it on NFL Network), and confirmed he will not have an answer to that question today. “Today’s a big day for our football team,” Stefanski said about the opportunity to review what went wrong in Sunday’s loss to the Steelers, and to correct those things. “It was a lot of little things,” that went wrong for Atlanta on Sunday, and those little things add up to big things like the Week 1 loss. The turnover margin was the first element of Sunday’s game Stefanski mentioned. Rush threw two picks, including TJ Watt’s pick-six. Bijan Robinson also fumbled twice — though he recovered one, and Jahan Dotson recovered the other. The turnover differential wasn’t huge — just -1 — but Stefanski noted that teams that end up on the wrong side of that turnover margin do not tend to win those games. This will be a point of emphasis for the Falcons this week and beyond. The most important news that came out of Stefanski’s Monday presser is injury-related; chiefly that the team is not ready to name a starter for Week 2 vs. the NFC South rival Panthers. I expect that announcement will come Wednesday, because they need to decide who’s taking those first-team reps in practice. In addition to the injuries up and down the quarterback depth chart, Stefanski shared two other major injury updates. Right guard Chris Lindstrom is in the concussion protocol. Da’Shawn Hand suffered a torn quad and is expected to miss the remainder of the season. While I do expect a starting QB to be named Wednesday, Stefanski made no such promises. “I need to get through today,” before committing to a starter, Stefanski said. I will be in Flowery Branch on Wednesday reporting on the quarterback situation and all other Falcons-Panthers related information right here in The Falcoholic’s Feed.

title: Falcons – Steelers recap: New faces, an all-too-familiar result
summary: Atlanta was dealt a tough hand going against the Pittsburgh Steelers on the road with a limited Cooper Rush under center. They looked at their cards, arched an eyebrow, and proceeded to play that lousy hand…well, let’s say not as well as you’d like. Rush was as abjectly bad, as you’d expect for a guy […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Cooper Rush #13 of the Atlanta Falcons hands the ball off to Bijan Robinson #7 during the second quarter of a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Atlanta was dealt a tough hand going against the Pittsburgh Steelers on the road with a limited Cooper Rush under center. They looked at their cards, arched an eyebrow, and proceeded to play that lousy hand…well, let’s say not as well as you’d like. Rush was as abjectly bad , as you’d expect for a guy who has been a career backup who didn’t have a job until training camp and had extremely limited first team reps and reportedly dealt with back spasms on Saturday. The Falcons were unwilling to expose Jack Strand to Week 1 game action as they look to develop him and ran one of the most conservative gameplans you’ll ever see for Rush, who had one sharp screen pass leading to a touchdown and a nice intermediate throw to Jahan Dotson sprinkled in between a lot of misses, near misses, and a hideous interception followed later by a pick six. I don’t think the team could have or would have asked for much more from Rush aside from a couple of decisions back, and the limits on the quarterback put limits on this offense that were very obviously difficult to overcome. That wasn’t all, of course. The offense and defense were both undone by penalties, with two defensive pass interference calls on A.J. Terrell and five holding calls (three accepted) on Atlanta’s offensive linemen outside of Ryan Neuzil. Special teams were a mixed bag after a summer that looked encouraging, with Nick Folk missing a pair of kicks, Jake Bailey missing the landing zone on a kickoff, and another penalty hurting Atlanta. It was the kind of effort that earns you a loss against a misfit Steelers squad, and the fact that Pittsburgh could only muster a touchdown win over this version of the 2026 Falcons does not bode well for them. That was largely because the defense, a question mark again heading into this game, held Pittsburgh to 20 points and just 264 yards, with both of Pittsburgh’s touchdowns coming off Rush turnovers. I’m upset primarily because this game was winnable in the right set of circumstances, but with a little distance from the effort I can only be so down about it. Rush starting was the kind of circumstance the Falcons exposed themselves two by having their top two quarterbacks being guys who have extensive injury histories, but needing him out there as the starter in Week 1 is absurd and unlikely enough as to simply be unlucky. It’s not hard to imagine more competent quarterback play making a huge difference, even if Chris Lindstrom needs to miss a little time with his concussion, and at least daydream of a decent season ahead. If they can get Michael Penix Jr. out there in Week 2, the passing game goes from an active liability to something approaching a danger. For all that, the penalties, the uncertainty around quarterback, and this team’s clearly future-looking ethos combine to make you think 2026 may once again be a year where flashes of hope and spells of frustration mellow into mediocrity. Perhaps that’s a bit harsh after one week. Though the coaching staff and front office do not bear the sins of those that came before them, these are still the Atlanta Falcons, and the Atlanta Falcons have been struggling so mightily and for so long that it’s difficult not to assume the first sign of another tough year is the sign. This team still has the talent and ability to right the ship, but it goes without saying that they’ll need to do so quickly to earn the fanbase’s trust and stay competitive, even with the NFC South once again looking like a mud pit. I hope we can look back at this as the day the Falcons fell prey to an inevitable tough road matchup with their third-string quarterback, rather than the start of something miserable and mediocre. On to the full recap. The Good Bijan Robinson is, of course, one of the very best players in football. He turned an errant Cooper Rush pass into seven yards early in this one, another errant Rush pass into a positive gain, and then a Rush screen and a couple of nice blocks by Charlie Woerner and Chris Blair into a touchdown just in the first quarter. He would finish with 21 carries for 83 yards and 8 catches for 90 yards and a touchdown, accounting for about two-thirds of Atlanta’s yardage. The Falcons need to be less one-dimensional, but Bijan gives you a fighting chance every week even if he’s your only dimension. Brian Robinson Jr. also ran reasonably well and was effective as a kick returner, which was nice to see. He averaged 32 yards on kick returns and had a couple nice runs, though he average just 3.4 yards per carry, and looks like the complement the Falcons were hoping to get when they scooped him out of free agency. The mar on his day was hesitation on his initial kick return, but everybody gets a Week 1 freebie. Drake London didn’t get much work, but made the most of it, with a six yard gain on a jet sweep and two grabs for 29 yards. He will have better weeks when he gets more chances, but he looked like the same top-tier player he’s always been when we saw him. I thought Jahan Dotson made a great first impression, which might seem like an odd thing to say about a player with one catch for 19 yards. You have to remember that Rush overshot him badly on his first interception for what should’ve been a quality gain in traffic, and that Dotson was the heads-up player who recovered Bijan’s screen pass fumble. I thought he showed the kind of awareness and ability to get open that should make him a legitimate factor with more competent quarterback play. The blocks from Chris Blair and Charlie Woerner on Bijan’s touchdown catch were fantastic. It beggars belief that Blair couldn’t get on the field for last year’s decimated offense when he’s a sure-handed target who can do that . Aside from one missed interception that went just beyond his hands, Divine Deablo looked really good in this one with a credited forced fumble and seven tackles. The fact that rookie linebackers Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. also showed up and delivered some big plays gives you real hope for this inside linebacker group as they try to navigate life post-Kaden Elliss. Atlanta put a lot of effort into stacking up their defensive interior, and I will say it looked like it paid off. Brandon Dorlus was really good in this one, and if he missed a sack, he still came up with multiple big stops and was aggressive and effective rushing from the interior. Maason Smith’s leaping effort on the second Steelers drive ensured they had to settle for three points, and it was both an impressive display of athleticism and extremely well-timed tip. He also had a coverage sack on Aaron Rodgers in the first quarter that was erased by an A.J. Terrell holding call. I thought LaCale London looked really good in this one, with a couple of big run stops and a non-stop motor that allowed him to keep impacting the game throughout. He’s slowly climbed the ladder with the Falcons and is now one of their essential interior defenders. Za’Darius Smith rocks. After retiring and un-retiring, dealing with awful loss, and working himself back into game shape, Smith came up with two sacks in this one to key a Falcons pass rush that was inconsistent but got home just enough to impact this game. What an effort from a player the Falcons are going to have to count on. The NFC South went winless in Week 1, so the damage here was not as bad as it could’ve been. The Panthers putting up 30-plus points, the Saints almost beating the Lions, and the Buccaneers hanging in against the Bengals may impact how good this one feels to you, though. The Ugly Cooper Rush looked like a third-string quarterback who hadn’t had enough time with this team, this offense, and also just was having…
author: Dave Choate

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 1: Wide receiver shuffling amidst injuries
summary: The Baltimore Ravens were victorious in the season opener yesterday, defeating the Indianapolis Colts in a 41-23 win. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense. Offense Jackson and the starting offensive line played all 68 snaps. Backup offensive tackle Carson Vinson saw seven snaps as an extra blocker […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Moore #17 of the Baltimore Ravens carries the ball against Cam Bynum #0 of the Indianapolis Colts during the third quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens were victorious in the season opener yesterday, defeating the Indianapolis Colts in a 41-23 win. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense. Offense QB: Lamar Jackson 68 RB: Derrick Henry 37, Justice Hill 31 WR: Rashod Bateman 53, Ja’Kobi Lane 27, Chris Moore 20, LaJohntay Wester 20, Zay Flowers 20 TE: Mark Andrews 49, Durham Smythe 42, Matthew Hibner 23, Josh Cuevas 6 OL: Ronnie Stanley 68, John Simpson 68, Jovaughn Gwyn 68, Vega Ioane 68, Roger Rosengarten 68, Carson Vinson 7 Jackson and the starting offensive line played all 68 snaps. Backup offensive tackle Carson Vinson saw seven snaps as an extra blocker in jumbo formations. In the backfield, Derrick Henry played just over half of the team’s offensive snaps and rushed for 144 yards with three touchdowns on 20 attempts. Justice Hill played 31 snaps and received seven touches in total. The snap counts at wide receiver are the biggest notable story. With Devontez Walker inactive due to an ankle injury, the Ravens suffered two more injuries at the position. Zay Flowers played 20 snaps in the first half before exiting with a hamstring injury, totaling 150 yards and a touchdown on five catches. Likewise, Ja’Kobi Lane was sidelined for the rest of the game after he too left early with a wrist ailment following 27 snaps. Lane’s first NFL touchdown catch was called back due to a penalty. With both players sidelined, Chris Moore and LaJohntay Wester took on elevated roles, each playing 20 offensive snaps. Moore had a long 53-yard catch and Wester caught two passes, in addition to both players’ duties as primary returners on special teams. Rashod Bateman started the game and played all but one snap, however he was targeted only once with no catches. Mark Andrews unsurprisingly led the tight end room with 49 snaps, catching four passes on six targets. Veteran Durham Smythe played 42 snaps as a primary blocker. Matthew Hibner is clearly third in the pecking order ahead of Josh Cuevas, out-snapping his fellow rookie 23 to six. Hibner caught one pass for 13 yards. Defense DL: Travis Jones 31, Calais Campbell 29, Broderick Washington 21, John Jenkins 13, Aeneas Peebles 10 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 44, Trey Hendrickson 40, Mike Green 17, Zion Young 12 ILB: Roquan Smith 54, Trenton Simpson 32 CB: Nate Wiggins 54, Marlon Humphrey 48, Keyon Martin 23, Chidobe Awuzie 6 S: Kyle Hamilton 54, Malaki Starks 54, Jaylinn Hawkins 52 All five of the Ravens’ defensive lineman saw 10+ snaps in this game as Nnami Madubuike’s return to action awaits. Travis Jones led the way with 31 snaps, closely followed by fellow veterans Calais Campbell (29) and Broderick Washington (21). John Jenkins and Aeneas Peebles combined to play 23 snaps. Tavius Robinson (44) and Trey Hendrickson (40) had a commanding snap share on the edge. Robinson had four quarterback hits and a sack, while Hendrickson was charted for eight pressures. Mike Green only played 17 snaps as the third banana, while rookie Zion Young’s debut saw him on the field for 12 defensive plays. Roquan Smith played every defensive snap and had a starring performance with an interception and team-high 11 tackles. Next to him, Trenton Simpson played 32 snaps and drew the start in the absence of Teddye Buchanan once again. Nate Wiggins did not leave the field and had a pass breakup in his 54 snaps. Marlon Humphrey’s 48 snaps were productive, as the veteran forced a fumble and had a key pass knockdown on a deep attempt in single coverage. Nickel corner Keyon Martin’s 23 snaps were third-most at the position. Surprisingly, Chidobe Awuzie only played six defensive snaps. T.J. Tampa suffered a knee injury and did not return to the game. The Ravens’ trio of safeties were on the field together for all but two plays where Jaylinn Hawkins was relieved. Hamilton and Starks each played 54 snaps. Hawkins occupying a near every-down role likely explains the lack of significant snaps for Martin and Awuzie at cornerback.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens vs. Colts: 9 Winners and 3 Losers
summary: The Baltimore Ravens opened the season on the road with a convincing 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The first game under new head coach Jesse Minter was a resounding success, but a few blemishes were apparent. Winners Lamar Jackson: The two-time MVP looked as sharp as ever against the Colts, completing 17-of-25 passes for […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Moore #17 of the Baltimore Ravens returns the ball against the Indianapolis Colts during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens opened the season on the road with a convincing 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The first game under new head coach Jesse Minter was a resounding success, but a few blemishes were apparent. Winners Lamar Jackson : The two-time MVP looked as sharp as ever against the Colts, completing 17-of-25 passes for 324 yards and a touchdown while adding another 40 yards and a score on the ground on seven rushes. After an injury-riddled season in 2025, Jackson reminded everyone what he is capable of with a Houdini-esque escape from a sack to convert a 3rd-and-16 with his legs. Zay Flowers : The Ravens’ No. 1 wide receiver showed why he deserved the $140 million extension he received this offseason with a monster first half against Indianapolis. The Colts had zero answers for Flowers as the shifty receiver racked up 150 yards and a touchdown on just five catches before unfortunately exiting the game with a hamstring injury. Flowers’ speed popped off the screen on his 54-yard catch-and-run touchdown. Derrick Henry : They say Father Time is undefeated, but it looks like he will have to wait at least another year to win his bout against Henry. The 32-year-old workhorse moved up to third in all-time rushing touchdowns with his three scores against Indianapolis to go with 144 rushing yards. A healthy Jackson and Henry in the backfield is nearly impossible to stop. Chris Moore : The 33-year-old special teams standout stepped up in a big way in his first game back with his original team, both as a returner and receiver. After Baltimore’s defense was walked down the field for a touchdown on the opening drive of the game, Moore responded with a 42-yard kick return to set the Ravens’ offense up at midfield. Moore later broke off a 49-yard return in the third quarter that was called back by a penalty. The biggest play of the day for the veteran came on offense, though, when Moore hauled in a 53-yard pass on third down. With rookie Ja’Kobi Lane set to miss time with a wrist injury and Flowers’ availability for the upcoming weeks unknown, Moore could find himself with more opportunities on offense. Tavius Robinson : Robinson started his contract year off with a strong game against the Colts. Robinson had one of the team’s two sacks on Daniel Jones and was a consistent force from the edge throughout the day with a team-high four quarterback hits. Roquan Smith : The All-Pro linebacker is looking to rebound from a down season in 2025, and Sunday was a good start towards doing so. After a poor first drive from Baltimore’s defense, which led to a touchdown, Smith quickly flipped the momentum on the next drive with an interception off of Jones. Smith led the team with 11 total tackles. Marlon Humphrey : Another player looking to bounce back after a poor season is the former All-Pro cornerback. Humphrey reminded everyone of his playmaking ability with a forced fumble on running back Jonathan Taylor and had an impressive pass breakup on a deep pass intended for Alec Pierce later in the game. The Ravens need their highly paid corner to continue to play at a high level. Tyler Loop : Perhaps the biggest concern for the Ravens entering the season was their kicking situation after a shaky preseason from Loop on the heels of his season-ending miss in Pittsburgh. While it would have been impossible to win back all of the goodwill in just one game, Loop certainly eased concern by making both of his kicks on Sunday, including a career-long 57-yarder. Declan Doyle : The praise for the first-time play-caller was sky high this offseason, and he showed exactly why in his first game. Doyle’s creativity was on full display against Indianapolis, particularly on Flowers’ 54-yard touchdown, where he started lined up next to Jackson in the backfield before running a route. Putting Jackson under center more and using play-action were both effective as well in Week 1. Baltimore may not have Doyle for long if he continues on this trajectory, so fans should enjoy the show while it lasts. Losers Offensive Line : While the offensive line’s performance was not terrible, it was the constant barrage of penalties that really held the unit back in their first outing together. Constant holding penalties and false starts killed momentum for an otherwise unstoppable Ravens’ offense. The unit combined for five penalties, two against left tackle Ronnie Stanley, one on center Jovaugn Gwyn, and two against rookie first-round guard Vega Ioane. The holding penalty against Gwyn nullified a touchdown catch for Lane, leading to a turnover on downs a few plays later instead. Penalties were to be expected in the first game of the season on the road, but Baltimore must fix the issue quickly if their offense is going to reach its true potential. Rashod Bateman : Much talk has been made this offseason about the potential for Bateman to bounce back in a new offensive system, but that was not the story on Sunday. Bateman finished the game with zero catches after his lone reception was called back due to a penalty. Following Flowers’ exit from the game, Bateman should have been the player to step up in the passing game instead of Moore. The Ravens need more from their former first-round pick if Flowers misses any games with his hamstring injury. Justice Hill : Hill did not have his best outing in Week 1, as the veteran running back had back-to-back penalties to kill a drive late in the third quarter. Hill had little success on the ground either, totaling just 18 yards on six carries, though he did add another ten yards on a catch.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 1: Encouraging start to the season as Ravens dominate all three phases
summary: The Baltimore Ravens began the 2026 season with a bang in Week 1, scoring 41 points en route to a 21-point victory over the Indianapolis Colts. While it was not a flawless performance, the Ravens never trailed after the first few minutes of the game and quickly opened up a three-possession lead, which they never […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens began the 2026 season with a bang in Week 1, scoring 41 points en route to a 21-point victory over the Indianapolis Colts. While it was not a flawless performance, the Ravens never trailed after the first few minutes of the game and quickly opened up a three-possession lead, which they never relinquished. Let’s break down how every position group fared in this week’s report card. Quarterback: A- Lamar Jackson had a strong performance to begin the season, completing 17-of-25 passes for 324 yards and a touchdown — with another 40 rushing yards and a score on the ground. Jackson connected with Zay Flowers for multiple chunk plays through the air and delivered another long 50+ yard pass in the third quarter. Jackson looked to be command of Declan Doyle’s offense and he’s clearly no longer compromised by injuries athletically. The lone blemish of Jackson’s day was a lost fumble where he was strip sacked in the Ravens’ own territory, which led to a Colts’ touchdown. Jackson was sacked almost immediately after turning around in play action, though, and fortunately the Ravens were up by three scores at the time, so it wasn’t a damaging sequence. Running Back: A It was just another day at the office for Derrick Henry in Week 1, who rushed for 144 yards on 24 carries with three touchdowns. Henry also added 19 receiving yards on a good catch-and-run reception. Henry’s longest run on the day went for 32 yards, and he grinded out chunk gains as the game progressed to help keep the Ravens’ offense on the field and put the game away. Justice Hill had 28 scrimmage yards on seven touches behind him, picking up a nice first-down gain through the air. Wide Receiver: A- Before exiting with a hamstring injury before halftime, Flowers had already set a new career-high in receiving yards with 150 on five catches. He had a long 54-yard touchdown catch and fell just a few yards short of scoring on the second drive of the game. Flowers was uncoverable and had he left the game early, there’s no telling what his final stat line may have been. His performance alone in just two quarters of action is enough to boost this position group’s grade. Chris Moore, who was a practice squad elevation, made an impact with a 54-yard reception in the third quarter. LaJohntay Wester had two catches, and Ja’Kobi Lane had one 11-yard catch before leaving the game early as well with a wrist injury. Lane would have had his first career touchdown reception, but it was called back due to a holding penalty. Surprisingly, Rashod Bateman was held to zero catches on just one target. Tight End: B – Mark Andrews’ first target resulted in a dropped pass, and he was also flagged for a false start in the red zone early in the game. That was a discouraging start, but he wound up reeling in four receptions for 49 yards overall. His six targets were tied with Flowers for most on the team. Matthew Hibner turned a short out-route pass into a 13-yard gain to help push the Ravens deeper into the red zone, setting up a score. Hibner wasn’t targeted again in the game, and rookie Josh Cuevas was not a factor in the passing game. Veteran Durham Smythe caught one pass for a short four-yard gain outside of the end zone. The Ravens’ tight ends as a whole seemed to do a good job of pass blocking and holding the edges in run blocking situations. Offensive Line: C – It was not the most encouraging start to the season for the Ravens’ new-look offensive line. While they did a good job in run blocking, the penalties from this group were rough and pass protection was spotty. Of the Ravens’ 10 penalties overall as a team, most of them were offensive line pre-snap calls, holding violations and in one instance a chop-blocking flag. It seemed like the Ravens were flagged for offensive line penalties on almost every drive and many times it negated a first-down gain or score. There were some instances where the Colts generated quick pressure up the middle, too, and they did get home on Jackson to force a fumble in the second quarter. Defensive Line: C+ Travis Jones was a force up front in this game with two notable tackles for loss, one of which he drove Taylor back several yards behind the line of scrimmage. Taylor was able to find running room against the Ravens’ defensive front a number of times, though, and the Ravens allowed 102 rushing yards overall and 5.2 yards per carry. Some of this can be attributed to the Ravens’ defensive scheme geared towards prioritizing pass rush and eliminating downfield passing plays. The Ravens used a lot of light personnel while they held a large lead for much of the game, essentially daring the Colts to run the ball. Broderick Washington had a nice pass breakup early in the game that was close to being an interception, and Aaenas Peebles had a quarterback hit as well. Edge Rusher: B Trey Hendrickson’s debut did not result in any splash plays, but he was close to getting home for a sack or possible forced fumble multiple times. Hendrickson had a handful of pressures on Jones and his presence may have helped opened things up a bit for Tavius Robinson, who had a big showing on the opposite side of the defensive front. Robinson racked up four quarterback hits with a sack and tackle for loss. In a contract year, this could be the start of a career-best season for the fourth-year edge rusher. Mike Green and Zion Young did not find their way onto the box score in this game. Linebacker: B+ Roquan Smith’s interception on the Colts’ second drive of the game was a thing of beauty, as he deceived Daniel Jones and tapped the ball to himself in the air before securing it. The Ravens added another touchdown a few plays later to open up an eight-point lead. Smith led the team in tackles with 11 and also had a quarterback hit. Next to him, Trenton Simpson had two tackles-for-loss, which was tied for the most of any defender. Cornerback: A- Marlon Humphrey had a starring performance with a forced fumble on Jonathan Taylor and third-down knockdown in coverage against Alec Pierce. Humphrey looked much more like his prime self than he did last season, which is an encouraging sign for this season. Nate Wiggins also an impressive pass breakup lined up against Pierce. Keyon Martin made a strong tackle in space against a much larger wide receiver. Overall, the Ravens’ corners did a good job limiting big plays in the passing game and were aggressive in coverage. Safety: B+ Following the defense’s first drive of the game, Kyle Hamilton began being used more as an extra pass rusher and his presence around the line of scrimmage made a noticeable impact. Hamilton finished with five tackles and a quarterback hit. Malaki Starks was victimized a few times against Taylor via a stiff arm and juke move, but also filled the stat sheet with seven tackles, a sack, two quarterback hits and one tackle for loss. Jaylinn Hawkins didn’t make any noticeable impact plays, but he appeared around the ball a few times on some positive defensive plays. The Ravens’ three safeties didn’t seem to leave the field very much at all. Special Teams: A Tyler Loop answered the bell in a big way, nailing a career-high 57-yard field goal attempt to close out the first half. That expanded the Ravens lead to three possessions, and he made a 45-yarder later in the second half, while also going perfect on all five extra points. Rookie punter Ryan Eckley’s three punts went for 140 yards, and Chris Moore had a couple long kick returns to set the Ravens up in good field position offensively. LaJohntay Wester also had a long 30-yard return on a kickoff as well and averaged 10.0 yards per punt return on three tries.
author: Frank Platko

title: Josh Allen earns my Week 1 game ball after leading Bills past Texans
summary: Josh Allen accounted for four touchdowns and delivered when the Bills needed him most The Buffalo Bills did not make their first win of the 2026 season easy. Buffalo’s defense struggled to contain the Houston Texans’ passing attack, the secondary appeared to have a target painted on it for much of the afternoon. Yet, when […]
full_text: Josh Allen accounted for four touchdowns and delivered when the Bills needed him most The Buffalo Bills did not make their first win of the 2026 season easy. Buffalo’s defense struggled to contain the Houston Texans’ passing attack, the secondary appeared to have a target painted on it for much of the afternoon. Yet, when the Bills needed someone to take control, Josh Allen once again reminded everyone why the ball belongs in his hands. Allen led Buffalo to a thrilling 36-31 victory, earning my first game ball of the season. Game ball: Josh Allen Allen completed 20-of-29 passes for 334 yards and two touchdowns while adding 23 rushing yards and two more scores. His 357 total yards and four touchdowns were impressive enough, but the situation in which he delivered made the performance even more meaningful. Houston took a 31-30 lead late in the fourth quarter, leaving Buffalo 96 yards away from the end zone with the game hanging in the balance. Allen responded by marching the Bills down the field and connecting with Joshua Palmer for a 34-yard touchdown with 1:36 remaining. It was the decisive score in a game featuring four fourth-quarter lead changes. That drive felt like vintage Allen. He was aggressive, confident and completely unfazed by the circumstances. Even after a potential interception slipped through the hands of Texans cornerback Kamari Lassiter, Allen came right back on the next play and attacked the same part of the field for the go-ahead touchdown. Opening week can produce some uneven football, particularly with a new head coach and several new pieces on offense. Allen provided the stability. Every time Houston appeared ready to take control, he gave Buffalo an answer. It was also Allen’s first win in Houston after entering the afternoon 0-4 there. More importantly, it gave Joe Brady a victory in his regular-season debut as Buffalo’s head coach. There were several deserving candidates, but Allen’s command of the offense and his work on the final drive made him the clear choice for Week 1. Honorable mention: Dalton Kincaid A healthy Dalton Kincaid looked ready to become one of the most dangerous pieces of Buffalo’s offense. Kincaid caught five of his six targets for 130 yards, averaging an incredible 26 yards per reception. His afternoon included gains of 35 and 40 yards as Allen repeatedly found him attacking Houston’s defense downfield. Kincaid in 2026, fantasy managers and Bills fans should both be paying attention. Honorable mention: DJ Moore DJ Moore’s first regular-season game in a Bills uniform provided exactly the type of performance Buffalo hoped it was adding to the offense. Moore caught five passes for 100 yards and a touchdown, giving Buffalo two 100-yard receivers in the same game. He showed an immediate connection with Allen and provided the offense with another dependable playmaker capable of creating yards after the catch. Buffalo spent much of the offseason talking about how Moore could expand the passing attack. It took only one game for him to demonstrate why. Honorable mention: Tyler Bass Tyler Bass quietly supplied 12 crucial points in a five-point victory. Bass was perfect against Houston, connecting on all three of his field-goal attempts and all three extra points. His kicks included a 46-yard field goal following Buffalo’s takeaway on Houston’s opening possession and a 33-yarder that tied the game at 20. After everything surrounding Buffalo’s kicking situation over the past year, a perfect opening performance deserves recognition. The defense delivered when it mattered Buffalo’s defense will have plenty to correct before Thursday night. Houston found favorable matchups against the secondary throughout the game, and C.J. Stroud threw for 274 yards and two touchdowns. Terrel Bernard finished with 12 total tackles, while Deone Walker and Greg Rousseau each recorded two tackles for loss. The run defense also settled down and performed better in the second half. For all the problems, the defense produced the game’s final answer. Rousseau recorded his second strip-sack of Stroud on Houston’s last possession, and Bernard recovered the fumble to secure the victory. The same combination had helped create Buffalo’s first points when Rousseau forced a fumble on Houston’s opening drive and Ed Oliver recovered it. It was far from a complete defensive performance, but the Bills made the decisive play when they absolutely needed one. A game ball that meant more The most meaningful moment may have happened after the clock reached zero. Inside the locker room, Allen presented Brady with the game ball from his first regular-season victory as an NFL head coach. Brady accepted it, but immediately redirected the recognition. “Only one person deserves this more than anyone else, and that’s Ed Oliver,” Brady told the team. Oliver has endured unimaginable personal loss during the offseason, making Brady’s gesture much larger than football. It was a heartfelt reminder of how closely this team has rallied around him. Allen earned my Week 1 game ball for carrying Buffalo to the finish line. Inside the Bills’ locker room, however, the most important game ball went exactly where it belonged. Buffalo is 1-0, Allen finally has his victory in Houston, and Brady has his first win as a head coach. Now the Bills have a short turnaround to prepare for the Detroit Lions and the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium.
author: Sara Larson

title: Josh Allen is not a reckless, YOLO, turnover-prone quarterback
summary: I’ll admit, it feels bizarre to be compelled to write this about Josh Allen in Year 9, especially after a 36-point eruption against that Houston Texans defense in the Buffalo Bills’ Week 1 win. Allen is not an overly reckless, YOLO, sugar-high quarterback bound to put the ball in precarious situations in critical moments of […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills runs off the field after 36-31 win against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ll admit, it feels bizarre to be compelled to write this about Josh Allen in Year 9, especially after a 36-point eruption against that Houston Texans defense in the Buffalo Bills’ Week 1 win. Allen is not an overly reckless, YOLO, sugar-high quarterback bound to put the ball in precarious situations in critical moments of every game. But is he ultra conservative? Ab-so-lutely not. I’m letting recency bias get the best of me here, because on Sunday, Allen certainly did make a poor throw the play before he ripped one of the best throws of his career to date to Josh Palmer on the eventual game-winning touchdown. And for as much praise as he’s rightfully received for the 34-yard touchdown — which was a 45 air-yard strike without room to step into the throw — the specific criticism for the jump ball the play before was out of control. Allen saw single coverage on Palmer with a chance for a go-ahead touchdown. The decision wasn’t brutal. The pass was simply underthrown and too far to the inside. Allen would undoubtedly admit that himself. The bad throw deserved to be shown. Without question. But to suggest “this is what you get from Allen every week,” is flat-out incorrect. My gameday column before Week 1 focused on first impressions, and how powerful they can be. And even after an MVP and an incredibly long stay in the NFL’s elite realm of quarterbacks, Allen still can’t shake the first impressions he made in this league. As a rookie, Allen’s 5.1% turnover-worthy play rate (a self-explanatory advanced metric) was the third-highest out of 39 qualifiers. Bad. And the first impression was made. The next season, when he did show clear signs of improvement, Allen’s 4.3% TWP rate was the ninth-highest out of 39 qualifying quarterbacks. That sophomore NFL season cemented the first impression in the minds of many. Heck, I remember going on radio shows after Buffalo’s Week 1 loss to the Jets to begin the 2023 season — in which Allen threw three interceptions and had a fumble — and having to ward off suggestions that he might be Jameis Winston. Check the following chart, and tell me if it reads like a super-careless quarterback. *lower rank is better Josh Allen Turnover-Worthy Play Rate (rank) 4th Q / OT Turnover-Worthy Throw Rate 2025 2.4% (7th / 43) 2.2% (8th) 2024 2.6% (15th / 44) 1.1% (4th) 2023 3.0% (20th / 41) 3.3% (12th) 2022 4.0% (31st / 41) 6.7% (30th) 2021 3.2% (19th / 38) 2.2% (2nd) 2020 3.4% (23rd / 38) Data unavailable Allen was the YOLO, sugar-high quarterback in his first two seasons. Since then, hardly. And he’s gradually improved how well he protects the football in each of the last four seasons. Four seasons is an eternity in the NFL! But it’s like many haven’t caught on to said vital advancement in Allen’s game. Maybe it’s because of the 18-interception 2023 campaign? Probably. Allen threw the second-most picks that year, but as you can see above, his Turnover-Worthy Play Rate ranked smack dab in the middle of all quarterbacks. Despite this clearly being a persuasive piece, it’s alright with me if you want to ignore the numbers because of your inherent faith in the old-fashion eyeball test. Because even if in your mind Allen is still a reckless, YOLO, sugar-high quarterback who puts the ball in danger every game in key moments, it is precisely what makes him such a daunting matchup for any defense. And, sure, you’ve heard about that dynamic before, but it’s probably not explored deeply enough. Here are Allen’s Big-Time Throw Rates — a metric that counts the most challenging, high-degree of difficulty throws, typically further downfield / through tight windows — and rank among quarterbacks with 200+ attempts since the beginning of 2020. Josh Allen Big-Time Throw Rate (rank) 2025 5.1% (9th) 2024 7.0% (1st) 2023 6.2% (2rd) 2022 7.6% (1st) 2021 5.9% (6th) 2020 6.1% (8th) Ridiculous, right? As you can probably imagine, Allen is the only quarterback in the NFL to finish in the Top 10 of that metric in each of the last six seasons. And it speaks directly to Allen squeezing everything humanly possible out of his offensive scheme and skill-position talent. He’s often had to make those challenging throws because the easy, wide-open tosses haven’t been available to him as frequently as the other top quarterbacks in football. Allen operating as the most full-throttle, all-gas, no-brakes quarterback in the NFL is the best possible scenario for the Bills offense and the worst possible scenario for each defense it faces. Allen’s bad plays may — see: probably — look different than other quarterbacks. Does that really matter? All interceptions and turnovers count the same. In golf, if you hit the ball one foot out of bounds or 20 yards out of bounds, you’re still taking the same penalty. I get it though — the ball that sails way right has more of a visceral impact on our brains. It’s a cognitive bias we naturally suffer from. The distinction between the psychological influence and real-life result of those occurrences needs to be acknowledged. And with any quarterback, I’d much rather chances being taken at a ferocious clip than essentially never looking for the big play, routinely erring on the side of caution. The timid, risk-averse quarterbacks are available in the undrafted ranks every April. And, heck, there are many passers who have the desire to play aggressively but lack the physical talent to match. Without being in defensive game plan meetings, I’m going to venture a guess that Allen’s willingness and ability to make big-time throws stresses a defense significantly more than his occasional tendency to give the ball away. There’s just no way a defensive coordinator fires up the film before playing the Bills and is giddy about his unit’s chances to force an Allen turnover. He’s almost assuredly far more unsettled about what Allen is capable of doing to his defense with his arm… and that’s before you factor in any of the quarterback’s legendary running talent. How do I stick the landing on this column? Maybe just with my take that Allen is absolutely not a reckless quarterback. In fact, he’s long been a player who understands, is comfortable with, and confident in his seismic talent, which has made him the best player in the NFL, in my opinion .

title: Buffalo Rumblings Tailgate Series: You haven’t really tailgated in Buffalo until you’ve found the Red Pinto
summary: There are tailgates you attend, and then there are tailgates you experience. If the first stop in our Buffalo Rumblings Tailgate Series, the Bills VIP Tailgate, represented the new, polished, all-inclusive side of game day in Orchard Park, our second stop takes us in almost the complete opposite direction. No admission ticket. No premium food […]
full_text: BUFFALO, N.Y. - OCTOBER 22 : Tailgating food cooked in inventive ways on the hood of a red pinto at the Hammer's Lot at the Pinto Ron tailgate party before the Buffalo Bills faced the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Orchard Park, N.Y. Ken Johnson, better known as "Pinto Ron", (born 1958) is a Buffalo Bills fan known for attending every single Bills home and away game and hosting a tailgate party since 1994. He is known for his red Ford Pinto and antics cooking food on his car hood in a variety of objects such as a shovel and army helmet; furthermore, he holds a tradition of being doused in ketchup and mustard. Most notably he served shots out of a bowling ball until he was forced to shut down by the National Football League (NFL) Johnson moved his tailgate party to private property next to the stadium where the NFL has no jurisdiction and was able to resume serving bowling ball shots. He has been featured in multiple NFL Films, as well as the made-for-TV movie Second String. (Photo by Marc Piscotty/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There are tailgates you attend, and then there are tailgates you experience. If the first stop in our Buffalo Rumblings Tailgate Series, the Bills VIP Tailgate, represented the new, polished, all-inclusive side of game day in Orchard Park, our second stop takes us in almost the complete opposite direction. No admission ticket. No premium food stations. No open bar. Instead, there’s a red Ford Pinto, pizza cooked in ways that probably weren’t envisioned by the filing cabinet industry, shots from a bowling ball and, eventually, a grown man getting absolutely drenched in ketchup and mustard. Welcome to the Red Pinto Tailgate at Hammer’s Lot And if you’ve been around Bills Mafia for any length of time, there’s a pretty good chance you’ve already seen it, even if you’ve never been there. Bills fans travel to Buffalo from across the country and around the world, and not everyone can pack a grill, tent, coolers and half their garage for the trip. That’s one of the reasons I’m spending this season highlighting the different tailgate experiences available around Highmark Stadium. Some are ticketed and all-inclusive. Some ask for donations. Some require nothing more than showing up and introducing yourself. We’ll cover where they are, what they cost, what you need to bring and, most importantly, what you can expect when you get there. I’ve now attended 102 consecutive Bills games, home and away, and one thing I’ve learned along the way is that you don’t have to arrive in Buffalo knowing everyone. When you’re among Bills Mafia, you’re rarely on your own for long. And few places demonstrate that better than Hammer’s Lot. The Red Pinto has a new view The Red Pinto Tailgate has been part of Bills game day for decades, but the opening of the new Highmark Stadium gives this longtime tradition a brand-new backdrop. Hammer’s Lot sits at 4170 Abbott Road, roughly a couple minute walk from the stadium. For the Bills’ home opener against the Detroit Lions on September 17, Hammer’s Lot officially opens at noon. Parking is $80 per vehicle, first come, first served. There are no parking reservations, so if Hammer’s Lot is part of your game-day plan, arriving early is probably a wise decision. You don’t have to park there to join the party This is an important distinction for traveling fans. The $80 is the cost to park in Hammer’s Lot, not admission to the Red Pinto Tailgate. The tailgate itself isn’t a ticketed event. So if you’re staying nearby, parking somewhere else or simply want to make the Red Pinto one of your pregame stops, you can walk over and experience it. That’s part of what makes this one so appealing for visitors. You don’t need to purchase an all-inclusive package to see one of Buffalo’s most recognizable game-day traditions. Just follow the crowd. Who exactly is Pinto Ron? You probably know him as Pinto Ron, a nickname founded on a mistake. Over the years the iconic “Pinto Ron” essentially grew out of a media mistake from decades ago. Rather than fight it, he embraced it, and the accidental nickname became inseparable from one of the most recognizable tailgates in professional football. He and his red Ford Pinto have been fixtures of Bills tailgating for decades. The traditions surrounding the car eventually became almost as famous as the man himself: unconventional cooking methods, bowling-ball shots and, of course, the ketchup-and-mustard ceremony. The Red Pinto Tailgate has been operating in some form since the 1990s and has attracted national media attention along the way. And that is exactly what you will see on Thursday night as Amazon Prime will be filming the ketchup and mustard ceremony live during their pregame show. Then there’s Pizza Pete At some point, someone apparently looked at a filing cabinet and asked whether you could cook in it. The answer, naturally, was yes. That experiment evolved into one of the Red Pinto Tailgate’s signature attractions, with Pizza Pete Papagelis turning a filing cabinet into a pizza oven. Over the years, the crew’s cooking equipment has included everything from shovels and watering cans to wheelbarrows and car parts. At most tailgates, you ask what’s on the menu. Here, you may want to ask what it’s being cooked in . Expect food coming off the Red Pinto, Pizza Pete’s creations and plenty of other food being passed around throughout the lot. This isn’t an all-you-can-eat package, though. There’s no guaranteed menu attached to admission because there is no admission. If you’re visiting, I’d still recommend bringing your own drinks and whatever food you need. Anything offered along the way is part of the experience. Yes, you can take a shot from a bowling ball Among the Red Pinto’s many traditions is one that requires a little explaining to anyone unfamiliar with Bills Mafia. The bowling ball. The tradition involves pouring a shot into the finger hole of a bowling ball and drinking it from there. Then dropping the ball on the ground and blowing as hard as you can into a horn. Is it elegant? Absolutely not. Will your friends understand the picture when you send it to them? Probably not. But you will have officially checked off one of the stranger items on the Bills Mafia bucket list! And then come the condiments If there’s one Red Pinto tradition almost everyone recognizes, it’s the ketchup and mustard ceremony. Before kickoff, Pinto Ron takes his position while ketchup and mustard rains down from above. That’s it. That’s the tradition. Trying to explain why doesn’t particularly improve the situation but it continues to draw huge crowds every home game. An old stadium “tradition” getting a different second act And because this is Pinto Ron, we’re talking about apparently preserving a piece of the old stadium couldn’t possibly involve something normal. There’s one more surprise, waiting at Hammer’s lot this season a certain very recognizable piece of the old Highmark Stadium has been rescued and repurposed into what may become the Red Pinto’s tailgate newest game day staple. Let me stop there. Pinto Ron plans to unveil the newest addition to the tailgate and I’m not spoiling this one. You’ll just have to come see it for yourself. There’s much more happening in Hammer’s Lot Pinto Ron might be the headliner, and the Red Pinto and Pizza Pete being an all star opening act, but it’s hardly the only reason to wander around. For the Lions game, Hammer’s Lot is expected to feature The Tubgaters, one of Eric Jones’ sand sculptures, Bank on Buffalo giveaways, Bud Light giveaways and an appearance from a former Bills player. The result is less like an organized event and more like a very large, slightly eccentric family reunion where several thousand additional relatives keep showing up. And that’s really the point. Hammer’s Lot offers a much better representation of what Buffalo tailgating actually feels like. Regulars return to the same places. People recognize each…

We “have a pulse, but you’re still trying to get a feel of how to use guys offensively, defensively, special teams, and to see the guys be able to make the adjustments; to see the guys be able to look through it all, be able to kind of play all the way through inside the red zone and figuring out, that’s what I was proud of,” Brady said . title: Coverage diversity something to watch under Buffalo Bills new DC Jim Leonhard
summary: First off, sample size caveat. I love week one of the NFL season. The vibes, the food, the weather…we talked about the things I love last week in my article. But I also kind of hate week one. Obviously, the phrase “week one is a liar” exists for a reason. We see weird and fluky […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Tight end Dalton Schultz #86 of the Houston Texans runs with the ball as safety Cole Bishop #24 of the Buffalo Bills readies for a tackle during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images First off, sample size caveat. I love week one of the NFL season. The vibes, the food, the weather… we talked about the things I love last week in my article. But I also kind of hate week one. Obviously, the phrase “week one is a liar” exists for a reason. We see weird and fluky phenomena during the first regular season game of a season every year. We look back at week one when the playoffs come around and frequently see results and play that make us wonder if we’re even in the same season. And if we’re trying to be intellectually honest (and we are), it makes it a necessity that every week one reaction conversation is absolutely dripping in a heavy pour of “but remember, it’s only week one”. With that statement as a precursor, one of the most interesting conversation points from the 2026 offseason surrounded what the Buffalo Bills’ defensive scheme would look like under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. After getting very used to a similar year-over-year look from previous head coach Sean McDermott (almost regardless of the person who held the “defensive coordinator” title), Buffalo was in for a change up under Leonhard, who came to the Bills most recently as the assistant head coach/defensive passing game coordinator for the Denver Broncos. But what would that change up look like? Through the first week, the main highlight from watching the game on broadcast and again on the all-22 was that there was a diversity in coverages being played on the back end on the Bills defense that showed a difference when compared to the coverage splits in 2025. That was reinforced by the coverage metrics from Fantasy Points Data Suite. Bills were charted as having 42 drop backs against them. Snap in Cover 0 = 0 (0%) Cover 1 – 3 (7.14%) Cover 2 – 5 (11.90%) 2 Man – 4 (9.52%) Cover 3 – 13 (30.95%) Cover 4 – 8 (19.05%) Cover 6 – 9 (21.43%) To put those numbers into perspective, here are the 2025 regular season coverage split percentages: Cover 0 = 2.83% Cover 1 – 15.33% Cover 2 – 16.22% 2 Man – 6.22% Cover 3 – 26.60% Cover 4 – 15.09% Cover 6 – 12.26% The spike in Cover 6 usage the first week of 2026 when compared to 2025 is the most interesting change here in coverage diversity splits (as a reminder, Cover 6 is half-field Cover 4 and half-field Cover 2, with the dividing line being the center line of the defense running end zone to end zone). What this means is that on a whopping 52.38% of all the Buffalo Bills’ defensive snaps against the Houston Texans in week one, the Bills appeared to have three defenders in deep coverages (two safeties and a corner in Cover 6, two corners and a safety in Cover 3). Why is this notable? The main point of pain for the Bills passing defense (when they didn’t miscommunicate and blow a coverage) was when dealing with in-breaking routes. Cover 3 and Cover 6 can both be had through in-breaker route combos like Cab (dig and drag from the same side of the field, see image below) or Shallow Cross (dig and drag from opposite sides of the field). Against dig and drag routes versus Houston, the Bills gave up 8 completions on 10 attempts for 111 yards, (11.1 yards per attempt, 112.9 passer rating against). As I mentioned above, it’s one game. I know nothing about how it will look moving forward. Is this just the way that Leonhard prefers his coverage splits or was this a Texans-only plan that leans towards Cover 2 against a Jared Goff-led Lions passing attack? As with all things after week one, it’s simply an interesting data point until we see more. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!
