title: Buffalo Bills OC Pete Carmichael reflects on “pretty special” effort in Week 1
summary: Many have wondered the true nature of Pete Carmichael’s role as the new offensive coordinator for the Buffalo Bills. Much of that comes from the fact that Joe Brady previously held that role, and he still calling plays on game day as the team’s new and current head coach. As part of his role, Carmichael […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael of the Buffalo Bills runs off the field at halftime of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Many have wondered the true nature of Pete Carmichael’s role as the new offensive coordinator for the Buffalo Bills. Much of that comes from the fact that Joe Brady previously held that role, and he still calling plays on game day as the team’s new and current head coach. As part of his role, Carmichael is Brady’s eyes and ears during the week where needed, should the head coach be unable to sit in for any portion of the prep work. He’s intimately involved in each week’s game plan, and he brings a ton of experience to the table as someone who worked alongside head coach Sean Payton. Essentially, Carmichael is implementing the system Brady wants to run, allowing the first-time head coach to then dive in on game days after having to spend equal time working with the defense and special teams units. So far, it’s working pretty well. Following Buffalo’s win against the Houston Texans, Carmichael spoke with reporters on Monday afternoon. To begin, Carmichael was asked about Austin Gunn, who quarterback Josh Allen specifically called out regarding his contributions to game planning. Carmichael praised the prep work done heading into Week 1, saying “Yeah, outstanding. We spent a lot of time on it. Austin, that’s uh, you know something, that’s his baby every week, and we sat in there as a staff and he took us through it and you know what he thought was the best plan, and obviously the players executed it. So yeah, shoutout to Austin for sure.” Carmichael was then asked about tight end Dalton Kincaid, whose play in Week 1 stood out to anyone paying attention to the game. Carmichael understands what Kincaid brings to the offense, and sees no limitations in his work due to lingering injury. There’s a chemistry between Allen and Kincaid that very few QB-TE duos manage to enjoy, which obviously pays huge dividends for the Bills. Carmichael knows that Kincaid will play a key role this season if the offense is to remain productive and successful. Though Carmichael is a consummate professional and a very laid-back veteran NFL coach, he did admit to being a bit of a “fan up in the press box” especially on the touchdown to wide receiver Joshua Palmer, understanding how rare that moment was given even he didn’t see things playing out as they did. Simply put, Carmichael said of Allen’s decision-making and execution: “That’s not where my eyes were. And obviously all of a sudden the ball went up and I was like ‘pretty special there.’ So it was awesome to see.” There’s little time to dwell on the past in the NFL, but that’s especially true for the Bills this week as they try to get ready for a short turnaround to host the Detroit Lions for the season-opening bout under the lights of Thursday Night Football on Prime . Carmichael explained that top priorities in situations like this to emphasize rest and recovery early on, followed by doubling up days the next two practice sessions ahead of Thursday. It’s a lot to fit in, but something veteran NFL coaches likely have down to a science. Check out the rest of Pete Carmichael’s latest press conference via the embedded video just below:

title: Bills DC Jim Leonhard excited, understands defense “not up to standards” yet
summary: Following a Week 1 win against the Houston Texans, Buffalo Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard fielded questions about the team’s defensive performance in Reliant Stadium. It’s at times easy to forget that Leonhard is a first-time NFL DC, and that up until Sunday he’d never called a defensive scheme at the professional level. Sure, he […]
full_text: Bills defense coordinator Jim Leonhard talks to someone on the sidelines before practice at Bills Training Camp at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford on Aug. 13 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Following a Week 1 win against the Houston Texans, Buffalo Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard fielded questions about the team’s defensive performance in Reliant Stadium. It’s at times easy to forget that Leonhard is a first-time NFL DC, and that up until Sunday he’d never called a defensive scheme at the professional level. Sure, he brings collegiate experience, but this is all still very new for Leonhard. Though not genuinely unique in the grand scheme, so, too, can be said of the defensive system’s newness, that the Bills fielded against a very talented Texans’ offense. Leonhard is a fun listen at the podium, poised and seemingly wise beyond his years as someone able to meaningfully articulate thoughts to an audience. Leonhard makes you want to suit up for him, lay a few hits, and then hit the sideline ready to cheer on the rest of the team. It’s easy to see why new head coach Joe Brady sought Leonhard when forming the nucleus of his coaching tree. When asked to give his first impressions of the defense following the win, Leonhard was tactful and pragmatic, of course recognizing the accomplishment but also refusing to gloss over the bigger picture. “I think it was awesome to get a win, find a way to close it out. Right? I love the way we started, obviously creating a turnover and then finishing it out with a big turnover. There was a lot of ugly in-between there, right? I mean, excited for the play style. Right? The energy was there, the effort was there. The detail has got to get better. Not up to the standards, right? It’s always great to get the win, but in a lot of ways it did feel like Week 1 where when things started to unravel a little bit at times — or just feel a little bit off — I thought guys looked around like they weren’t sure what the answer should be.” The positive news is that Leonhard believes all things are possible in time, saying “I think it’s very correctable. I left watching the tape going ‘alright, we’re closer. We’re closer than it looked.’ And, I’m excited for where we’re going. Right? There’s gonna be some bumps in the road, and, again, to go into a place like that and find a way to close it out and get a win? Take that for what it’s worth. We have to improve, right? The standards are higher for what we want this defense to be. And it’s our job to get there. There’s a lot of things I want back myself, as I’m sure some players want some snaps back. And that’s the fun part of this game, man. We get a chance to go do it again on Thursday.” Following that, Leonhard was asked if anything surprised him, to which he said: “No, not necessarily. You know, the thing early in a year here when you get some unscouted looks, right, you always want to see how guys respond. And that’s the thing, you can go back to last year and you study teams knowing that, like, they’re also trying to fix their flaws, they’re changing their tendencies and personnel. And we have to be quicker to adjust and adapt, and I thought that was the one thing that the first half, both from myself and from a player standpoint just an awareness like ‘we gotta get there faster.’ And I thought we made some adjustments in the second half, and were a little bit more aggressive and stopped the run better, which led us to some 2nd & Longs, some 3rd & Longs that helped us get off the field.” Leonhard also discussed linebacker Terrel Bernard’s new role as an inside linebacker in the 3-4 alignment — which saw him tally a team-leading 12 tackles — stating that he “thought he handled it really well.” He noted that there were “very few situations that were just big-time communication errors, and there’s some things we gotta clean up,” but took ownership for a lot of that happening: “I didn’t like the two minute. I did not like the way I called the two-minute in the end of the half and kind of put us in some panicky situations. So, that’s the number-one thing that I’m like, ‘alright, that’s on me and I’ll fix that.’ And outside of that, I mean, the situations… if we keep them out of 3rd & 1 and 3rd & 2s, obviously we’re gonna have a little bit more success on third down. And then red zone is obviously an area that we have to correct in a huge way going forward.” That was all shared in only the first few minutes of Leonhard’s presser on Monday. It’s clear he owns his role as defensive coordinator, understanding that the players’ work is a direct reflection of his coaching. We may not see the full intent of Leonhard’s defensive scheme in year one simply due to the fact that certain players may still need to be added. Yet, Leonhard seems confident that the right people are in-house to get the job done even when the chips are down. Leonhard had much more to say during Monday’s media availability, which you can dive into in full below via the embedded video:

After their first games of the season the standings are as follows: Buffalo Bills 1-0 New Jets 1-0 Miami Dolphins 0-1 New England Patriots 0-1 […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Adonai Mitchell #15 of the New York Jets celebrates against the Tennessee Titans during the second quarter of the game at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images As week 1 comes to a close in the National Football League, we got to see an early look on what the AFC East may look like throughout the season. After their first games of the season the standings are as follows: Buffalo Bills 1-0 New Jets 1-0 Miami Dolphins 0-1 New England Patriots 0-1 The Bills were finally able to pick up a win in Houston for the first time since 2006. For Josh Allen it marked his first win in that stadium and he had to earn it that’s for sure. Allen finished the day with 334 passing yards with two touchdowns through the air and another two touchdowns on the ground. It was not a pleasant day for the defense allowing 31 points but shoutout to Deone Walker and Greg Rousseau for clutch sacks on the last drive of the game to clinch the victory. New York got themselves a road victory as well to start the season in the Robert Saleh Bowl defeating the Tennessee Titans. Who knows what the expectations are for the Jets but after one week there could be some hope. Geno Smith had a productive day at quarterback with no turnovers, and Breece Hall had a 100 yard rushing performance with a touchdown. This is a big season for coach Aaron Glenn because another bad season will likely lead to a new head coach for Gang Green while the team hopefully drafts their quarterback of the future. The Patriots lost and Bills fans can point to the reason being that they played a “real opponent,” but I would be quick to hold that judgement. Remember a couple seasons ago, Josh Allen threw away a game against the Jets to open the season with silly interceptions giving a victory to Zach Wilson. The same can be said about Drake Maye who was in control for the majority of the game until a string of three fourth-quarter picks. New England showed that they still have a great defense so they can still prove themselves to be contenders again this season. The issue will be that the talk of the offseason was that the team needed a number one receiver. After finally getting one in AJ Brown, he finds himself on IR with a high ankle sprain and will most likely miss six games according to reports. Lastly with the Dolphins, this marked the beginning of the Malik Willis era at quarterback. Willis showed off the big arm at times but also showed some poor decision making throwing an interception and taking some sacks that could have been avoided. Running back De’Von Achane was held to only 36 rushing yards which is not the recipe for success for Miami. The defense did force a couple of interceptions from Kirk Cousins but could not stop Ashton Jeanty who had 100 yards rushing and two touchdowns as a receiver.

title: Panthers vs Bears Game Review: Hasty generalizations
summary: The full story of an NFL season is not written after a single game. Even one where you are force fed a 50-burger in your own stadium. It was a hard one to stomach for anyone rooting for the Carolina Panthers, but despite a lopsided final score and number of concerning takeaways, it’s probably the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates touchdown with Jalen Coker #18 against the Chicago Bears during the third quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The full story of an NFL season is not written after a single game. Even one where you are force fed a 50-burger in your own stadium . It was a hard one to stomach for anyone rooting for the Carolina Panthers, but despite a lopsided final score and number of concerning takeaways, it’s probably the best start to a season in the last 5 years. If I had to sum up the reason why, it’s that even when things looked bad, they still looked competitive. We are all mindful that that is a shamefully low bar, but the point remains that it’s a vast improvement over what has been the recent quality of football coming out of Charlotte, North Carolina. So, let us all not jump to the conclusions that we may want to after a single week. Even if this one week stirs up some still unresolved trauma from the 2024 Panthers defense that allowed almost 32 points per game. Let us look on the bright side and decide that even if the Panthers defense is that bad, scoring 37 points a game means the Panthers will still win an average football game. Feel better yet? No? Then in the spirit of overreacting to Week 1, let’s make some hasty generalizations based on what we saw on Sunday afternoon. Jalen Coker will be the best Panthers receiver of all time A receiver putting up 8 receptions for 138 yards and 2 touchdowns a game? That’s 136 catches for 2,346 yards and 34 touchdowns in a whole season. Make room Steve Smith, there’s another triple-crown winner coming through. He doesn’t even need separation to make it happen, either. According to NFL’s NextGenStats, Coker only had an average 1.9 yards of separation at the time of catch or incompletion – 8th worst total in the league. The Offensive Line is the most consistent in the entire NFL If you thought that both tackles being out for Week 1 and starting a new budget free agent acquisition at center was going to be a problem, you were wrong. In fact, the Panthers offense line looked about as good as it possibly could have given the circumstances as no starter had a run blocking or pass blocking grade considered below average. Hats off to the winners of PFF’s Offensive Line of the Week . Give Bryce Young all of the money If Baker Mayfield is going to sign for 3 years, $165 million to only put up 217 yards and 0 touchdowns, surely Bryce Young’s 361 passing yards and 4 total touchdowns must be worth $60 million a year? Young is currently 3rd in the NFL in passing yards, tied for 2nd in passing touchdowns and top 10 in a bevy of other important stats including EPA/Play (9th – +0.27), completion % over expected (9th – 6.6%), yards per attempt (4th – 9.3) and average depth of target (10th – 9.8 yards). Strip Derrick Brown of his captaincy The Bears scored 8 touchdowns, but 2 of them came on the back of some rough decisions from one of the purported team stalwarts. Mistake number one was leveling Caleb William’s on cheap shot that was flagged for unnecessary roughness after a throwaway that ultimately turned a 3rd and 20 into 1st and goal. I can almost forgive that one as William’s must have been immensely frustrating to deal with the entire afternoon. Williams had nearly a 20% completion percentage over expected and had 10 scrambles for 65 yards and 2 rushing touchdowns. Every time they though they had him, he pulled a Houdini act to get away. But you know what is unforgivable? Taking away a big man interception because you lined up offsides. Do you know how rare it is for a 332 lb defensive lineman to intercept a football? Neither do I, but I know it’s not often, much less from the literal 1 yard line. A big man shows soft hands and a hero’s heart to pluck a ball right out of the air in the Panther’s time of most dire need – and it’s called back because your helmet was over the line? Derrick Brown deserves a lot of love for what he has done for the Panthers, but this is an outrage that cannot be tolerated. It’s not all over yet and there is still plenty of road ahead on this journey. We’ll see you next week after the Panthers take on the Atlanta Falcons. Until then, Keep Pounding

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: KJ Bolden
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: ATHENS, GA - NOVEMBER 15: Defensive back KJ Bolden #4 of the Georgia Bulldogs tackles wide receiver Emmett Mosley V #3 of the Texas Longhorns during the college football game between the Texas Longhorns and the Georgia Bulldogs on November 15, 2025, at Sanford Stadium in Athens, GA. (Photo by Jeffrey Vest/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Georgia Bulldogs safety KJ Bolden. Bio Bolden (6’0”, 185 lbs.) was a consensus five-star recruit out of Buford, GA and the top ranked safety coming out of high school. He played both sides of the ball for his high school football team and was an anchor on the track team. Bolden had originally committed to Florida State, but he decided to switch to his hometown Bulldogs late in the process. True freshman don’t normally see the field much at programs like Georgia, but Bolden was an exception. He played in all 14 games his true freshman season, even finishing fifth on the team in tackles. He added a sack, a forced fumble, and an interception, helping him earn an SEC All-Freshman nod. After starter Malachi Starks left for the NFL last year, Bolden stepped up in his place. He finished second on the team in tackles as the full time starter with 76 stops, also tallying two interceptions, five passes defended, a fumble recovery, and a blocked punt. His performance earned him Second Team All-SEC honors and a spot on many of the defender award watch lists for this season. A couple games into this season, Bolden has three tackles and 1.5 for loss in two blowout wins against cupcake opponents where he was taken out early in the game to let the backups get some experience. Strengths/Weaknesses Bolden’s athleticism jumps off the tape as he boasts legitimate 4.33 speed. He uses that athleticism to full effect both in the box and in single-high situations, breaking on passes and filling in run gaps as good or better than any other safety in college football. He is a competent and willing tackler, only tagged with four missed tackles last season on about 80 chances. Bolden does an excellent job of keeping his eyes on the quarterback, reading and planting to jump routes and contest catches. He also has positional versatility as a box safety, a deep safety, and even a slot defender. Bolden’s slight frame at just 185 lbs. is the most concerning flaw in his game. Bigger bodied backs and receivers can really test his strength because of his lass of mass. Along those lines, he struggles at times against NFL caliber tight ends in man coverage. Those guys are typically larger and heavier, bullying him a bit in coverage. Many scouts would also like to see more takeaways this year from Bolden: he has the range and ability to take the football away, just needs to do it more consistently. Projection Bolden’s combination of speed, tackling, and versatility make him a likely first round selection. He should be able to put some mass on his frame at the next level, so even if he doesn’t ever become an Ed Reed type of playmaker on the backend he’ll have a spot in the NFL. After the Panthers defense allowed 59 points and over 250 rushing yards against the Bears, having a sure tackling center fielder would help out a lot. Regardless of whether Ejiro Evero’s scheme is still in Carolina next year or not, Bolden’s versatility allows him to still be on the Panthers radar come April. What do you think, Panthers fans? If KJ Bolden is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
author: Daniel Belton

title: The Optimist: Worst Luke Kuechly tribute ever
summary: Former Carolina Panthers linebacker Luke Kuechly, who famously wore the #59 jersey for his entire career, entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame this year. He was one of the best defenders in Panthers history, famous for being a stout, athletic, and cerebral linebacker who turned the middle of the field into a nightmare for […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jimmy Horn Jr. #15 of the Carolina Panthers is tackled against the Chicago Bears during the first half of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Carolina Panthers linebacker Luke Kuechly, who famously wore the #59 jersey for his entire career, entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame this year. He was one of the best defenders in Panthers history, famous for being a stout, athletic, and cerebral linebacker who turned the middle of the field into a nightmare for opposing offenses. Yesterday, in a loving, if misguided, tribute to Luke’s absence on the field, the Carolina Panthers kept anything stout, athletic, or cerebral from touching the field on defense and allowed a symbolic 59 points to the Chicago Bears in the season opener. It was the most points allowed in franchise history and, combined with the Panthers own 37 points, the highest scoring Week 1 game in NFL history. If we told you even two days ago that Bryce Young was going to throw for 361 yards and account for four touchdowns then you would have been pretty optimistic about the Panthers chances in their season opener. Unfortunately, baffling penalties, inopportune turnovers, and an embarrassing defensive effort turned a shoot out into a firing squad. The defense It’s tough sledding when you open your season against what is expected to be one of the best offenses in the NFL and you’re starting your third string outside linebacker. You’ll be expected to struggle rushing the passer, containing scrambles, and holding the edge in the rushing game. It’s also tough when you have multiple starters and contributors on defense who were not with the team in training camp. Tough is one thing. Giving up four touchdowns, out of a total eight surrendered, on plays of twenty yards or more is another flavor of avalanche entirely. Caleb Williams averaged 6.6 yards per attempt and was the Bears least efficient rusher with more than one carry. D’Andre Swift (6.9 yards per attempt) and Kyle Monangai (10.0 yards per attempt) combined with Williams for 289 yards rushing and six touchdowns on the ground. If Ejiro Evero’s seat wasn’t hot coming into the season then it certainly is now. That said, there were flashes of pressure and good linebacker play. We know the secondary has the talent to compete. They did manage to hold expected super star tight end Colston Loveland to a whole two targets and zero catches in the game. Give these guys the Panthers’ traditional four to five weeks to pull themselves together and they could be a good unit down the stretch. Could be. I hope. Jimmy Horn, Jr That wasn’t it, Jimmy. One more week of this, at most, and the Panthers should be looking for new blood in the return game. The offense Atlanta Bryce made a rare appearance in Charlotte yesterday, blasting a mile ahead of his career average game and captaining the offense to a largely respectable showing in Brad Idzik’s debut as play caller. There are some kinks to work out and zero guarantee that they’ll look like this again before December, but you could hardly have asked for a better realistic start on offense. Jalen Coker was everything we had hoped for when Tetairoa McMillan was blanketed. McMillan still managed to find success in the second half despite an abundance of attention from the Bears secondary. And that was all with more production from the tight end position than it feels like we have ever seen in Dave Canales’ tenure. It’s funny how many yards and targets there are to go around in a 37 attempt, 361 yard day. The volume is probably exaggerated, but if that’s the gist of what we can expect in the air with Idzik calling plays then color me excited. Unfortunately, it wasn’t a balanced effort. The ground game struggled heavily. As with the defense, multiple injuries along the line depressed expectations for the rushing attack, but what we saw was still disappointing. A limited ability to gain even three yards when the chips were down hampered this offense and kept them from keeping up with the Bears. The only bright side, and I’m scared to even publish this lest it changes today, is that Jonathon Brooks escaped the game without further injury. Same as with the defense, the seeds shined through in the season opener. There is still a lot of work for them to do to prove that they can be a consistent threat to opposing teams with their offense. Well, not the same as with the defense. Maybe there is less work to do on this side of the ball. @ Atlanta There’s not much more I can say about 59 points. That’s bad. We’re not going to change schemes or onboard 11 new starters. We also, as a fan base, as promised, are not going to overreact to Week 1. Now, to overreact to Week 1, scoring 37 points a game—the Carolina Panthers current 2026 regular season average—would have seen them as a 15-2 team with at least one playoff win in 2025. That’s statistics. On the one hand, I’d expect both sides of the ball to come back to Earth over the course of September before landing on an actual identity through October. That story arc will be true for most teams in the NFL. On the other hand, the sky’s the limit if this is the team’s cold start to the 2026 season. Next week will be an interesting test against Bijan Robinson and whatever dime store quarterback the Falcons think looks healthy. Even if the defense manages to pitch a shutout, we still might not know a lot about them entering Week 3 against the Cleveland Browns. Losing a season opener is nothing new. Losing one while showing promise, sadly, is. I’ll take it for now.
author: Walker Clement

title: Do the Chicago Bears need to aggressively add to their defense?
summary: Soak it in. The Bears’ offense is what everyone has been asking for since Rex Grossman laid a 2006-sized egg. A modern offense capable of scoring at any time and in any manner. And yet, this roster does not look ready to compete for a championship. Why? The defense remains flawed. While there were still […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers runs with the ball during the second quarter against the Chicago Bears of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Soak it in. The Bears’ offense is what everyone has been asking for since Rex Grossman laid a 2006-sized egg. A modern offense capable of scoring at any time and in any manner. And yet, this roster does not look ready to compete for a championship. Why? The defense remains flawed. While there were still some standout performances, namely from rookies Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad, the defensive line and defensive backfield have major holes. Do the Bears need to make a trade and add to their defense? I’m 95% there. There are only a few remaining reasons to be optimistic that the Bears defense can still improve. First, they are still missing some key players in Kyler Gordon and Coby Bryant. However, the severity of Bryant’s injury and lack of clarity around Gordon means that you can’t necessarily count on either of them. If (very big if) Gordon can return and make the impact he is capable of, that could help lock up the middle of the field and push someone like Muhammad outside where he might be more comfortable. If (another big if) Bryant can return 3/4 of the way through the season, he can bring some range and playmaking to the back end. Hard to rely on either of those realities, but neither are impossible. Another reason for tepid optimism is the early returns on the young players. Both Thieneman and Muhammad had standout performances. Still, there were things that need cleaning up, particularly Muhammad’s coverage in the slot. He was beaten a few times on quick crossers — proof that he still needs time to get better at this new position. Add in preseason stars Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving, and there is still potential for some real growth along the defensive front. My final plea for patience is simply that the Bears defense was put in a few bad situations, giving the Panthers short fields. The Panthers had drives start at the Bears 42, Panthers 40, Bears 21, and Panthers 42. This is unsustainable for any defense — and a sticking point I am sure Head Coach Ben Johnson will make during the upcoming week. Still, the Bears surrendered 24 first downs, 478 total yards, 7.7 yards per play, and four touchdowns on four trips to the red zone. This defense has a lot of issues that need to be addressed. So what needs the most attention? I think two things come to mind. The Bears still need an EDGE to complement Montez Sweat. Dayo Odeyingbo looked slightly better yesterday, but made mistakes and still lacked necessary impact. Austin Booker was remarkably absent during the game yesterday. Any optimism that he could be the game wrecker on the DL was put into question after his performance. So at a minimum, the Bears need a DE2 opposite Sweat to help generate pressure from the opposite side. Ideally, the Bears can secure an EDGE that can be a primary pass rusher and shift Sweat to DE2. A Kayvon Thibodeaux could be a more affordable option. Shifting focus to the defensive backfield, and what was previously viewed as a team strength looks like a defensive weakness after Week 1. Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson were both burned on several instances, leading to chunk plays by players like Jalen Coker, Darren Waller, and Tetairoa McMillan. While the DL needs to put pressure on QBs sooner, both Johnson and Stevenson appeared to have a difficult time keeping up in man coverage. Given the importance of Johnson in particular, this should be sounding alarms across the Bears organization. He hasn’t looked quite right since his groin and core injuries early in the 2025 season. While the addition of Kyler Gordon or a quick return of Coby Bryant could help cover the issues on the outside CBs, I am walking away deeply concerned with the issues at starting CB. If the Bears are going to take a swing, I am more inclined to do so on an impact CB. A guy like Joey Porter Jr. could push Jaylon Johnson to CB2 and give him better matchups. I think this type of addition could go a long way in improving the pass defense for the Bears. The Bears already have a ton of resources wrapped up in the defense, but given the initial returns on offense, Ryan Poles should pull out all of the stops to ensure that the defense can contribute to a legitimate championship run. Now it’s your turn! Do the Bears need to aggressively add to their defense? Sound off in the comments!

title: NFL Power Rankings Week 2: Not Overreacting To Kickoff Weekend
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season is underway, and with that, Week 1 is in the books. As usual, the opening week of football has proven to be one of the most unpredictable in the football calendar. Unlike previous seasons, the opener kicked off on a Wednesday, followed by the NFL’s first game in Australia. While […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter against the Houston Texans of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season is underway, and with that, Week 1 is in the books. As usual, the opening week of football has proven to be one of the most unpredictable in the football calendar. Unlike previous seasons, the opener kicked off on a Wednesday, followed by the NFL’s first game in Australia. While it’s great to have football back, it’s always important not to overreact too much to the results from the weekend. With that in mind, let’s dive into our WCG Week 2 NFL Power Rankings as we turn the page on the season opener. 1. Seattle Seahawks (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: Thank God Sam Darnold’s Injury Is Short-Term. Pulling out a 13-10 victory is one thing, but without the long-term health of Darnold secured, their season looks much different moving forward. The good news is that while there’s no definitive diagnosis for the Seahawks’ quarterback quite yet, the consensus is that he avoided anything long-term or season-ending. Assuming this doesn’t end in an IR stint, Seattle will be just fine, and the best is yet to come. 2. Buffalo Bills (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: D.J. Moore is going to make a big difference for Josh Allen. That might be enough to get their offense back to a Super Bowl level. The bigger focus will be on the defense. Despite their win, they still gave up 31 points. The talent is there; it might just take some time with a new coaching staff to get things firing correctly. 3. Baltimore Ravens (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: The reports of Lamar Jackson’s demise were premature. He’s back. The bigger question is whether their defense can return to form under head coach Jesse Minter. This is a highly talented team that underachieved last year, but they must get a better return on investment from some of their higher-paid players if they hope to return to Super Bowl contention this season. 4. San Francisco 49ers (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: If Thursday night was any indication, a healthy defense could make a world of difference this season. The 49ers looked dangerous, fast, and well-rounded on both sides of the football. Barring better health than previous seasons, San Francisco could contend for the NFC West title this season. 5. Los Angeles Rams (0-1) Initial Week 1 Thought: With Myles Garrett on IR for four-to-six weeks, how quickly Aaron Donald can get into shape might dictate whether or not they can hang in the division race once Garrett returns. The Rams might have to rely on other veterans like Matthew Stafford, Davante Adams, and Puka Nukua to keep this team on track while they wait for their defense to take shape. 6. Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: Browns or not, quarterback Trevor Lawrence’s growth under head coach Liam Coen does not appear to be a half-season fluke. Even more impressive is the defense’s continued improvement. Despite Deshaun Watson’s overall numbers, the game was well out of hand before the Browns offense did anything of note. This is a well-rounded team with a potential Top 5-7 quarterback reaching his peak. 7. Chicago Bears (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: The offense’s Year 2 jump under Ben Johnson is evident, but the defense might keep them from being a legitimate Super Bowl contender. The Bears must find some defensive balance, and it must happen in a hurry. Better health will help, but for now, the offense will face continued pressure to produce 30-plus points per game. 8. Kansas City Chiefs Initial Week 1 Thought: Are the Chiefs back or were they ever gone? The defense looked great, but plenty of questions remain on offense, including how to get their pass catchers open. With that in mind, Kenneth Walker III sure looked good in his Kansas City debut. 9. Denver Broncos (0-1) Initial Week 1 Thought: The Broncos’ blowout loss on the road in Kansas City felt like a prime example of a game that nobody should overreact to. That said, that was about as bad as Denver has looked in a few years, so hopefully it was a fluke rather than the regression some have been expecting in 2026. 10. Houston Texans (0-1) Initial Week 1 Thought: Houston’s early-season struggles continue into another year, but C.J. Stroud’s 274-yard passing performance was promising after how the playoffs ended. Assuming the defense can get back on track, they should have more than enough talent on both sides of the ball to compete with Jacksonville for another AFC South title. 11. New England Patriots (0-1) Initial Week 1 Thought: This year’s top regression candidate will have to contend with a (0-1) start and one of the league’s toughest schedules. Even so, don’t bail on the Patriots quite yet. There’s plenty of talent on both sides of the ball, and it’s hard to imagine that Drake Maye will experience the same struggles he did on Wednesday night in Seattle. 12. Detroit Lions (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: Even if it shows 31 points in the box score, there’s going to be some patience needed with Drew Petzing taking over the play calling. Part of that comes from blowing a 21-point lead, but Jahmyr Gibbs was the only offensive player with typical production against a Saints team still trying to find its footing. We’ll see how they look on a short week in Buffalo. 13. Cincinnati Bengals (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: With four sacks and four takeaways, over time the Bengals may finally prove to have a Super Bowl-caliber defense. Now, it’s time to get Ja’Marr Chase and their highly paid receivers going in the passing game. Regardless, there’s plenty to be excited about in Cincinnati. 14. Philadelphia Eagles (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: Despite scoring 24 points, the Eagles’ lack of killer instinct on offense should still concern folks, even after bringing in yet another offensive coordinator. Saquon Barkley looked better than he did for most of last season, but has still yet to show the same burst. The same could be said for quarterback Jalen Hurts and the passing attack as a whole. 15. Green Bay Packers (0-1) Initial Week 1 Thought: The organization put its faith in head coach Matt LaFleur with an extension, but their inability to finish games is becoming a very concerning trend that cannot be ignored. In fact, the Packers have four losses that all had 90% or better win probabilities heading into the fourth quarter. Now they must figure out whether they are the league’s unluckiest team or have a systemic issue that needs to be addressed. 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-1) Initial Week 1 Thought: Without overreacting, it’s fair to say that the Chargers’ Week 1 offensive output was highly disappointing. That’s the key to them getting back to the playoffs and finding some success this season. It’s fair to expect things to improve, but it was also fair to expect a much better product in their first game. We’ll see how Jim Harbaugh plans to get his team to respond. 17. Minnesota Vikings (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: How serious is Kyler Murray’s concussion? Their season-long success might rely on it. In the short-term, they pulled off an impressive victory against the Packers and have a chance to get to 2-0, with both wins coming in the division if they can take care of business on Sunday in Chicago. We’ll see if Kevin O’Connell sticks with Carson Wentz or decides to give J.J. McCarthy a spot start while waiting on Murray to clear concussion protocol. 18. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: The defense still has some juice, but how concerned should we be that they couldn’t handle the lowly Falcons on their third quarterback more convincingly? A lot of that comes down to an underwhelming offense, led by a well over-the-hill Aaron Rodgers. This roster has an older core, and it’s fair to wonder what their ceiling is moving forward. 19. New York Giants…

title: Reviewing the Bears’ PFN grades from Week 1 vs. Panthers
summary: The Bears came away from Week 1 victorious, marching into Carolina and picking up the 59-37 victory. The game marked the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history, and it also marked the most points the Bears have scored in a single game in the 21st century. As one could expect by the score, the Bears’ […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Chicago Bears running back D'Andre Swift (4) scores a touchdown in the fourth quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Bears came away from Week 1 victorious, marching into Carolina and picking up the 59-37 victory . The game marked the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history, and it also marked the most points the Bears have scored in a single game in the 21st century. As one could expect by the score, the Bears’ offense was incredible on Sunday. The defense? Not so much. There’s a lot to nitpick from how Chicago looked defensively, but given how dominant it was on offense, it’s hard to come away from the Week 1 matchup and not feel optimistic about this team. The analytics tend to back up the eye test. But which players fared the best? Each week, I’ll be reviewing how each of Chicago’s eligible performers graded by Pro Football Network’s Impact Scoring model. Here’s what Week 1 looked like. Offense Caleb Williams: 85.5 (4th of 30 QBs) D’Andre Swift: 87.3 (2nd of 45 RBs) Kyle Monangai: 81.4 (5th of 45 RBs) Kalif Raymond: 72.4 (40th of 64 WRs) Luther Burden III: 64.2 (62nd of 64 WRs) Cole Kmet: 70.4 (20th of 31 TEs) Braxton Jones: 77.2 (28th of 62 OTs) Joe Thuney: 66.7 (54th of 57 OGs) Garrett Bradbury: 67.3 (26th of 30 Cs) Jonah Jackson: 82.6 (7th of 57 OGs) Darnell Wright: 83.9 (2nd of 62 OTs) All told, a lot of these grades pair up with how the Bears looked on tape. Caleb Williams was the star of the show on Sunday, scoring four total touchdowns and not giving up any interceptions. His 72.4% completion percentage and 124.1 passer rating were each among the best on the offensive side of the ball. I was admittedly surprised to see Joe Thuney so low, but for the most part, Chicago’s offensive line held up pretty well. I came away impressed with their ability to generate movement and take precise angles in the run game. As one could expect given how many points they score, the Bears had the highest PFN Offense Impact Score in the league at 92.5. Their 0.36 EPA per play tied for the most in the NFL, as did their 7.9 yards per play. Coincidentally, the team the Bears tied with in the latter statistic was the Ravens, whose offensive play-caller is former Chicago offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. It was a good week for the Ben Johnson tree. Defense Montez Sweat: 76.7 (28th of 99 EDGEs) James Lynch: 60.7 (60th of 99 EDGEs) Kentavius Street: 79.9 (9th of 84 DTs) Grady Jarrett: 68.4 (36th of 84 DTs) Austin Booker: 52.0 (94th of 99 EDGEs) Dayo Odeyingbo: 51.2 (96th of 99 EDGEs) Devin Bush: 79.1 (20th of 62 LBs) Malik Muhammad: 81.5 (8th of 86 CBs) Jaylon Johnson: 65.4 (76th of 86 CBs) Tyrique Stevenson: 59.3 (86th of 86 CBs) Dillon Thieneman: 75.0 (19th of 75 SAFs) Cam Lewis: 71.3 (47th of 75 SAFs) It’s not particularly shocking that the Bears didn’t grade incredibly well on defense. Their only two defenders to finish with a top-ten score at their respective positions were Kentavius Street, who had a sack on Sunday, and Malik Muhammad, who had an interception in his NFL debut. Muhammad was particularly impressive, as the rookie allowed a targeted passer rating of just 39.8 against Carolina. However, both Jaylon Johnson and Tyroque Stevenson finished as below-average starters, with Stevenson finishing Week 1 with the lowest PFN CB Impact Score in the league. Heading into Monday Night Football , the Bears rank just No. 24 among 30 defenses with a 68.2 PFN Defense Impact Score . Their 68.7 pass-defense score ranks No. 24 in the NFL, though their run-defense score of 74.4 ranks higher with a serviceable No. 17 ranking. The 7.7 yards per play they allowed tied for the third-most in the league, which is surely a mark Chicago will look to improve upon in future matchups. Special teams (for the sickos) Cairo Santos: 77.6 (14th of 26 Ks) Tory Taylor: 76.7 (19th of 29 Ps) Cairo Santos was penalized twice on Sunday for having his kicks fall short of the landing zone on kickoffs, giving the Panthers improved field positioning. That said, his 8-for-8 mark on extra points and converted field goal try from 40 yards out give him an average score. Conversely, Tory Taylor only punted twice, granting the Bears +3 net yards over expected. His 51.0 net yards per punt tied for ninth in the NFL on a small sample size.

full_text: Chicago had an amazing performance from its offense, putting up 59 points and earning the team its first win of the season. These sorts of things get noticed, and so it’s not surprising that a pair of Chicago Bears have been nominated for the FedEx Air and Ground players of the week. As of Monday afternoon, Caleb Williams has the highest QBR (94.9) and EPA (12.3) of any quarterback in the league, and his passer rating and adjusted net yards per attempt are also in the Top 5. Here, his primary competition is Josh Allen—who amusingly enough had two rushing touchdowns, just like Caleb. The nominees for the @FedEx Air & Ground Players of the Week. Vote for your winners below! ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/nCbaZBQ81e — NFL (@NFL) September 14, 2026 The other Chicago candidate is, of course, D’Andre Swift. Swift was recently extended by Chicago, and he rewarded their confidence with 134 yards from scrimmage and three touchdowns. Swift was an absolute monster blocking for Chicago, as well, and his place being nominated alongside Derrick Henry and Jahmyr Gibbs is well-earned. There were many who had doubts when Ben Johnson said that he wanted to have the highest-scoring offense in NFL history, but behind QB1 and RB1, the Bears have gotten out to a significant headstart on that goal. Sound off below on what you think is the limit for this offense (if there is one), and when you get a chance, go vote for Williams and Swift here .

title: Bears vs. Panthers Game Balls: 2026 Campaign Opens With Historic Start
summary: The 2026 Chicago Bears season is underway, and Bears fans have never quite had a week one victory Monday like this one. In scoring 59 points against the Carolina Panthers, the Bears achieved their highest point total since 1980 (a Week 14 victory over the Green Bay Packers, 61-7). That point total was also tied […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears reacts to touchdown against the Carolina Panthers with D'Andre Swift #4 during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 Chicago Bears season is underway, and Bears fans have never quite had a week one victory Monday like this one. In scoring 59 points against the Carolina Panthers , the Bears achieved their highest point total since 1980 (a Week 14 victory over the Green Bay Packers, 61-7). That point total was also tied for second-place all-time in an NFL week one game, only trailing a 1973 performance by the Atlanta Falcons that saw 62 points scored. There have only been three games in franchise history where the Bears have scored more points than they did against Carolina this week. The previously mentioned 1980 contest against the Packers, 61 points against the San Francisco 49ers in 1965 (the famous 6 TD Gale Sayers game), and the 73-0 victory over Washington in the 1940 NFL Championship. That’s the list. The Bears offense was dominant in every way possible. Caleb Williams ran for two touchdowns, and he passed for two more. The rushing game itself was electric, putting up 291 yards. The only thing missing was Colston Loveland, but the fact that the team could achieve these kinds of statistics without a single catch from TE1 says a lot about the talent level this team has on that side of the ball. The defense left a lot to be desired, especially in the first half. Even with the historic offensive output, you don’t want to routinely give up almost 40 points. For his part, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen did seem to adjust at halftime, and the Bears only gave up 13 points in the second half. Hopefully some lessons were learned and we can build off of them. Let’s get to the game balls. Offense Game Ball: RB D’Andre Swift This could have gone to a number of players. Caleb was incredible. Kyle Monangai rushed for 100 yards and a touchdown, but his presence was mostly felt in just the second half. I have to go with the featured running back who was terrific from bell to bell. Fresh off a new contract, D’Andre Swift went out there on Sunday and earned every cent of that new deal (and then some). He took the very first play from scrimmage 17 yards on a handoff to the right side, which was whistled back for a Rome Odunze holding penalty. Swift didn’t let that deter him, though. He racked up 124 yards rushing on 18 carries (6.9 YPC) and three rushing touchdowns. He also caught one pass for 10 yards. Swift ran with determination and quick decision making on Sunday. He was a clear difference maker for the offense each and every time out, and for that, he gets our offensive game ball this week. D'Andre Swift EVERY RUSH Week 1 Highlights 2026 Chicago Bears vs Carolina Panthers pic.twitter.com/Fi2oljj4Hk — BEARSKIFILM (@BearskiFilm) September 13, 2026 Defense Game Ball: S Dillon Thieneman There were a lot of negatives when it comes to the Bears defense in their 2026 debut, but the rookies shined at times. Safety Dillon Thieneman and CB Malik Muhammad were both in the running for a game ball here. Muhammad looked like the best CB on the field Sunday. Tyrique Stevenson had an absolutely abysmal game, getting burned and whiffing on multiple tackles. Jaylon Johnson wasn’t much better, though he showed more effort at times than Stevenson. However, it was Thieneman that really stood out in his debut. He led the team in tackles (10), while also having a pass defended and QB hit. Those 10 tackles tied for the league high among safeties in week one. Thieneman made his presence felt all over the field, flashing that high end speed and making some physical hits. Despite the rocky start from the defensive unit as a whole, Thieneman and Muhammad both gave us some reasons to believe things will improve as the season goes on. Dillon Thieneman All-22 rookie debut Kid is going to be in Chicago for a long time https://t.co/0xMBeEwySw pic.twitter.com/Hcfsm78weM — Dave (@davebftv) September 14, 2026 Bryan Orenchuk and myself will have plenty to say about this game this week on a new episode of Bears Over Beers on Wednesday evening. It will be available on the 2nd City Gridiron YouTube channel or via your favorite podcasting platform. Our 2nd City Gridiron Podcast Channel is available on Apple , Spotify , iHeart , Audacy , and other popular podcast platforms. Who would have received your game balls? Let us know in the comments section below.

title: This could be the most unstoppable offense in Chicago Bears history
summary: Let me add this one to overreaction Monday takes about the Chicago Bears’ 59-37 curb-stomping of the Carolina Panthers in Week 1: What we just saw on Sunday has me ready to say Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams are about to orchestrate the greatest offensive season this franchise has ever seen. Was it just because […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after their 59-37 win against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let me add this one to overreaction Monday takes about the Chicago Bears’ 59-37 curb-stomping of the Carolina Panthers in Week 1: What we just saw on Sunday has me ready to say Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams are about to orchestrate the greatest offensive season this franchise has ever seen. Was it just because the Panthers’ defense is really bad? Is it just a one-week wonder? Is that kind of scoring sustainable, especially if the defense is going to give up 30 points a game? Just stop. You’re asking the wrong questions. “Should we start fitting Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams for their gold jackets?” “Should we make D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai the two highest-paid running backs in the league?” Now that’s what I’m talking about. Okay, seriously though, wow. Williams, who barely played at all in the preseason, looked every bit like a third-year quarterback about to destroy the entire league. No completion percentage concerns in this one, as he hit on 21 of his 29 pass attempts (72.4%) for 269 yards and two scores. Throw in the two rushing touchdowns, and I absolutely cannot wait to see what his grades come out to this week. We could be looking at the highest marks of his career for a single game. The Bears’ run game, meanwhile, was an absolute monstrosity. Swift (124 yards, 3 TDs) and Monangai (100 yards and a TD, including a 61-yarder) could not be stopped, combining with Williams to give Chicago six rushing touchdowns on the day. Rome Odunze sonned a guy after we wondered how effective he was going to be while battling injury. Cole Kmet, the lesser-heralded of the Bears’ two tight ends, stole the show with an insane touchdown grab. (Also, what a f—g throw by Williams.) Aside from Luther Burden’s early fumble (which he bounced back from) and some penalties, you couldn’t ask for a whole lot more from this unit. The great part: it’s been building toward this ever since Johnson became the head coach here. From the tenacity of the run game to Williams’ development as a passer, we saw the vision even as early as last season. Now, the vision is here, and it looks incredible. From the roster to the mentality, this offense is built to beat defenses into submission and solve problems. You have to commit to full 60 minutes of stopping the run every time you play them, for one thing, and you still might not stop them even if you do. And if Williams is going to rip zone coverage to shreds and punish aggressive pass rushes with his legs like this? The best you can do is slow a machine like that down. The only thing that can stop an offense on that level of efficiency is itself. What’s more: we already know this is what Johnson does. This is his track record—explosive, physical offense. Now, he has the talent to take it to a level even he hasn’t yet reached with Williams rounding into a possible MVP-level player right before our eyes. Johnson said he wanted to have the highest-scoring offense ever, and his team just emphatically announced it does, too. Sure, it’s only one game. The NFL is a fickle league, and things can change from week to week. But I think we can be sure of this: Johnson, Williams, and Co. have a chance to rewrite every offensive record this franchise has—and not just because they’ve been offensively challenged for so many years. No. This is the real thing.
author: Khari Thompson

title: 10 Bears Takes: Run Game Dominance, Caleb Williams Improvement, History Made
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season is under way, and I’m not sure the Chicago Bears could have had a more emphatic offensive performance than they did on Sunday afternoon in Carolina. Now, it’s always important not to overreact to anything that happens in Week 1 (we’ll take more on that in a few), but the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball against Bobby Okereke #58 of the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season is under way, and I’m not sure the Chicago Bears could have had a more emphatic offensive performance than they did on Sunday afternoon in Carolina. Now, it’s always important not to overreact to anything that happens in Week 1 (we’ll take more on that in a few), but the offense did something we’ve never seen before. Without getting too much into the weeds right now, let’s dive into our first regular season edition of 10 Bears Takes for the 2026 regular season. 1. Once again, the 2026 opener continues to prove how unpredictable Week 1 can be. Man, what a weekend, huh? Once again, the NFL showed why they are king, even if the two opening games of the weekend didn’t deliver the same way many had hoped. Across the league, plenty of results didn’t match expectations, starting with Thursday’s game, where the Los Angeles Rams were run out of Australia by the San Francisco 49ers. To make matters worse, offseason prize Myles Garrett will miss at least four games after undergoing a knee scope. Surprises on Sunday included the New Orleans Saints taking the Detroit Lions down to the wire in overtime, the New York Jets dominating the Titans in Tennessee, and the Atlanta Falcons on their QB3 hanging with Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers on the road. While the results of the week make it easy to conclude, no matter how “crazy” things might feel in the moment, we should have learned to let things play out for a few months into the season. For example, the Las Vegas Raiders beat the New England Patriots 20-13. A few months later, the Patriots were in the Super Bowl, and the Raiders were firing their head coach (and staff) after a disastrous first season. Heck, even Justin Fields went off for a 9.9 yards-per-attempt average and three total touchdowns, before being benched two months later. Long story short, it’s best to hold all of our hot takes for at least a few more weeks. Even for as exciting as the Bears’ win was on Sunday, let’s see how things play out into October. 2. Don’t be fooled by last year’s results; the Carolina Panthers’ defense should be much improved. No matter the opponent, 59 points is something Bears fans have never seen this team accomplish before. Seriously, what the Bears’ offense did on Sunday is something fans have never seen their favorite team accomplish before. In total, Chicago hung 59 points, 552 yards, and 70 plays. Even more impressive, they ran for 291 yards on 39 carries for a 7.5-yard average, and six touchdowns on the ground. Through the air, they were as efficient as they have been with Caleb Williams going 21-for-29 (72.4%) for 269 passing yards and two passing touchdowns, while adding 65 yards and two touchdowns on the ground. Even more impressive, he averaged 9.3 yards per attempt. In total, the offense scored nine times on 14 drives, punting just twice. One of those drives came at the end of the half, and it was a run play. We’ll dive into more specifics on each aspect of their offensive attack here in a few, but what this group did, especially in Week 1, should not be overlooked, even if it’s unlikely to be replicated many times this season. During the offseason, head coach Ben Johnson went on record saying he wanted to have the league’s highest-scoring offense ever. While that might feel like some super lofty expectations, it’s worth noting that the team with the current record (the 2013 Denver Broncos) did not crack 59 (or more) at any point during their impressive 16-game campaign. They did, however, hang 50-plus three times, as well as 40-plus. Although lofty, the Bears are technically out-pacing the Broncos one game into the season. Even if I don’t believe they can break the record for points-per-game, it’s a great start, and again, not something we’ve ever seen a Bears offense accomplish. Buckle up, Bears fans. The defense is likely to struggle, which means these types of offensive outbursts will be musts for them to win ball games. 3. Speaking of the offense, the subtle differences in Caleb Williams’ game were noticeable and, more importantly, promising. As noted above, Williams was above the high-water mark set by his head coach, with a 72.4% completion rate. A big part of that, beyond an impressive offensive outburst, was how often he simply took the checkdown. He started five-for-five before throwing one away, and finished the first half 12-of-15 for 196 passing yards, a touchdown, and a 141.0 passer rating. For those who believe “settling” for checkdowns results in lower efficiency numbers, Sunday was his second-highest yards-per-attempt in his career, and a 15.19 total EPA (best of his career). Simply put, Williams taking what the defense gave him resulted in higher efficiency, fewer incompletions, and was a good contribution to Week 1’s highest-scoring offense. Expanding out further to the entire offense, Sunday’s game was a great example of how much opposing defenses are going to struggle to contain this group all season. Everyone, including me, agrees that tight end Colston Loveland is one of, if not the best, offensive weapons the team has. After all, he was their most dangerous pass catcher down the stretch last season. Yet, somehow, the Panthers’ defense held Loveland to no catches (or yards) on two targets, but still found a way to give up 552 yards and 59 points. In the passing game, veteran Kalif Raymond led all pass catchers with eight catches for 88 yards. Luther Burden factored in with five catches for 63 yards, and Rome Odunze had the catch of the day, mossing Carolina’s rookie cornerback. In total, the Bears had 261 total yards through the air, despite not getting Loveland or rookie Zavion Thomas involved. The only touchdown came from Jahdae Walker’s 1-yard catch to ice the game. What should scare defensive coordinators is that Johnson cannot only feature less-likely heroes like Raymond and Walker, but also bludgeon opposing defenses on the ground. We’ll get into the team’s rushing attack and D’Andre Swift’s much-deserved extension later, but hanging more rushing yards (291) than passing yards (261) shows how versatile and unpredictable this group can be. Even if fans shouldn’t expect 59 points or 500-plus yards, they can expect their head coach (and offensive play caller) to find every potential avenue to success for his offense on a weekly basis. 4. Much was made of how the Bears handled their defensive acquisition this offseason; after one week, there’s plenty to be concerned about moving forward without serious adjustments from defensive coordinator Dennis Allen. Make no mistake: there’s plenty to be excited about in 2026 for this Bears team. That said, if Sunday was any indication of how much this defense will struggle, everyone should have serious concerns moving forward. I’m not one to sit here and continue to poo-poo Bryce Young and his development heading into Year 4. In fact, I’m someone who believes the conversation for the top quarterback in the 2023 class between Young and C.J. Stroud is closer than many want to admit. That said, allowing him to go for 361 yards, a 110.3 rating, and a total EPA of (9.18) is just not going to win this unit many awards. Many, including myself, expect the Panthers’ offense to take a step forward this season, but that big of a step forward? Highly unlikely. The lack of pressure on Young was a concern, but the missed tackles and lack of gap integrity were more concerning. The open-field tackling at the second level was atrocious, and the team’s top-2 cornerbacks looked slow and overmatched. Outside of the two takeaways, there wasn’t a whole lot to like about the Bears’ defensive performance on Sunday. The…
author: Aaron Leming

title: Bears vs. Panthers: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and Everybody Blocks
summary: The Chicago Bears’ 59-37 win over the Carolina Panthers was a perfect way to kick off the season because, while so much went right, there’s still plenty that didn’t for head coach Ben Johnson to focus on. Most notably, the defense that allowed Carolina to get 478 yards of offense and 24 first downs. In […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after his rushing touchdown against the Carolina Panthers in the first quarter of a game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears’ 59-37 win over the Carolina Panthers was a perfect way to kick off the season because, while so much went right, there’s still plenty that didn’t for head coach Ben Johnson to focus on. Most notably, the defense that allowed Carolina to get 478 yards of offense and 24 first downs. In his postgame press conference, Johnson was asked how they can solve some of their defensive issues, and he used that as a way to discuss them getting better overall. “We talked about with the team, find a way to get to the plane with a win. And we did that,” Johnson said in his postgame press conference. “We accomplished that. Now we’re in a race to improve — in all three phases and collectively as a team. That’s what we gotta do. So we’ll take a look at the tape. What can we get better at? You know, it only gets harder from here on out. And yet, I told those guys, you’d like to think in a long season like this, we’re playing our worst football early on, and we continue to get better and better and better. That’s really the message right there. All three phases, we all got to get better each and every week.” Johnson has set a high bar for his team in 2026, and his offense’s performance will obviously make him happy. They racked up 552 yards of offense, had 26 first downs, and were 71.4% (10-14) on third-down tries. But the defense’s woes and their 12 penalties (for 57 yards) matched the 12 times his team was penalized in Week 1 last season. One aspect of the game that everyone will be pleased with is the 291 yards rushing, Chicago’s most in a game since getting 302 on September 9, 1984. Johnson acknowledged how his entire offense had a hand in it. “The story of the game ended up being the rushing and, so, the offensive line — shout out to them,” he said. “But it was collective with the tight ends, the receivers were blocking their tails off as well. And Swifty (D’Andre Swift) and (Kyle) Monangai both were able to do a great job there. Caleb added quite a bit with his feet also.” Ben gave the offensive line a game ball in his locker room speech, and their o-line spokesman, right guard Jonah Jackson, made sure to spread the love, saying, “It took all of us, tight ends, wideouts, backs, QB, and a shout out to the playcaller.” The 59-37 win was good, but the Bears are a long way from being the best. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing time breakdowns and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE Caleb Williams is just the 4th quarterback in NFL history with at least 250 passing yards, 50 rushing yards, 2 touchdown passes, 2 rushing touchdowns, and a passer rating over 120 in the same game. He also hit 70% completion for the sixth time in his NFL career, but for the first time under Ben Johnson. His 10 rushes, 65 rushing yards, and 2 rushing TDs are all career highs. Kalif Raymond’s 8 receptions are a career high, as was Kyle Monangai’s 61-yard run. Jahdae Walker only had one catch for a touchdown, but he left an impact on this game in other ways, including the final block on Monangai’s touchdown. “I saw Jahdae chasing down and making sure that wasn’t just a big play, but a touchdown,” Kalif Raymond said via the team site. “I mean, it’s a huge play for Kyle, but Jahdae’s out there taking guys to make sure it happens. I mean, it goes from a big play, a first down to a touchdown. That’s a testament to the guys blocking. I think Lu (Luther Burden III) had a big block too … so just all the stuff working together, and that’s what you want, especially for the backs we have.” Jahdae Walker combined video. Block on special teams, block on offense, and touchdown catch. pic.twitter.com/7S24DcVoIQ — ✶Ⓜ️𝕒𝕣𝕔𝕦𝕤 ▶️✶ (@_MarcusD3_) September 13, 2026 DEFENSE Tyrique Stevenson, who had a rough game in coverage, led the Bears with 9 tackles on defense. Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman had 8 tackles on defense, a QB hit, and a pass defended, plus 2 more tackles on special teams. Rookie Malik Muhammad II, who started at nickel but kicked outside to corner when Stevenson was dinged up, had 3 tackles, 2 pases defende, and an interception. Cam Lewis, who got the start at safety but also got some reps at nickel, had 6 tackles. Devin Bush has 6 tackles, a fumble recovery, and a QB hit. Jaylon Johnson had 3 tackles and a forced fumble. Montez Sweat had 2 tackles, a tackle for loss, and a sack. Kentavius Street also had 2 tackles, a tackle for loss, and a sack. SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos missed the landing zone a couple of times, drawing penalties, but he made all 8 extra points and a 40-yard field goal. Tory Taylor (2 punts for 102 yards) hit a banana ball that the Panthers muffed, leading to a Kaden Davis recovery. Raymond had a 23-yard punt return. Josh Blackwell had 4 kickoff returns and a 21.3 average. Roschon Johnson had 4 special teams tackles. Long snapper Beau Gardner had a tackle. Walker had a couple of special teams tackles. Dayo Odeyingbo blocked an extra point. What is this "banana ball" Ben Johnson is talking about? Look at the angle Tory Taylor strikes this punt. It starts outside towards the sideline, but then comes all the way back inside the hashes. Hard to track, especially with this kind of hang time. Huge play. pic.twitter.com/X5CCeOJqea — Adam Hoge (@AdamHoge) September 14, 2026 To check out the complete Bears vs. Panthers box score, I find ESPN’s site is easy to navigate.
