title: The Broncos’ poor run defense and tackling are major concerns
summary: The Denver Broncos’ defense was atrocious last night vs. the Chiefs. They allowed Kenneth Walker to rush for 173 yards, including a 60-yard 4th-down touchdown run, and average 7.5 yards per carry. They also allowed a hobbled Patrick Mahomes in a knee brace to rush for 23 yards, including a 15-yard first-quarter touchdown. A big […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Emmett Johnson #10 of the Kansas City Chiefs stiff arms Alex Singleton #49 of the Denver Broncos during an NFL football game on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos’ defense was atrocious last night vs. the Chiefs. They allowed Kenneth Walker to rush for 173 yards, including a 60-yard 4th-down touchdown run, and average 7.5 yards per carry. They also allowed a hobbled Patrick Mahomes in a knee brace to rush for 23 yards, including a 15-yard first-quarter touchdown. A big reason for the Chiefs’ rushing success was the 28 missed tackles by the Denver Broncos defense. This was the most missed tackles by a defense in a game since at least 2018, according to Next Gen Stats. Yes, more than their abysmal 70-point loss to the Miami Dolphins in 2023. It was downright embarrassing and a pathetic effort by what is considered a top-ranked defense. The Broncos defense missed 28 tackles against the Chiefs, allowing 247 yards after missed tackles, the most yards allowed by any defense in a game since at least 2018. The Broncos had eight different defenders miss multiple tackles on the night. #DENvsKC | #ChiefsKingdom — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) September 15, 2026 The Broncos’ struggles vs. the run are, unfortunately, nothing new. In the AFC Championship Game vs. the Patriots, they allowed 141 yards rushing, and in the Divisional Round game vs. the Buffalo Bills, they allowed the Bills to rush for 183 yards. Now, in Week 1, with their run-it-back defense, the results were equally bad, as they allowed a whopping 220 yards on the ground to an Andy Reid-coached Kansas City Chiefs team. Every big play the Chiefs had on offense was aided by poor tackling. Mahomes touchdown run saw two defenders whiff on tackles in the backfield. Kenneth Walker slashed through the Broncos’ defense and shrugged off multiple defenders with ease. His 60-yard touchdown on 4th down was aided by a missed tackle by cornerback Riley Moss. The Rashee Rice touchdown saw two Broncos defenders whiff on a tackle and allow Rice to scamper into the end zone. The missed tackles and lack of effort were evident throughout the night. If you want to place blame on anyone, it should be on the two team captains in the middle of the Broncos’ defense. Veteran linebacker Alex Singleton and nose tackle DJ Jones. These two captains are the main players in the middle of the Broncos’ defense and simply have not been good enough lately. We saw it in the playoffs, and the Broncos still re-signed Singleton and preached how important he is to this team. They also brought back Justin Strnad, and the results vs. the run remained the same. As for DJ Jones, you’re supposed to be a run-stuffing nose tackle, but the Broncos’ run defense continues to be a weak point for this team. We saw it vs. the Bills two years ago; it was the theme last season in the playoffs, and it has continued into the season opener vs. the Chiefs. Broncos tackling effort tonight was pathetic pic.twitter.com/QCG7v1B0Sm — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 The issue here is that things do not get easier for the Broncos moving forward. This Sunday, they play the Jacksonville Jaguars, the only team last season to beat them by double digits. They had trouble against the Jaguars’ offense even when they were playing their best last season. If they play anywhere near as bad as they did last night this week, that game could get ugly quickly. Then you have the Rams and 49ers, two offenses that are going to establish the run and usually are successful at it. They are going to watch the tape and attack the defense the same way the Bills, Patriots, and Chiefs have in recent games. The Broncos’ strong pass rush and secondary are weakened if they cannot stop the run consistently. Vance Joseph needs to correct these issues with the Broncos’ defense, and he needs to do it quickly. If not, things could get bad for the Broncos early on this season. Especially with the offense looking like a mess as well.
author: Scotty Payne

title: Davis Webb’s debut as a playcaller was an epic failure
summary: This offseason, Denver Broncos Head Coach Sean Payton did what many people thought he would never do. He handed over play-calling duties to newly hired/promoted offensive coordinator Davis Webb. After being a highly sought-after coach this offseason, Webb returned to the Broncos and was supposed to help the offense take the next step this season. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Bo Nix (10) of the Denver Broncos speaks to offensive coordinator Davis Webb during the second quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images This offseason, Denver Broncos Head Coach Sean Payton did what many people thought he would never do. He handed over play-calling duties to newly hired/promoted offensive coordinator Davis Webb. After being a highly sought-after coach this offseason, Webb returned to the Broncos and was supposed to help the offense take the next step this season. He was going to be more aggressive, bring new ideas, and continue to develop his strong working relationship with quarterback Bo Nix. There was a lot of hype and anticipation about Webb’s debut as a play caller, and well, his debut was an epic failure. "Ask me in another half." 😅 —Sean Payton on not calling plays pic.twitter.com/s8rE5dDYfU — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) September 15, 2026 Where do we begin? It looked off from the very first snap. Nix, who has been historically good at avoiding sacks, was sacked on the very first play and was sacked a total of 4 times last night. He would go on to throw an ugly interception to end the opening drive and finish the night with multiple turnovers. Nix played one of the worst games of his Broncos career last night. Now, let us talk about the run game, or lack thereof. While the Chiefs ran for 220 yards on the ground last night, the Broncos could only muster 61 yards rushing and seemingly abandoned it early on when it was no more than a one-score game. Veteran JK Dobbins was out-snapped by RJ Harvey last night and had just 8 carries for 36 yards. Remember Jaylen Waddle? They made a blockbuster trade for him during the offseason, spent all of camp hyping him up and talking about how he’s going to change this offense. Remember that guy? He was targeted just 3 times and had 1 catch for 2 yards. Even after the Chiefs lost starting rookie corner Mansoor Delane after the opening-drive INT. Courtland Sutton was targeted 5 times and had 2 receptions for 11 yards. Combined, the Broncos’ top two wide receivers in their new and improved offense totaled 3 catches for 13 yards. That’s not what you want. The offensive line was bad too. I haven’t seen the tape, and I am no offensive line guru, but the pressure was getting to Nix throughout the night. Veteran defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo simply out-coached Davis Webb last night. Now, let’s talk play calls. It’s 3rd and 1 in a close game, and the Broncos go 5-wide? You have a fullback on your roster, paid Adam Trautman to be a blocking tight end specialist, kept Nate Adkins on the roster, and re-signed JK Dobbins (Kenneth Walker was a free agent), and you decide not to run the ball? Meanwhile, the Chiefs faced multiple short-yardage situations and went to their heavy package, dominated the Broncos at the LOS, and converted multiple first downs. It is just one game, and Webb has been an impressive coach thus far, but there is no beating around the bush on this one. His debut as a play caller was an epic failure. Can he improve? Of course. Teams and play callers have bad games and bad starts to the season. Sean Payton’s teams are known for their slow starts. However, Webb needs to turn things around quickly or else Sean Payton, who looked edgy on the sidelines last night, is going to takeover play calling duties sooner rather than later.
author: Scotty Payne

title: Horse Tracks: ‘Just a nasty wake-up call’
summary: Well, that sucked. Not only did the Broncos lose the game, they were spectacularly awful in all phases. “Obviously not a good evening,” said Sean Payton, stating the obvious after the game. “Didn’t do a lot well at all in the game.” Nope. Tackling was abominable; pass pro was suspect; the run game was absent; […]
full_text: Well, that sucked. Not only did the Broncos lose the game, they were spectacularly awful in all phases. “Obviously not a good evening,” said Sean Payton, stating the obvious after the game. “Didn’t do a lot well at all in the game.” Nope. Tackling was abominable; pass pro was suspect; the run game was absent; Bo Nix looked no better than a JV quarterback; and Davis Webb left us wondering what all the offseason hype over his play-calling genius was actually about. Davis Webb, what are we doing? https://t.co/n3qXkBQzpD — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 And all that on national, prime-time TV. It’s hard to imagine a worse Week 1 game. Payton offered the expected, “it starts with me, it starts with the coaches” as some attempt at accountability, but that’s not even close to enough. There was no reason for the 2025 AFC champions to look so inept in a Week 1 matchup against their most-hated division rival for a decade. And that is 100 percent on Payton. His offensive coordinator was pathetic, and his defensive coordinator was humiliated. The players did not execute, but the coaches clearly did not have a game plan proving any serious preparation for the Chiefs. It was no secret that the Chiefs were going to run the ball. After all, they went out and got a Super Bowl-winning running back to pair with a three-time Super Bowl MVP coming back from a season-ending injury last year. Of course, they were going to run the ball. But somehow our (previously) top-ranked defense could not find a way for 173 yards to bring down Kenneth Walker III. In fact, the yards given up on missed tackles all game (248) were the Broncos’ third-most since 2018. However bad you thought the Broncos' tackling was against the Chiefs, it was even worse Denver's 248 missed tackle yards allowed were the most in a single game in @NextGenStats ' database. Their 29.8% missed tackle percentage is the third worst single-game score since 2018 https://t.co/Kd0zQjfUFl — Trevor Sikkema (@TampaBayTre) September 15, 2026 And of course the Chiefs defense was going to pressure Nix. So instead of establishing the run, or using the “secret weapon” talked about all offseason in Jaylen Waddle, what did the Broncos’ offense do? Bubble screens. “There are a number of places we have to look,” Payton said of the horrendous performance. “Our third-down numbers weren’t good. Our rushing numbers weren’t good. Pick your spot. “We didn’t tackle well enough then the game became one-dimensional,” the head coach added. “Really, the antithesis of how you beat a good team on the road.” “We literally gave ourselves no chance to succeed today and made it easier for them. Just a nasty wake-up call today.” BO Nix Nix noted the same. “When you give a good team too many chances, they’re going to exploit it,” he said. “Honestly from just a whole offense, whole team perspective, we just really didn’t play very good.” The QB also believes the play-calling wasn’t the issue, just the execution. “We just didn’t put anybody in a good spot today,“ Nix said, adding that the penalties and negative plays didn’t allow the offense to take advantage of most of the planned play calls. ”The players did not make it easy on [Webb] today. We just didn’t execute and then we were behind and then we didn’t do a whole lot of good consistently enough to win the game at all.“ Nix added that the loss was more disappointing than frustrating, but ownership of the poor play will get them back on track. “We literally gave ourselves no chance to succeed today and made it easier for them,” Nix said. “We know we need to be better. We don’t have a choice. Just a nasty wake-up call today. We know this is not going to be the whole season.”
author: Laurie Lattimore-Volkmann

title: Winners and losers from the Denver Broncos’ 31-10 blowout loss to the Kansas City Chiefs
summary: What an ugly showing. There are no winners. We are talking all losers tonight, and nobody is safe. The Broncos played awful on both sides of the ball and were embarrassed on the national stage vs. their divisional rivals. Blown out and looked awful while doing it. Super Bowl caliber team? This didn’t even look […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Kansas City Chiefs dives for a first down against Jahdae Barron #23 of the Denver Broncos during the second quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images What an ugly showing. There are no winners. We are talking all losers tonight, and nobody is safe. The Broncos played awful on both sides of the ball and were embarrassed on the national stage vs. their divisional rivals. Blown out and looked awful while doing it. Super Bowl caliber team? This didn’t even look like a playoff team. Everything that was supposed to be good about this team sucked tonight. Plain and simple. Let’s get this over with. Here are your losers from tonight’s blowout loss to the Chiefs. LOSER – OC Davis Webb Webb taking over the play-calling duties was a big talking point this offseason. The highly sought-after coordinator stayed with the Broncos and was handed play-calling duties from head coach and veteran play caller Sean Payton. There was a lot of hype about his potential, and we would see a new and improved Broncos offense. Well, after one game, the offense took a step back. Everything looked bad. Bo was taking sacks and turned the ball over multiple times; they abandoned the run, dropped passes, and could not block. They had a 1st and GOAL at the 5-yard line after a Mahomes INT and could not get a touchdown. Remember the big trade for Jaylen Waddle? He was barely targeted, and when he was, he dropped the ball on 3rd down. Courtland Sutton did not get his first catch until the 3rd quarter. Unacceptable. LOSER – Broncos defense/tackling This was the worst Broncos defensive showing since their 70-burger vs. the Miami Dolphins. They allowed the Chiefs to rush for over 200 yards (and counting as I write this with 6:40 left in the 4th quarter) and could not make a tackle at all tonight. Whiffs were the theme of the night and a reason for all the Chiefs’ big plays on the night. However bad you thought the Broncos' tackling was against the Chiefs, it was even worse Denver's 248 missed tackle yards allowed were the most in a single game in @NextGenStats ' database. Their 29.8% missed tackle percentage is the third worst single-game score since 2018 https://t.co/Kd0zQjfUFl — Trevor Sikkema (@TampaBayTre) September 15, 2026 What else is there to say? They looked awful and could not tackle at all. Embarrassing, pathetic, and unacceptable. LOSER – Bo Nix I have defended Bo Nix all offseason, but tonight, he gave all the ammo to his haters. He played one of the worst games of his career, was sacked at least 4 times, and turned the ball over at least 2 times. This could go up as I type this. The offense was 2/12 on 3rd downs. That’s not just a Bo Nix issue, but I am including it here. LOSER – The entire Broncos organization The entire organization takes the L tonight. From the top down. You were one game away from the Super Bowl and, frankly, should have been in the Super Bowl. All offseason, we play the what-if game after a magical 14-3 season where they won the AFC West and were the one seed. You go on to make a big splash for Jaylen Waddle, bring back pretty much every free agent, and fail to go out and sign many outside free agents. Then you unveil your new training facility, have the media hype you up all offseason, and enter Week 1 with a ton of hype…and you play like that? They looked unprepared and like a shell of the team we saw last season. The Broncos lost by double digits just once last season (to the team they play next Sunday), but they start the 2026 season with a blowout loss. 0-1 with a tough schedule ahead. Unacceptable.
author: Scotty Payne

title: Instant reaction: Broncos blown out by Chiefs on Monday Night Football
summary: The Denver Broncos took on the Kansas City Chiefs on the road at Arrowhead Stadium to start the season under the bright lights of Monday Night Football. When the clock struck zero, the Broncos found themselves on the wrong side of the scoreboard and were embarrassed 31-10. Here are some instant reactions from tonight’s performance. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Emmett Johnson #10 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs with the ball against Alex Singleton #49 of the Denver Broncos during the fourth quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos took on the Kansas City Chiefs on the road at Arrowhead Stadium to start the season under the bright lights of Monday Night Football . When the clock struck zero, the Broncos found themselves on the wrong side of the scoreboard and were embarrassed 31-10. Here are some instant reactions from tonight’s performance. An unimpressive debut for Davis Webb and the Broncos’ offense One of the big storylines fans across Broncos Country had their eyes on tonight was how the offense would look with the return of Bo Nix and Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb calling plays. The Broncos vowed to start off fast. Alas, that didn’t happen. Truth be told, they were awful. Color me unimpressed and very concerned with what transpired this evening. Nix started out rough tossing an interception right into the hands of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane while targeting Courtland Sutton on the first drive of the game. On the second drive of the game, he rebounded and helped guide the offense on 10-play, 63-yard scoring drive that ended in a 19-yard touchdown strike to tight end Evan Engram. After that? It was Murphy’s Law for Nix and the offense. In their four second quarter drives, they ran just 22 plays for 51 yards. Penalties and a key drop by Pat Bryant on third down stalled two drives. On another, the Broncos went empty set on third and short and Jaylen Waddle couldn’t get enough yards on his reception to move the chains. Overall, the Broncos toted the rock just six times in the first half for 23 yards. Considering the stakes of the game and being in a hostile road environment, opting not to establish the run was a bad choice by Webb. Even Head Coach Sean Payton mentioned his disappointment in that in a post-half time sideline interview. Things didn’t look much better in the second half. Waddle had a key drop on the team’s opening drive of the second half and was essentially invisible all game long. How about shooting themselves in the foot in the red zone after Brandon Jones’ interception on the subsequent drive? Just comical. It’s amazing that they had two weeks to prepare for the game after the preseason and ended up looking this flat. Moreover, I didn’t like the number of personnel changes and how long it took for the Broncos to snap the ball. It’s just the first week, but it’s clear Webb and his players on offense have a lot to work to do. Credit to Steve Spagnuolo for a good defensive game plan for Kansas City—they showed up and played well and had Nix rattled all evening long. Poor tackling and execution plague Broncos’ defense With Patrick Mahomes coming off an ACL injury, there was no doubt the Chiefs were going to show a dedication to the run. They utilized extra lineman early and often along with a healthy dose of carries from free agent acquisition Kenneth Walker III. The results speak for themselves—they dominated the Broncos’ defense with their ground game. While the Chiefs’ offense struggled to get things done through the air in the first half, Walker’s rushing prowess was hard for the Broncos to stop. By the end of the first half, the Super Bowl MVP had 89 yards on 14 rushes. His dominance continued with a 60-yard touchdown scamper on 4th and 1 on the Chiefs’ first drive of the second half. He would finish the game with 23 rushes, 173 yards, and 1 touchdown and added 3 catches for 18 yards and 1 touchdown through the air. This was one of the most undisciplined efforts I’ve seen from the defense in quite some time. You’d have to go back to the 70-point debacle versus the Miami Dolphins in 2023 to see such poor execution. Cornerback Riley Moss had two blown missed tackles which resulted in touchdowns for the aforementioned Walker and wide receiver Rashee Rice. He wasn’t the only one. A handful of other players on defense failed to execute at a high level. I’d highlight inside linebacker Alex Singleton as a terrible performer tonight as well. Anyone care to remind me why they brought him back and rewarded him with an extension? He look This was an embarrassing performance by Vance Joseph’s defense. Sure, it didn’t help that the offense put them in bad situations, but I expect better from a group who has been of the best in the National Football League the past two seasons. They’ll have their work cut out for them on a short week preparing for a Jacksonville Jaguars offense who looked great against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday and put up the most points against Denver last season in December. Miscellaneous thoughts and tidbits: There really isn’t anything positive to write home about. However, two players I thought looked fairly decent with their opportunities were Evan Engram and RJ Harvey. Perhaps the Broncos will try to find a way to get them more involved in the offensive plans moving forward. The Broncos offensive line ranked highly last year. But tonight was a rough outing for them. One area they struggled with routinely was picking up interior pressure and blitzes by Spagnuolo’s defense. This caused Nix to bail out of the pocket early on numerous occasions and contributed to his erratic play. I’m slightly concerned this formula will be something other defensive coordinators will take note of and exploit moving forward. The Broncos had just 177 yards of total offense. They were an appalling 2 of 12 on third down conversions. Completely unacceptable. Meanwhile, the Chiefs racked up nearly 400 yards of total offense and were 9 of 17 on third down. They had 19 first downs compared to just 9 for Denver.
author: Christopher Hart

title: Denver Broncos vs. Kansas City score & highlights from Monday Night Football
summary: Well that didn’t go as planned. While most of us expected a new offense under Davis Webb, instead we got a discombobulated play-calling effort and absolutely zero offensive efficiency on the night. We should certainly be talking about that tonight, but the real issue was on defense. I’m not sure what the record is for […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos warms up prior to the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well that didn’t go as planned. While most of us expected a new offense under Davis Webb, instead we got a discombobulated play-calling effort and absolutely zero offensive efficiency on the night. We should certainly be talking about that tonight, but the real issue was on defense. I’m not sure what the record is for missed tackles, but Denver’s defense tonight may have come close to it. This tweet below dropped in the third quarter and they missed plenty more tackles before the night was over. All kinds of bad for the Broncos and there isn’t much to say other than to see if they can improve on all of these issues within the next six days… The Denver Broncos had a 25.0% missed tackle rate in Week 3 of 2023 when they allowed 70 points to the Miami Dolphins They have a 24.5% missed tackle rate against the Chiefs so far tonight, per @SumerSports — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) September 15, 2026 Broncos vs. Chiefs final score Team 1st 2nd 3rd 4th Final Denver Broncos 7 0 3 0 10 Kansas City Chiefs 7 7 10 7 31 First Quarter The game started out looking like a disaster for Denver. An ugly interception by Bo Nix followed by a power run game from Kansas City that resulted in a Patrick Mahomes scramble and score to put the Chiefs up early. Nix settled in, however, and responded with a strong drive going 5/5 for 55 yards and this 19 yard touchdown strike to tight end Evan Engram BO NIX FINDS EVAN ENGRAM FOR A TOUCHDOWN pic.twitter.com/jV4BEedp1o — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 Both teams drew blood early and it looked like the game would turn into a dogfight. Broncos 7, Chiefs 7. Full first quarter recap . Second Quarter The game quickly devolved into a defensive battle in the second quarter with both teams trading punt after punt after punt. It wasn’t until late in the first half that a team got an offensive drive moving with the Kenneth Walker just dominating the Broncos’ defense to get the team into scoring position. Denver’s defense seemed to have forgotten how to tackle on that drive with so many missed tackles including a short pass to Rashee Rice who turned those missed tackled into a 13-yard touchdown catch and run. Overall, it was an ugly half of football for the Broncos offense outside of that one scoring drive. Many of the issues we complained about much of last season remained an issue through one half of the first game in 2026. Chiefs 14, Broncos 7. Full second quarter recap . Third Quarter As frustrating as the offense was in the first half, the defense probably had the most concerning issues show up. After Kenneth Walker housed a fourth and one for 60 yards, this little stat showed up in my feed that made me even more irritated… Kenneth Walker III has already forced nine missed tackles through the first half, the most missed tackles forced by a Chiefs running back in any game since 2021. #DENvsKC | #ChiefsKingdom — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) September 15, 2026 Walker would add two more missed tackles on that fourth down run. Not ideal. A fantastic punt by Jeremy Crawshaw pinned the Chiefs to their own three yard line. On their first play, Mahomes would gift the break the Broncos needed with a deep pass that was intercepted by Brandon Jones and returned all the way to the Chiefs five-yard line. BRANDON JONES INT pic.twitter.com/ASgl5SAEFX — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 However, much like the Broncos offense all night. They flubbed the opportunity and nearly fumbled it back to Kansas City. Instead, they were fortunate to escape the drive with a Wil Lutz field goal. They would give it all back with more missed tackles resulting in a 59-yard catch and run by Travis Kelce. Denver would hold to a field goal, but man, this defense couldn’t tackle to save their lives in this game. Chiefs 24, Broncos 10. Full third quarter recap . Fourth Quarter A Bo Nix strip-sack fumble to end the third quarter gave the Chiefs great field position early in the fourth quarter. And while I’m not sure how many different ways I can talk about how the Broncos’ defense couldn’t tackle to save their lives – they would add several more missed tackles on this drive that would end with the Chiefs going up by three scores to put the blowout into full effect. Broncos' offense since the 1st quarter. no good. pic.twitter.com/kH3wzCJphf — Zac Stevens (@ZacStevens) September 15, 2026 When the offense wasn’t stinking up the joint, the defense was missing multiple tackles per play. The rest of the fourth quarter was played, but the outcome was fairly obvious by the late third quarter. At 0-1, the Broncos need to turn things around quick because it doesn’t get much easier next week. Chiefs 31, Broncos 10.

title: Broncos vs. Chiefs third quarter recap
summary: The momentum shift was significant late in the first half with the Kansas City Chiefs seizing all of it to take the lead, while the Denver Broncos offense racked up four straight three-and-outs to end the half. Getting the ball first, Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs’ offense were slowed early in their first drive. On […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Kansas City Chiefs breaks a tackle by Brandon Jones #22 of the Denver Broncos to score a 60 yard touchdown during the third quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The momentum shift was significant late in the first half with the Kansas City Chiefs seizing all of it to take the lead, while the Denver Broncos offense racked up four straight three-and-outs to end the half. Getting the ball first, Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs’ offense were slowed early in their first drive. On third and seven, Mahomes hit Rashee Rice just shy of the first down marker. They would go for it inside their own 40 and would pick it up easily with Kenneth Walker bouncing it outside for a 60 yard touchdown run to blow the game wide open. KENNETH WALKER 60-YARD TD DENvsKC on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FewiswX7K5 — NFL (@NFL) September 15, 2026 Chiefs 21, Broncos 7. The Chiefs running game had out-paced Denver by a mile a game. So finally JK Dobbins broke one outside to basically double the Broncos rushing yards on one play to get Denver across midfield on the first play of the next drive. The drive would again be derailed by themselves after a Delay of Game penalty pushed them back on a third and what was going to be a short three that would turn into a fourth down and yet another punt. A fantastic punt by Jeremy Crawshaw pinned the Chiefs at their own two yard line. On their first play, Mahomes fired a deep pass over the middle that was intercepted by Brandon Jones who returned it all the way back to the Chiefs’ five yard line. BRANDON JONES INT pic.twitter.com/ASgl5SAEFX — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 An immediate holding call would push them back to the 15 yard line followed by a near fumble six by Bo Nix. He was fortunate the Chiefs player being out of bounds when he touched the football. Denver was lucky to escape this drive with a field goal attempt. Chiefs 21, Broncos 10. The Chiefs keep the big plays going as Denver’s defense couldn’t tackle the broadside of a barn in this game. A 59-yard catch and run by Travis Kelce setup a first and goal and a GG for Denver. TRAVIS KELCE WITH A HUGE GAIN DENvsKC on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/szJhTx75WG — NFL (@NFL) September 15, 2026 The defense would clamp down from there sacking Mahomes to bring out the field goal unit for the Chiefs. Chiefs 24, Broncos 10. The third quarter would come to an end with Denver finally committing to the ground game – probably too little too late – but picked up a first down and got near midfield. An offensive pass interference call on Troy Franklin sucked all the wind out of that drive and on third and forever the pass rush would get to Bo Nix and knocked the ball loose where Chris Jones would recover.

Look at #70 https://t.co/gKfu5kYfUE pic.twitter.com/vLlxg3BRPs — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) September 15, 2026 Denver’s defense would come up big on the Chiefs’ next drive with Malcolm Roach tipping a third down pass near midfield to force another punt. Starting from their own 12 yard line, Bo Nix and the Broncos offense opened things up with a checkdown to Adam Trautman for a six yard gain and a quick toss outside to Pat Bryant was an easy first down but he took his eye off the ball just long enough to drop it. On third down and four, Nix hit Jaylen Waddle finally but was immediately hit and tackled a yard short of the first down marker. After a short two yard run for the Chiefs, Que Robinson exploded off the edge and nearly sacked Patrick Mahomes who threw the ball into the dirt to avoid the sack. On third and eight, Mahomes was pressured again and somehow picked his way through the line and gained just enough for the first down. That would be all they would get and would be punting a few plays later. A nice punt return by Marvin Mims Jr. finally got the Broncos starting position outside of the 20 yard line for a change. An end around by Troy Franklin picked up five, then an outstanding spin move by RJ Harvey picked up four yards. On third and one, Nix from an empty backfield was immediately pressured and had to scramble to throw it away for yet another punt. Denver’s defense finally buckled. Giving up a third and 10 conversion to Kenneth Walker who then took the ball on the next play for 28 yards up the middle into Broncos’ territory. Kenneth Runner 😤 DENvsKC on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/AoxxMVX0Fh — NFL (@NFL) September 15, 2026 Walker continued to dominate into the two minute warning get the Chiefs just outside the red zone. That drive would be capped by more missed tackles on a short pass to Rashee Rice for a 13-yard touchdown to put Kansas City back out in front. Chiefs 14, Broncos 7. With 90 seconds left, Nix and the Broncos tried to mount a drive. They would go three-and-out instead and give the Chiefs the ball back with time left to do something with it. A holding penalty on the punt pushed them back to their own 10. They wouldn’t get a chunk play and ended up running the clock out.

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Can the Buffalo Bills finally win the AFC?
summary: For the first time this season, the Detroit Lions hit the road, heading to Orchard Park, New York, to face the Buffalo Bills. The Bills have a brand-new home in Highmark Stadium, and what a game to open it, primetime on “Thursday Night Football.“ Detroit is coming off an overtime thriller at home against the […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates fumble recovery during the fourth quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time this season, the Detroit Lions hit the road, heading to Orchard Park, New York, to face the Buffalo Bills. The Bills have a brand-new home in Highmark Stadium, and what a game to open it, primetime on “Thursday Night Football.“ Detroit is coming off an overtime thriller at home against the New Orleans Saints, needing a stop on a two-point conversion to win. Buffalo defeated a tough team in the Houston Texans in a shootout on the road. Both teams are top Super Bowl contender in their conferences, and this game is a rare good game for a Thursday night. This could be a statement win for whoever comes out on top. If Detroit wins, they are moved up the chain as a threat in the NFC. If Buffalo wins, they’ll reinforce the belief around the league that they’re the team to beat in the AFC. Let’s dive in on the Bills and see why they’re the toughest team on the Lions’ schedule this season. Buffalo Bills 2025 Season 12-5 record (2nd in AFC East) 4th in points for, 12th in point allowed Overall DVOA: 8th (4th on offense, 20th on defense) 2025 was a slight step back for the Bills compared to 2024, as they lost to the Denver Broncos in overtime in the AFC Divisional Round. In 2024, they reached the AFC Championship Game, where they lost to the Kansas City Chiefs. The team, once again, failed to live up to the offseason hype, and their inability to reach the Super Bowl despite the talent on the roster cost their head coach, Sean McDermott, his job afterward. Quarterback Josh Allen was coming off his MVP season in 2024, and while his stats were similar to the year before, he was sacked the most times ever in his career: 40. Allen threw for 3,668 yards (11th in the league) with 25 touchdowns and 10 interceptions. His success on the ground continued, as he rushed for 579 yards and 14 touchdowns, averaging 5.2 yards per carry. Speaking of running the ball, Allen got a big help in running back James Cook, who led the NFL in rushing yards with 1,621, a career high. He also found the end zone 12 times and averaged 5.2 yards per carry. His ability to move the rock between the tackles helped take some of the weight off Allen’s shoulders, who had previously had to do all the heavy lifting. It also strengthened their read-option play calling, as teams accounted for Cook more than Allen. For the passing game, Allen struggled to have a dominant top receiver on the team, as Khalil Shakir led the team in catches (72) and yards (719), but only scored four touchdowns. The touchdown leader was tight end Dalton Kincaid, who got 39 catches for 571 yards and five touchdowns. Defensively, the Bills didn’t really stand out in anything particular. EDGE Joey Bosa was one of their top contributors, getting five sacks and leading the league in forced fumbles with five. EDGE Gregory Rousseau led the team in sacks with seven, and safety Cole Bishop led the team in interceptions with three and tackles (85). Buffalo had the 17th-ranked passing defense and 12th-ranked run defense per DVOA, so that side of the ball wasn’t their best, and they relied on their offense to win games. 2026 offseason Key additions: EDGE Bradley Chubb, CB Dee Alford, S Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, WR DJ Moore (trade) Key losses: G David Edwards, EDGE Joey Bosa, EDGE A.J. Epenesa, CB Cam Lewis, HC Sean McDermott 2026 NFL Draft picks Round 2: EDGE TJ Parker Round 2: CB Davison Igbinosun Round 4: OT Jude Bowry Round 4: WR Skyler Bell Round 4: LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr Round 5: S Jalon Kilgore Round 5: DT Zane Durant Round 7: CB Toriano Pride Jr. Round 7: P Tommy Doman Jr. Round 7: G Ar’Maj Reed-Adams Buffalo did more addition than subtraction, starting with the firing of McDermott. With McDermott gone, the Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach. On the defensive line, the Bills needed veteran help and upgrades, and they believe they got some. While losing Epenesa to free agency and Bosa to possible retirement, the Bills signed Chubb to a three-year deal worth $43.5 million. The secondary got some help as well, getting cornerback Dee Alford and former Lions safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson. The Bills’ biggest loss was guard David Edwards, and losing two veterans on the defensive line forces them to shake things up there. Cornerback Cam Lewis was the biggest loss in the secondary for Buffalo. The Bills addressed most of their losses in the 2026 NFL Draft, taking EDGE TJ Parker and cornerback Davison Igbinosun in the second round. The Bills gave up one of their second-round picks for Chicago Bears wide receiver DJ Moore, giving Allen a boost in the passing game and a clear WR1 for the team. The rest of the draft was for depth purposes, snagging multiple offensive linemen and secondary players, while getting a new punter as well. Overall, the Bills roster doesn’t have as much turnover as other teams, with the biggest change at head coach. They believe they are close to winning a Super Bowl, so I get the few moves they made. 2026 season thus far (1-0) Week 1: Defeated Houston Texans, 36-31 Stats: 5th in points scored, 22nd in points allowed Overall DVOA: 4th (2nd on offense, 23rd on defense, 3rd on special teams) What a game to start the year for the Bills; going on the road and defeating the Texans isn’t easy. The Texans’ defense is tough, and the Bills needed to score on their final drive to win and put up 36 points. Allen had a solid game, throwing for 334 yards and two touchdowns, rushing for 23 yards on six carries and scoring two more times. Cook was limited most of the game, rushing for 57 yards, averaging 4.4 yards per carry, and had three catches for 12 yards. Allen didn’t take long to find success with his new weapon in Moore, as he finished with five catches for 100 yards and a touchdown. Kincaid finished as the leading receiver with five catches for 130 yards, and wide receiver Joshua Palmer found the end zone on his only catch for 34 yards. Defensively, the Bills had a rough day in slowing down the Texans offense, allowing quarterback C.J. Stroud to throw for 274 yards and two touchdowns. While Stroud played well, former Lions running back David Montgomery led the charge, rushing for 60 yards and two touchdowns while also catching three passes for 19 yards and a touchdown. If the Texans needed to score, they gave the ball to Montgomery. The Bills forced two fumbles and recovered both; one turned into a field goal early in the game, and the last came on the final drive, leading to the Bills kneeling it out. Rousseau finished with two sacks, and both fumbles were caused by him, making him the most impactful player on the defense on Sunday. If not for his big day, the Bills might have lost the game. Injury notes Key players ruled out : None Key players to monitor : DT T.J. Sanders (knee), RB Ty Johnson (hamstring) Injuries haven’t really affected the Bills much at the start of the year. Defensive tackle T.J. Sanders and running back Ty Johnson missed Week 1, but both could potentially play in Week 2 (both listed as limited on Monday). Johnson is dealing with a hamstring injury, but it appears the team held him out to get him ready for Week 2. Sanders is dealing with a knee injury after popping up on the injury report late last week, and Brady downplayed the severity of the injury, saying he missed last week as a precaution. Biggest strength: Quarterback Facing off against a former MVP in Allen, it’s hard not to see him as the team’s biggest strength. The offense runs through Allen overall, and without him, this team wouldn’t be the same. Allen isn’t your typical dual-threat quarterback; the man acts like a bulldozer while running with the football. Allen isn’t afraid of contact like most quarterbacks, and his agility is…
author: Brandon Knapp

title: Lions vs. Saints Song of the Game: ‘Paradise by the dashboard light’ by Meat Loaf
summary: The rush to judgment in the NFL after Week 1 is maddening. We enter the season fully aware that September football is ugly, and Week 1 lies. Yet the dizzying speed, emotion, and overall cacophony of the NFL’s return creates monsters of us all. FIRE THIS GUY! THAT QUARTERBACK SUCKS! I TOLD YOU THEY WERE […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions celebrates 31-30 win against the New Orleans Saints with Chuck Clark #36 after the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The rush to judgment in the NFL after Week 1 is maddening. We enter the season fully aware that September football is ugly, and Week 1 lies. Yet the dizzying speed, emotion, and overall cacophony of the NFL’s return creates monsters of us all. FIRE THIS GUY! THAT QUARTERBACK SUCKS! I TOLD YOU THEY WERE GOING TO BE TERRIBLE THIS YEAR! The Detroit Lions eked out a win over the New Orleans Saints, and no matter what your expectations for the team were in 2026, this game confirmed those greatest fears and/or highest expectations. The first half proves the Lions, when firing on all cylinders, are capable of blowing out anyone. Or the second half definitively shows Kelvin Sheppard is a fraud, the secondary stinks, and the Lions’ Super Bowl window is closed. Y’all, can we just sleep on it? Detroit Lions Week 1 Song of the Game: “Paradise By The Dashboard Light” by Meat Loaf Yes, “Song of the Game” is back due to popular demand me just wanting to do it again and bring some fun back to the site. If you weren’t around or don’t remember, Song of the Game is exactly what it sounds like: a song that attempts to capture the essence of the Lions’ game. We talk about it here, do it weekly, and then we have a crazy, disjointed playlist by the end of the season. If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016 , 2017 , 2018 , 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 . And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here . It’s only appropriate that the first song to kick off this playlist is one that matches the Lions’ season opener in length. Meat Loaf’s most iconic duet stretches nearly eight-and-a-half minutes, taking the listener through a journey of love, thrills, painful indecisiveness, and regret. Yeah, that sounds about right. Now, I’m going to admit right here that this song is overtly sexual, and it’s going to make for some awkward metaphors. So buckle up. This one isn’t for the faint of hearts. We’re glowing like the metal on the edge of a knife Glowing like the metal on the edge of a knife The Lions’ 2026 season got off to a somewhat strong start. After shaking off a three-and-out, the offense put together an impressive 13-play, 89-yard drive. Jahmyr Gibbs had gains of 11, 21, and 11 yards before eventually walking in untouched for the season’s first score. The rushing lanes were occasionally gaping, the blocking schemes were complicated, and the offensive line—despite losing Christian Mahogany halfway through the drive—was humming. Oh, baby, we were cookin’. After Meat Loaf and Ellen Foley spend the first 3:30 glam rocking to each other about the sex their characters are about to have, the song kicks in a funky beat and a faux radio call of a baseball game is laid over the track. It’s about as blatant a sex metaphor as you can get, as the not-so-convincing radio announcer describes a series of plays in which the runner crosses each base and nears home. He’s taking a pretty big lead out there Almost daring him to try and pick him off The Lions were inching closer and closer to a decisive Week 1 win. Derrick Barnes, interception. Gibbs, touchdown. Roger McCreary, sack fumble. Amon-Ra St. Brown, touchdown. Ford Field was feeling it, Lions fans were in awe of the team’s defense finally coming together with a marriage of pass rush and coverage. It was starting to feel like Detroit’s offseason plan was coming together perfectly. Stop right there Just before we find out whether this “base runner” is “safe at home,” Foley screams out to stop everything. The song comes to a screeching halt. Before the baseball player is ready to “consummate” his trip around the bases, she begs for long-term commitment and faith. And just like the Lions failed to seal the deal cleanly, Meat Loaf struggled to find an answer. I gotta know right now, before we go any further Do you love me? Will you love me forever? Baby, baby, let me sleep on it Well, let me sleep on it I’ll give you an answer in the morning As with every NFL fanbase after every game, the noise following the Lions’ 31-30 win has been loud and exaggerated. The doubters now have definitive proof the Lions are doomed. The endlessly faithful point to the first half as irrefutable evidence everything is going to be fine once things settle in. Me, I’m not so sure. I’m not ready to give an answer. There were promising developments in the run game, offensive line, and pass rush. But there were troubling, ominous signs in the secondary, defensive game plan, and offensive inconsistency. Everyone is in a rush to find out answers and come to undeniable conclusions. Why can’t anyone just admit: we still don’t know. We need more time. Let’s sleep on it. Meat Loaf’s marathon of a song ends in tragedy. The male character expresses grief, regret, and sorrow for those exciting days. He’s stuck in a relationship bonded by carnal pleasure instead of true love. He’s tormented by his past, hasty choices and just wants it all to end. Unlike the narrator, though, the Lions have a chance to quickly put the past behind them. Thursday is a new opportunity to recapture that glowing edge of a knife and find true success—not just fleeting sparks. You can follow along with this year’s playlist with this direct link to Spotify , or the embedded player below.

title: Film study: How Drew Petzing helped Detroit Lions’ recapture their run game vs. Saints
summary: If the Detroit Lions want to reestablish themselves as Super Bowl contenders, improving the run game has to be at the top of the priority list. Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints was a strong start. Throughout the season, I plan on writing these film studies to breakdown different elements of the game. Each […]
full_text: If the Detroit Lions want to reestablish themselves as Super Bowl contenders, improving the run game has to be at the top of the priority list. Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints was a strong start. Throughout the season, I plan on writing these film studies to breakdown different elements of the game. Each week will focus on something different or build on a previous film study. Some weeks it will be the offense, others the defense. It could be a single play in great detail, a critical series, or anything that catches my eye and that I think will be interesting to dig into. This week its the run game that will be put under the microscope. With that said, I want to make one thing clear: I do not have all of the answers . The approach to this series will be one where I am learning, studying the film and growing my own knowledge of the Lions and the ever-evolving game of football. So if you have questions, disagree with something, or have constructive criticisms and corrections, please join the discussion in the comments section. Main takeaways After watching all of the Lions’ run plays from Week 1, there are three main takeaways I came away with: Occasional “key breaker” changeups A detailed approach in making similar schemes look different Isaac TeSlaa is a difference-maker “CRUNCH” key breaker My favorite run play of the game is in this first one featured below. This run scheme is known as a “CRUNCH” concept. Fundamentally, the concept involves cross-blocks with roots in trap and belly schemes. This concept, visually shown below, hinges on backside trap blocks (yellow) from the tight end as well as both the left and right guards. The run is designed to hit the strong-side C gap, between right tackle Blake Miller and tight end Brock Wright. Miller (green) kicks out the wide-9 edge defender, while the Wright follows behind and traps the inside 3-technique defensive tackle. This cross-block concept continues down the line as center Juice Scruggs and left tackle Penei Sewell (orange) glide up to the second level. This run scheme creates two advantages worth highlighting. First, the cross-blocks between the right tackle the tight end gives each blocker an advantageous angle for his respective assignments, putting each player in a better position to succeed. Those angles create a natural wall in the C-gap alley, similar to classic belly and trap schemes. Second, linebackers are often given keys to follow pulling guards. This CRUNCH concept is designed to break those keys. On this play, both guards give pull to their left, while the intended run gap is to their right, creating a false read for the linebackers. When you watch the video clip of the play below, keep your eyes on linebackers No. 55 and No. 20. No. 55 immediately points in the direction of the pulling guards and hesitates, while number 20 is off to the races to filling in the direction of the pulling guards. Key breaker plays are a great changeup to have in any good scheme, both for the current game and for future opponents to be cognizant of while game planning. The next play shows a slightly similar action, but in a zone-blocking scheme. Watch right tackle Blake Miller similarly kick out the edge defender, while tight end Sam LaPorta slides inside with a lead fold block into the play-side zone scheme. A critical takeaway here is that the good coaches make the same schemes look different while making different schemes look the same. Drew Petzing gives a small taste of that with those blocking actions above. In the series of plays, its taken to another level. Heavy personnel shell game Throughout Dan Campbell’s tenure as the Lions’ head coach, the team has consistently used six offensive lineman personnel packages, previously featuring Dan Skipper. Now Skipper is wearing a headset, but the heavy personnel packages are here to stay. Petzing called heavy personnel five times in Week 1, each with a different twist. Now, I don’t know the exact verbiage for these plays, but for sake of clarity in showing the differences in each variation, I’ll use some of my own terms to define elements. Play 1 – Heavy Left, Tackle Swap, Power Right The Lions’ first touchdown of the season grabbed plenty of attention as Petzing pulled out a wrinkle by swapping Penei Sewell back to the right side with Blake Miller to the left, while sixth offensive lineman Larry Borum checked in and declared as eligible. The Lions immediately ran right behind the All-Pro with a power concept. Note LaPorta’s strong combination block with Sewell, initiating the double-team before peeling off to block the second-level linebacker allowing Gibbs to walk in untouched. Heavy Left: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the left. Tackle Swap: left and right tackles swap positions. Power Right: run concept. Play 2 – Heavy Right, DUO Right, “tag” Man On the second called play with heavy personnel, the Lions did not line up with any personnel deception. Sewell was in his normal left tackle position, with Miller and Borum to the right. This is where I will be honest, I am not entirely sure what the run concept initially called here was, but my suspicion here is that it was a DUO scheme with a “man” tag based on the defensive alignment. The Saints respond to the heavy personnel with two 2i-techniques in the A gaps. This throws a wrench in traditional DUO concept. DUO typically presents with double-teams of the guard and center against the A-gap defender, with a second double team of the other guard and tackle against the opposite B-gap defender. With both A gaps occupied and neither B gaps occupied, adjustments have to be made. Borum and Miller double the strong-side C-gap defender, while the “man” tag calls for each guard to take a man base block of the 2i-techniques. Center Scruggs immediately releases to the second-level linebacker. Heavy Right: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the right. DUO, “tag” Man: run concept. Play 3 – Heavy Left, Miller Extra, Inside Zone Right Next, a new variation of heavy emerges, with Blake Miller is the “extra” sixth offensive lineman and lining up outside of and next to left tackle Sewell. The Lions also ran this with an unbalanced alignment, putting two tight ends on the Heavy Left side. With all the attention of the tight ends and both starting tackles on the left side, Petzing calls the an inside zone run concept to the weak side with Borum at right tackle. Heavy Left: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the left. Miller Extra: Blake Miller becomes the extra lineman. Inside Zone Right: run concept. Play 4 – Heavy Right, Sewell Extra, DUO Right, “tag” Man The fourth iteration of heavy is a blend of Plays 2 and 3. Heavy Right: six offensive linemen, with the sixth lined up to the right. Sewell Extra: Penei Sewell becomes the extra lineman. DUO, “tag” Man: run concept. Play 5 – Heavy Left, Tackle Swap, Power Right Same as Play 1, and almost another Gibbs touchdown. A few key notes here. On all five of the heavy personnel plays, Larry Borum declared as the eligible receiver, regardless of the various alignments. Given that the Lions varied how they aligned all three tackles, it is not hard to image how difficult this could be for a defense to track. Who is eligible? Where is the eligible receiver aligned? Where is the strength? It’s a game of Three-Card Monte, but with Sewell, Miller, and Borum. Isaac TeSlaa shoutout The last play of this film study is a quick shoutout to the wide receivers and their role in the run game, particularly Isaac TeSlaa. While TeSlaa was limited to zero receptions on a single target, he was still a difference-maker in the game. This outside zone toss sweep only works because TeSlaa down-blocks on edge defender Tyree Wilson. TeSlaa strains and maintains his block until Gibbs rounds the corner. Despite finishing the play on his tail, TeSlaa will earn the respect of his teammates and coaching staff for doing the dirty work.

title: Discussion: What was the biggest surprise from the Detroit Lions’ Week 1 win?
summary: Week 1 in the NFL is thrilling for so many reasons. For one, it’s just the return of football, the passion of millions of people around the world. But for a league with the longest offseason, it’s also the culmination of months and months of work from each team’s front office. Every free agent signing, […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: Detroit Lions guard Tate Ratledge (69), Detroit Lions guard Juice Scruggs (70), and Detroit Lions guard Ben Bartch (78) block during a play during a regular season NFL football game between the New Orleans Saints and the Detroit Lions on September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Week 1 in the NFL is thrilling for so many reasons. For one, it’s just the return of football, the passion of millions of people around the world. But for a league with the longest offseason, it’s also the culmination of months and months of work from each team’s front office. Every free agent signing, waiver wire claim, draft pick, undrafted free agent signing—it all comes together to paint a picture when the teams finally take the field. I’ve likened it before to Christmas morning. After seeing these gifts under the tree for months, we finally get to unwrap it and see what we’ve got. Since early January, we’ve all outlined how we would’ve approached the offseason, criticized and/or praised every move Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes opted to make, and it was all just educated guessing. On Sunday night, we finally had a data point that matters. Was Holmes’ plan the best to set the Lions up for current and future success? We got a taste in their 31-30 victory of the New Orleans Saints. Some things went as expected, others most certainly did not. So today’s Question of the Day is: What was the biggest surprise from the Lions’ Week 1 win over the Saints? My answer: I’m going to stick with the positive here, because—quite frankly—most of the negative things from Sunday’s game were somewhat expected. The secondary struggled, the defense gave up more explosive plays, and the offense looked like a product that was still putting pieces together. Perhaps the biggest negative shock was the rough day from Jameson Williams, particularly after a strong training camp. But the biggest surprise to me was just how effective the Lions’ running game was. I thought it was fully reasonable and expected for the offensive line to take some time to come together. With Cade Mays’ injury, a left guard battle that never really got off the ground, and a rookie right tackle, everything was set up for some early chemistry issues. And when Ben Bartch, who barely got any first-team work in training camp, had to step in for an injured Christian Mahogany in the first quarter, I only expected more trouble. Instead, we saw the Lions post a rushing success rate better than they averaged during Ben Johnson’s best years in Detroit: Per NFL Pro stats: Lions rushing attack success rate by year: 2024: 44.9% (7th) 2025: 40.7% (21st) 2026 (1 game); 51.5% (2nd) This is your biggest reason for optimism this Monday morning. — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) September 14, 2026 Through Week 1, the Lions rank eighth in PFF’s team run blocking grade (69.7), fifth in adjusted line yards (5.16), and third in yards before contact (73). Those are all serious indicator that the Lions were moving people in the run game. I credit the players themselves for creating a cohesive unit through some early adversity. Certainly offensive line coach Hank Fraley deserves some credit. And new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, who has been widely praised specifically for his scheme in the run game, clearly put his players in the best position to succeed. While the overall offensive performance was inconsistent, and there are legitimate questions to have about Petzing’s play calling, I was extremely encouraged and somewhat surprised that Detroit’s running game appears to be back—especially against a Saints team that ranked eighth in run defense DVOA, second in run defense EPA, and ninth in success rate allowed last season. What was your biggest surprise from Lions vs. Saints? Share your thoughts in the comment section below by joining our community for free! Join the conversation! title: Lions OT Blake Miller ‘optimistic’ about playing despite knee injury
summary: Detroit Lions first-round pick Blake Miller gained a reputation at Clemson for being an iron man. In three years in college, he didn’t miss a single game, starting 54 consecutive contests. When the Lions’ injury report dropped on Monday, it appeared Miller’s NFL streak could be broken after just one game. With only a walkthrough […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions offensive tackle Blake Miller (76) during pregame warmups before their game against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Detroit Lions first-round pick Blake Miller gained a reputation at Clemson for being an iron man. In three years in college, he didn’t miss a single game, starting 54 consecutive contests. When the Lions’ injury report dropped on Monday, it appeared Miller’s NFL streak could be broken after just one game. With only a walkthrough practice, Miller was estimated as a non-participant with a knee injury. And with Detroit on a short week—scheduled to play the Bills on the road this Thursday—it could be too quick of a turnaround to make the field. However, the rookie right tackle spoke with the media after practice and sounded more optimistic about his chances of playing due to progress already made on Monday. “I’m doing everything I humanly can to get my body feeling the best it can feel. Even with the progress just today that I’ve made, I’m happy, and I’m optimistic,” Miller said. Lions coach Dan Campbell said it was possible Miller could play vs. the Bills, but he was a little more cautious in his optimism. “It’s really tough to say. We’re going to know a lot more tomorrow,” Campbell said. “I mean, we really will. It’s really hard to say.” Miller didn’t point to a single play or moment in the game in which he suffered the injury. He noted, rather, that there was a moment on the sidelines where something felt “weird,” and when the adrenaline wore off after he had gone home, he started to feel it more. So Miller was proactive about it. He came in “as early as I could” to start working on the rehab and “nip this in the bud.” If Miller can’t go, the Lions do have veteran Larry Borom to step into the role. Borom has 38 starts in his five-year NFL career, including 11 starts last year for the Dolphins. Elsewhere, it sounds like it’s less likely that starting left guard Christian Mahogany will play this week. Campbell acknowledged that his injury should not be considered serious or long-term, but his chances of playing are worse than Miller’s. “I don’t think this is something serious long-term, but it could be tough to get him ready for Thursday,” Campbell said. In Mahogany’s place, the Lions played Ben Bartch for over three quarters on Sunday. Campbell said the veteran guard needed to knock off some rust against the Saints, but he’s confident in him moving forward. “I thought there was some real good and there was some that wasn’t so good. Just inconsistent, a little rusty, which I wouldn’t say was that abnormal,” Campbell said. “I mean, he got a few reps, he got that last week, and so he’s only going to be better as we keep going here. He’s played; he’s a veteran in this league, and the good was really good, and I anticipate that’s what we’re going to see a lot more of moving forward.”

title: Detroit Lions RB Isiah Pacheco has surgery, will miss ‘significant’ time
summary: Isiah Pacheco isn’t going to be in the Detroit Lions lineup anytime soon. While he’s required to miss three more games after the team put him on injured reserve to start the season, Lions coach Dan Campbell made it sound like his absence will extend much longer. On Monday, Campbell revealed that Pacheco’s back injury […]
full_text: Detroit Lions running back Isiah Pacheco (10) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Isiah Pacheco isn’t going to be in the Detroit Lions lineup anytime soon. While he’s required to miss three more games after the team put him on injured reserve to start the season, Lions coach Dan Campbell made it sound like his absence will extend much longer. On Monday, Campbell revealed that Pacheco’s back injury required surgery. “It’s going to be a while,” Campbell said. “Yeah, it’s going to be a while. I mean, I really can’t (provide a timeline). It’s going to be a significant amount of time, though.” NFL reporter Ian Rapoport gave a more substantive update, noting that Pacheco could be targeting a December return . “Isiah Pacheco had surgery to remove a body that was pressing on a nerve in his back, source said. It’s a 12 week recovery with a chance he’s back by early in December,” Rapoport tweeted. This offseason, the Lions signed Pacheco to a one-year, $1.81 million contract in the hopes he could take over the RB2 role following the trade of David Montgomery. With Jahmyr Gibbs taking over a bigger role, Detroit obviously put less investment in the backup position. On Sunday, the Lions gave the backup job to Sione Vaki, who received his first significant action on offense since entering the league in 2024. Vaki only had three touches in the game—two rushes for 7 yards and one catch for 10. But it was his pass protection struggles that stood out the most, including a play in which he got in Penei Sewell’s way, leading to a pressure and quarterback hit. “He was inconsistent,” Campbell said. “There were some things in there that he’s got to be better at. I know the one that everyone’s talking about. I know that was — can’t do that, he knows that, and we’ve got to get him cleaned up. And so it was inconsistent, but he did have some reps in there that were good. He had a couple of carries that I thought were pretty good. He got a ball on a checkdown that wasn’t bad. We’ve just gotta tighten this stuff up with him a little bit, because we’re going to need to be able to use him. That’s the bottom line: he and (Jacob) Saylors.” It will be interesting to see how the Lions handle that backup role moving forward. Campbell insisted after Sunday’s win over the New Orleans Saints that he was unbothered by having Gibbs set a career high in rushing attempts (29) and touches (34) . “You know what I like? Winning the game, man, and we were going to win this game. That guy’s our hot hand,” Campbell said. “Ultimately, do I want to set records with how many carries? No, that’s not something I want to do. When you look at a guy, and you feel like, ‘Alright, man.’ He’s in good shape. I mean, he had a really good camp, and he is in phenomenal shape. He’s in the best shape I’ve seen since he’s been here. Now that doesn’t mean we’re not going to monitor, and we’re going to keep an eye on this guy because we understand that too, but we did what we had to do today.”
