title: The Lions found a way to win, but the time to clean things up is overdue
summary: What happened at Ford Field on Sunday felt far too messy for a team with the kind of expectations they have for themselves. After a first half where the Detroit Lions scored just seven points and punted the ball four times, they found themselves up three scores in a hurry. A strip-sack fumble forced by […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions reacts during the first quarter against the New Orleans Saints of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images What happened at Ford Field on Sunday felt far too messy for a team with the kind of expectations they have for themselves. After a first half where the Detroit Lions scored just seven points and punted the ball four times, they found themselves up three scores in a hurry. A strip-sack fumble forced by a blitzing Roger McCreary and recovered by DJ Wonnum felt like a fever dream only Brad Holmes could have conjured. Things were suddenly, and finally, clicking into place for a Lions team that was a full-touchdown favorite over the New Orleans Saints. Everything felt back on track. And then, somehow, the Lions nearly gave it all back. Maybe that’s the most fitting way to describe Sunday: Detroit found a way to win, but it also found a whole lot of reasons to wonder how much it actually learned from last season. As soon as it felt like everything was coming together, things started to unravel. 47 yards to Chris Olave, and the Saints flip the field. A few plays later, they score their first points of the afternoon. No worries, the Lions offense is up and off the ground, they’ll… promptly go three-and-out for the third time. Jack Fox’s punt and the Lions punt coverage leaves something to be desired, and the Saints are already near midfield. But you know what, that Lions defense, it had pitched a shutout in the first half. They recorded a sack, an interception, and held the Saints to fewer than 115 total net yards— the first time Detroit had done that since December of 2015 —so put ‘em out there and… watch New Orleans score seven plays later—eight if you remember the 21-yard defensive pass interference penalty on Rock Ya-Sin. Alright, turd quarter flushed, the Lions offense is their bread and butter, time to… fail to convert their second third-and-short on the day, this time after Kool-Aid McKinstry broke up a pass to Amon-Ra St. Brown. Fox, from the Lions’ 45-yard line, punts the ball 31 yards to the 24-yard line of New Orleans. A methodical 11-play, 66-yard drive turns into a field goal and the Saints find themselves down just four points, 21-17, with a lot of football still to be played. The Lions were not playing complementary football. Offense, defense, special teams, it was all bad—like nothing good—for nearly 16 minutes of football on Sunday. That’s all it took for the game to get flipped on its head. Seeing things break down the way they did over that stretch is interesting when you hear Dan Campbell’s post-game speech from the locker room : “We did not play our cleanest, but when we had to have it, all three phases—it’s what we talked about last night, man—when we needed somebody to pull us back out of the water—our head’s underwater—we did that. In all three phases, and your teammates, one by one. That was the difference, men.” Campbell is right that the Lions found a way to win, but “finding a way to win” and “playing complementary football” aren’t necessarily the same thing—and over the course of 16 minutes Sunday, the Lions almost let it slip away. According to Campbell’s summarization, the Lions “had” to have it to start the second half, and when they forced an interception, only up 7-0, and the offense turned it into a touchdown. When the defense forced a fumble on the Saints’ very next drive, the Lions’ offense puts them up by 21. All of that only lasted for about six minutes of actual game time, but in that moment of football harmony, you couldn’t have imagined New Orleans felt anything other than completely demoralized. But they weren’t. Tyler Shough looked poised beyond his starts, and Kellen Moore proceeded to dial up explosive play after explosive play. We had seen this movie before last year in Detroit, but talked ourselves into a more aggressive defense, one more committed to the pass rush, would cover up for a secondary under repair. Detroit finished Week 1 as the fourth-fastest team to pressure—2.40 seconds—across 61 pass plays, a marked improvement from finishing last year 30th at 2.86 seconds, so where does that leave us? Brian Branch is still at least a month away from returning, who knows what the future holds for Kerby Joseph, and Ennis Rakestraw was presumably a healthy inactive. “The biggest thing right now, guys, is you find a way to get the win,” Campbell continued to say in the locker room after the game. “It’s Week 1 and then you clean [expletive] up, because it feels a hell of a lot better than the loss to have to clean it up. That’s the thing: we found a way to win, we will clean this up, and there’s a lot to clean up.” That’s where Campbell’s postgame message could be misconstrued. Most people will hear “a lot to clean up” and immediately think that’s commentary about the defense, but it’s not contained to just that side of the ball. Outside of the Lions’ two short-field touchdown drives to begin the third quarter, their offense was largely unable to sustain itself. They were an abysmal 5-of-13 on third down, even worse than their 38.7% conversion rate a year ago that had them finish 19th in the NFL. Nine of the Lions’ 14 drives lasted five plays or fewer—one of those was a three-play touchdown drive—but that is just not part of the formula for complementary football. Where Campbell was spot on in his assessment of Sunday’s game was the work the Lions have ahead of them, the messes on both sides of the ball they’ll need to clean up in hurry. They can’t afford to bring the baggage of this game against the Saints with them on the plane to Buffalo before their Thursday night showdown with the Bills. This iteration of the Lions once again proved they know how to handle adversity, but they only need a mirror to see who put themselves in that position, coaches and players included. Navigating adversity is a strength and a skill this team has honed over the years. Needing to “find a way” because all three phases stopped functioning is a problem. Detroit has just four days to figure out which one Sunday was.
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Detroit Lions stock report: 13 risers, 7 fallers vs. Saints
summary: After a long Detroit Lions offseason—and finding themselves on the wrong end of a 24-3 second-half run—the Lions scraped by the skin of their teeth thanks to a missed Daniel Carlson 62-yard field goal attempt at the end of regulation and defending a failed two-point conversion attempt in a 31-30 overtime victory. Not exactly how […]
full_text: After a long Detroit Lions offseason—and finding themselves on the wrong end of a 24-3 second-half run—the Lions scraped by the skin of their teeth thanks to a missed Daniel Carlson 62-yard field goal attempt at the end of regulation and defending a failed two-point conversion attempt in a 31-30 overtime victory. Not exactly how it was scripted. It was mostly a lethargic first half offensively, but after taking a 21-0 lead midway through the third quarter, there was almost a feeling that the Lions might step on the accelerator and floor it past the Saints. That made the dramatic, anxiety-ridden, thrilling finish feel a little disappointing. But survive and advance as far as Week 1 goes. It’s an oddball NFL slate that often isn’t an accurate indicator of what’s to come. Just last year, the eventual Super Bowl champion Seahawks lost 17-13 and started the season 0-2, the eventual first-overall-pick Las Vegas Raiders beat the eventual AFC champion New England Patriots, and J.J. McCarthy was NFC Offensive Player of the Week. Dan Campbell was level-headed and appreciative of the victory, showing little concern both in the locker room and during his postgame press conference. This stock report will carry a similar non-overreactionary approach. Stock up: Jahmyr Gibbs, RB Gibbs got his contract extension, and in his new “bell-cow” role, accounted for 50.4% of the Lions’ 369 total yards and 57.7% of their 26 first downs. His 183 total yards are the fourth-most by a Detroit Lions player in a season opener in franchise history. On a day when the Lions’ offense went through some lulls and wasn’t quite firing on all cylinders, Gibbs willed them down the field and into the end zone. While the offensive line and play design deserve some credit for the run game, it was truly a masterful display from Gibbs, with his vision, patience, pacing, and acceleration all fully on display to the tune of seven runs of 10-plus yards, 12 missed tackles forced, and 82 yards after contact. The team rode him when they needed it most, accounting for 35 yards on their final overtime touchdown drive. For a Saints defense that finished top-10 in the second half of last season in a number of run defense metrics, the Lions rushing attack looked more comfortable and consistent than last season. The lone negative was a fumble that was overturned on replay review, but Gibbs remains fully primed for a career season as a strong Offensive Player of the Year contender. Stock up: Derrick Barnes, LB Barnes, taking on the role of the team’s second linebacker in his sixth season, played a career-high 77 snaps while successfully filling the shoes of his long-time good friend Alex Anzalone. Barnes stepped up and was flying around like a bat out of hell in the second half and overtime. He did so while evolving beyond the SAM linebacker role on the line of scrimmage in five-down fronts that he had become accustomed to over the last two seasons, instead playing the majority of his snaps as an off-ball, stand-up linebacker next to Jack Campbell. Barnes kicked off his playmaking by jumping the route and intercepting Tyler Shough’s pass intended for Noah Fant on the first play of the Saints’ opening drive of the second half. On the next drive, he cleaned up Shough for a sack. Later, he brought down Travis Etienne at the line of scrimmage, corralled Shough on a third-down scramble, shut the door on another drive by bringing Etienne down on a third-down red-zone reception to force a field goal, and forced an incompletion along the side of the end zone in overtime. Finally, Barnes even stepped up to take away Shough’s first-read on the two-point conversion. Overall, Barnes stuffed the stat sheet with six tackles, two quarterback pressures, a sack, an interception, a pass breakup, and three run stops. He looked like the best version of himself—the player the Lions envisioned when they signed him to an extension last offseason and entrusted him with added responsibility while confidently moving on from Anzalone. Stock down: Jameson Williams, WR Williams might have had the most apparent and unexpected poor performance of the day. He had one deep pass over the middle—his original bread and butter—that was dropped, another intermediate shot over the middle that was potentially tipped by the defender and couldn’t be hauled in, and he bobbled a reverse that appeared well-designed for him to jettison his way into an explosive gain, if not a touchdown. Williams also had two other third-down targets on routes near the sideline that were almost within reach. He could’ve created more separation, the throws could’ve been better placed, or both, but Williams and Jared Goff simply couldn’t connect, with both plays resulting in punts. Williams and Goff just couldn’t get on the same page for most of the afternoon, despite Drew Petzing at least appearing to have a good idea of how to play to Williams’ strengths. A runway route at some point would’ve been nice, but the yards-after-catch opportunities just weren’t as available. Williams started the first two months of last season, outside of Week 2 against Chicago, with fairly cold and disappointing performances. There’s plenty of evidence to believe that won’t be the case again, but Sunday was still surprising after how impressive Williams looked throughout training camp, when he appeared to be the most polished and dominant version of himself. To his credit, Williams responded with an unbelievably clutch 22-yard catch on a corner route in overtime, setting up the offense at the 5-yard line. It was Goff’s only completion of the day on a pass traveling 10-plus air yards downfield and outside the numbers. Williams finished strong when the Lions needed him most, and hopefully that play is something to build on after he managed just 23 receiving yards on eight targets in regulation. Stock up: Aidan Hutchinson, DE While his presence wasn’t always felt, one of the qualities needed most from an elite-level pass rusher is getting home when his team needs him most, and Aidan Hutchinson rang the bell there against the Saints. His undressing of left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. with a timely chop-spin move to sack Tyler Shough and knock the Saints out of field goal range on their final drive of the second quarter was colossal. So was taking advantage of a one-on-one matchup against running back Kendre Miller for his second sack late in the fourth quarter when Detroit desperately needed it. It took Hutchinson almost two full quarters to really get going, but his impact extended beyond the sacks. He beat right tackle Taliese Fuaga for a pressure that led to Derrick Barnes’ sack, had another clean spin-move win against Fuaga in the red zone before the Saints’ first touchdown on a quick slant, bull-rushed his way into the pocket to force a checkdown to Travis Etienne, and blasted Shough on a twist during the Saints’ late fourth-quarter 42-yard completion to Chris Olave. Too many defensive snaps played is going to be a theme for a handful of Lions defenders from this game, but all things considered, Hutchinson playing 83.3% of the snaps (75 of 90) is an improvement from the workload he carried in the majority of his games over the last few seasons. Stock neutral: D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Avonte Maddox, and Chuck Clark, starting secondary Tyler Shough having over 60 dropbacks is going to leave some bad plays on tape for any secondary. So will playing 90 total defensive snaps—the most of the Dan Campbell era—while deploying a top-10 man coverage rate and blitz rate in Week 1. That approach also contributed to Shough having the second-fastest time to throw (2.44 seconds) of the week, especially as the Saints’ offense cranked up the pace in the second half. Add in the cornerbacks not always having safety help over the top, and this gray-beard, veteran-laden defensive back group understandably had its share of ups and downs. Each player had plenty of highlights early before the lowlights began to pile…

title: Detroit Lions Week 1 snap counts: Several defensive rotations unveiled
summary: The Detroit Lions needed overtime to secure a 31-30 win over the New Orleans Saints in Week 1, but a win is a win in September as teams adjust to a new season. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) is sacked by Detroit Lions defensive tackle Alim McNeill (54) during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions needed overtime to secure a 31-30 win over the New Orleans Saints in Week 1, but a win is a win in September as teams adjust to a new season. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can glean moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 77 snaps (100%) Josh Dobbs: Did not play (DNP) With the Lions’ run game clicking, Goff had an average day at the office on Sunday, though the Saints’ fast tempo sped up the game and created more opportunities for both offenses. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 57 (74%) Sione Vaki: 22 (29%) — 24 special teams (71%) Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 24 (71%) We were told Gibbs would be the workhorse back, and he certainly was in the opener, carrying the ball a league-leading 29 times and rushing for a league-leading 156 yards. He also added five receptions for another 30 yards for good measure. Despite Gibbs touching the ball a ton, he was still on the field only 74% of the time, leaving 20 opportunities for Vaki and two snaps when they were on the field simultaneously. It was an up-and-down day for Vaki’s first run as RB2, showing well in pass protection and as a receiver, but in the locker room after the game, he was left frustrated with the mistakes he made. When I asked him to point out the parts of his game he was happy with, he had this to say: “To be honest, I couldn’t tell you. I feel like there’s nothing but improvement that needs to happen.” It’s worth noting that, according to PFF, 20 of Vaki’s 22 reps came on passing downs, which points to coaches’ confidence in his ability to hold up in one of the more critical components of a running back’s responsibilities. Wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown: 69 (90%) Jameson Williams: 65 (84%) Isaac TeSlaa: 52 (68%) Tay Martin: 0 (0%) — 24 (71%) Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 11 (32%) The Lions rolled with just three receivers on offense, with Martin and Kennedy taking on starting roles on special teams. Martin was fantastic as a gunner on punts and on kickoff coverage, securing a career-high three special teams tackles. “I just wanted to make sure I made Dan (Campbell) right for believing in me,” Martin said of using special teams to make the active roster. “I’ve been waiting on this chance my whole life, to go out there on the 53-man roster and make some plays.” Tight end Sam LaPorta: 62 (81%) Brock Wright: 39 (51%) — 11 (32%) Tyler Conklin: 10 (13%) Jackson Meeks: 0 (0%) — 18 (53%) No real surprises here, as the Lions were expected to utilize all three of their top tight ends, and the distribution of snaps is very similar to what we’ve seen in previous years. Offensive line LT Penei Sewell: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) C Juice Scruggs: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) RG Tate Ratledge: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) RT Blake Miller: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%) G Ben Bartch: 66 (86%) — 5 (15%) LG Christian Mahogany: 11 (14%) OT Larry Borom: 9 (12%) — 5 (15%) G/T Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 5 (15%) Mahogany got the start, but an awkward injury on the 11th offensive play cost him the rest of the game. The initial scan of his knee was negative, and Mahogany was in good spirits in the locker room , suggesting it’s not a long-term injury, but on a short week, the Lions may continue to lean on Bartch to start at left guard. Borom found the field nine times in Jumbo sets, and offensive coordinator Drew Petzing was very creative in his usage, lining him up as a tight end and at left tackle. That gave the Lions the opportunity to move Sewell all over the formation, create mismatches in the run game, and was a catalyst in both of Gibbs’ rushing touchdowns. Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 83 (92%) — 5 (15%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 47 (52%) — 5 (15%) DT Tyleik Williams: 35 (39%) — 5 (15%) DL Ben Stille: 9 (10%) 3T Mekhi Wingo — INACTIVE McNeill seeing the field on 92% of defensive snaps is borderline insane for a big man. So why do it? His positional versatility and ability to impact the game from multiple spots is a massive advantage for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. With the Lions maintaining a double-digit lead for most of the game, the Saints threw the ball often. That situation led the Lions to lean on rookie Gill-Howard more than starter Williams. After the game, he talked with Pride of Detroit about his impact on the game: “I think I need to pass rush way better. There were times when I was rushing too down the middle, or I got stuck in a gap—I had a few decent rushes for sure, but I felt like the area I took a step (forward) was in the run game. I didn’t get moved (off the ball) at all.” Gill-Howard’s assessment is backed up by PFF, who assigned him a 76.8 grade for his run defense, the second-highest on the team in Week 1. EDGE EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 75 (83%) Rush End DJ Wonnum: 69 (77%) — 5 (15%) EDGE Derrick Moore: 18 (20%) Big End Tyler Lacy: 15 (17%) Rush End Eric O’Neill: 4 (4%) — 17 (50%) Big End Ahmed Hassanein — INACTIVE Like McNeill, Hutchinson played a ridiculous amount of snaps in this game, but it was surely hard to take him off the field when he was so dominant. Not only did Hutchinson secure two sacks, but he leads the NFL in pressures in both PFF (10) and NFL Pro’s (10) metrics. With the Lions electing to play more nickel defense in this game, that meant more Wonnum, and he rewarded Sheppard with his performance, forcing six pressures (tied for seventh best in the NFL, per NFL Pro) and a couple of pass breakups at the line of scrimmage. O’Neill, who was active over Hassanein, showed why with his special teams performance, securing two special teams tackles at critical moments. Linebacker MIKE Jack Campbell: 90 (100%) — 5 (15%) SAM Derrick Barnes: 77 (86%) — 13 (38%) WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 20 (22%) — 19 (56%) WILL Devin White: 18 (20%) SAM Trevor Nowaske: 8 (9%) — 29 (85%) MIKE Joe Bachie: 0 (0%) — 18 (53%) MIKE Jimmy Rolder — INACTIVE While Campbell played every down on defense, the rest of the linebackers were used more situationally, with Barnes getting the most opportunities because of his versatility—and he didn’t disappoint. Barnes secured an interception, was credited with three run stops and two pressures (per PFF), while also adding a sack for good measure. Rodriguez and White split WILL linebacker duties, each finding the field in situation-specific roles. Nowaske came on for more bulk at the line of scrimmage, while Bachie was relegated to special teams. Cornerback CB D.J. Reed: 89 (99%) CB Rock Ya-Sin: 89 (99%) — 5 (15%) NB/CB Roger McCreary: 39 (43%) — 16 (47%) NB Keith Abney: 25 (28%) — 5 (15%) CB Khalil Dorsey: 0 (0%) — 23 (68%) CB Ennis Rakestraw — INACTIVE Reed and Ya-Sin only missed one rep each on a grueling 90-play afternoon, while McCreary took over the Christian Izien every-down role in the slot with Abney backing him up in obvious passing situations. Overall, the Lions played nickel roughly 70% of defensive downs, and while some of that was adjusting to the Saints throwing the ball, it also reflects what we have seen in training camp. Safet y S Avonte Maddox: 85 (94%) S Thomas Harper: 54 (60%) — 17 (50%) S Chuck Clark: 41 (46%) — 5 (15%) NB/S Christian Izien — INACTIVE One of the interesting wrinkles to come out of this game is how the Lions utilized their safeties. While Maddox and Clark were the clear starters all training camp, coaches alluded to Harper increasing his role and competing for starter-level snaps. We saw Harper start the majority of the time the Lions were in nickel, while Clark appeared to be the preferred option in the Lions’ base defense. This approach looked effective, as each allowed only one reception on two targets, while Clark also secured an…

title: Green Bay Packers News: Matt LaFleur has a lot of problems to navigate
summary: Bad losses tend to put everything in the larger universe of Packers-related takes in free fall for a while, but at a certain point, it feels like even the most outlandish takes aren’t exaggerating anymore. Dating back to last year’s Broncos game, the Packers have collapsed again and again, week after week, and every time […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 28: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers looks on against the Arizona Cardinals in the second half during a preseason game at Lambeau Field on August 28, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bad losses tend to put everything in the larger universe of Packers-related takes in free fall for a while, but at a certain point, it feels like even the most outlandish takes aren’t exaggerating anymore. Dating back to last year’s Broncos game, the Packers have collapsed again and again, week after week, and every time it happens, it feels like we reach a new critical mass of takes. I’ve heard from readers and listeners since Sunday suggesting all manner of causes for the Packers’ trouble, ranging from the implausible (the league told the refs to penalize the Packers as retribution for the hit on Kyler Murray) to the absurd (the Packers lost because Jordan Love has bad body language). But the weirder and more gut-wrenching ways in which the Packers lose, the harder it becomes to dismiss anything. Are the Packers just cosmically unlucky? I mean, even if you think Matt LaFleur is the worst coach in the world, you’d think things would break his way a couple of times in the span of what’s now a six-game losing streak. How many random drops or weird bounces or phantom flags can possibly go against one team in one stretch? All that to say, as exhausting as the wild and wacky and weird takes might be right now, it’s almost impossible to find your way out of the fever swamps, too. Much like the Packers, we’re going to have to ride this out to the bitter end. title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on kicks in Week 1
summary: There was a lot of long snapper discourse during the preseason, mainly centered around the Green Bay Packers’ incumbent Matt Orzech and the challenger Cal Adomitis. This all stemmed from the fact that rookie kicker Trey Smack did not miss a kick in the preseason with Adomitis as his holder. I – a denizen of […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images There was a lot of long snapper discourse during the preseason, mainly centered around the Green Bay Packers’ incumbent Matt Orzech and the challenger Cal Adomitis. This all stemmed from the fact that rookie kicker Trey Smack did not miss a kick in the preseason with Adomitis as his holder. I – a denizen of the internet – saw calls for Orzech to be released. I saw multiple people saying that Orzech was bad, and it led me to a very important question? Is Orzech bad as a long snapper on field goals and extra points? I found I did not know, so I tried to find out. That’s a long intro, but that search led us all here, to a column where we look at the location of snaps on field goals and extra points. Congrats to you, a massive weirdo, who has decided that you are also interested in this. I watched some videos and dug through some books about this and came up with a quadrant. I sketched something up, and I will share that with you now. If you can’t tell, that’s a stick figure in a position of holding for a field goal. I spent entirely too much time on it. I tried to color code the best I could to indicate the good and the bad. The best place for a snap is off the ground, over the place where the snap is to be held. The next best place is off the ground on the body. The ground at the snap point or at the body is worse than those, but still kind of in the green because it gives the holder a chance to get the ball in the vicinity of where the ball is to be placed, but being on the ground is less than ideal. The worst are the areas where the holder has to move his body and put himself off balance. The two zones behind him are bad, and the head/above the head is a disaster area. You don’t want that one. There’s a whole rotation of the ball element to make sure the holder can catch it and easily place it with laces out, but that’s simply a level we’re not tracking here (yet). I will say that all of Orzech’s snaps we’re looking at today were good on that front. Good rotation. With that in mind, how did Orzech do in Week 1? As you can see from my very official numbers, he did well! I looked at all 6 of the field goal/extra point attempts, including the one they ended up wiping off the board with the defensive offsides. All 6 attempts were snapped squarely in the green zone, with 4 of those 6 (66.7%) in the ideal quadrant. There is the matter of the missed extra point. Where did that one hit? That’s the ideal quadrant, right there. Snapped up, above the place where the ball is going to be placed for the hold. For the hold itself, we talked about that a bit in a preseason post . In a situation with no wind, most kickers tend to like the ball held with a slight forward lean, away from the kicker. Looks good on both fronts. I am not an expert in kicking mechanics, so the miss itself is beyond me. What I can say is that the snap-to-hold operations looked good. I have no idea what form this column will take going forward. Will I abandon it because there is limited interest? Maybe! The goal now is to keep writing it weekly, provided it’s something you all actually find some value in. Sound off in the comments, I guess. I’ll be tracking in regardless; how much digital ink I spill on it will likely be up to you. Albums listened to: Nine Inch Nails – With Teeth

title: Packers move WR Bo Melton back up to 53-man roster
summary: The Green Bay Packers have added receiver Bo Melton back to the team’s 53-man active roster after moving him down to the practice squad late last week. Melton was released due to his status as a vested veteran for the purposes of termination pay, but he was called up for Sunday’s action against the Minnesota […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 27: Green Bay Packers cornerback Bo Melton #16 during the first half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Thursday, November 27, 2025 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have added receiver Bo Melton back to the team’s 53-man active roster after moving him down to the practice squad late last week. Melton was released due to his status as a vested veteran for the purposes of termination pay, but he was called up for Sunday’s action against the Minnesota Vikings. Essentially, had Melton been a member of the 53-man roster in Week 1, he would have been able to claim pay for his entire minimum salary for the 2026 season, even if he were released at a future date. Because the Packers didn’t have him on the 53-man roster, his salary is not guaranteed, and he doesn’t have the option to claim termination pay moving forward. Green Bay’s 53-man roster is now full. The Packers also released long snapper Scott Daly from the practice squad, leaving just Matt Orzech at the position (on the 53-man roster). Green Bay was the only team with a long snapper on their practice squad in Week 1. With the promotion of Melton and the release of Daly, Green Bay has two open practice squad spots up for grabs going into Week 2. Generally, the team makes additions to the practice squad after workouts on Tuesday, the Packers’ “off” day during the regular season. Right now, here’s how Green Bay’s practice squad shapes up: QB: Kedon Slovis RB: Pierre Strong Jr. (hamstring injury), Damon Bankston (signed last week) WR: Isaiah Neyor, Chris Hilton Jr. TE: Drake Dabney OL: Josh Gesky, Dalton Cooper, Dillon Wade DL: None ED: Nyjalik Kelly, Arron Mosby LB: Kristian Welch (called up last week due to Ty’Ron Hopper’s injury) CB: Domani Jackson S: Kahlef Hailassie (signed last week) K: Lenny Krieg (international exemption) Last week, the Packers worked out a quarterback, a tight end and two running backs and defensive backs, before ultimately signing a running back and defensive back . — Update: #Packers worked out Eric Johnson and Cam Miller — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) September 14, 2026 The Packers have worked out two players, defensive lineman Eric Johnson II ( a former pre-draft visitor for the team back in 2022 ) and quarterback Cam Miller. Miller was with the Miami Dolphins in camp this past year. Worth noting: Green Bay has had two defensive linemen poached to 53-man rosters in Jaden Crumedy (Houston) and Nazir Stackhouse (Tennessee). They might need an extra body there, even with seven guys (six healthy) on the 53-man roster.

summary: If you missed the Green Bay Packers’ Week 1 loss to the Minnesota Vikings…congrats, actually. The offensive line was very bad. Obviously, a lot of today’s press conference with head coach Matt LaFleur centered around questions about the offensive line, which he mostly chalked up to mental mistakes leading to pass protection busts. When he […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you missed the Green Bay Packers’ Week 1 loss to the Minnesota Vikings…congrats, actually. The offensive line was very bad . Obviously, a lot of today’s press conference with head coach Matt LaFleur centered around questions about the offensive line, which he mostly chalked up to mental mistakes leading to pass protection busts. When he was asked whether teams would try to replicate the Vikings’ blitz-happy blueprint against Green Bay, he said, “I think there’s things that we definitely have to get cleaned up that we’ll see this week.” Both the Lions and Vikings were top 3 in Week 1 in rush/coverage disguise rate, based on pre-snap alignment. pic.twitter.com/3nkiAKsrEC — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 While the New York Jets don’t lean into the blitz as much as Brian Flores’ Vikings (no one does), they are one of the highest blitz-rate teams in the league. This week will give the Packers an opportunity to prove that they’ve learned from Week 1 and improved. If they fail that opportunity, LaFleur might need to call in the National Guard. "We had a few protection busts that absolutely should not and cannot happen." – Matt LaFleur after Jordan Love was sacked 4 times and hit 15x #packers #vikings #nflopener #offensiveline pic.twitter.com/4B5l8OnW3s — Dave Schroeder (@SchroederWBAY) September 14, 2026 When asked if the team could go another direction at guard, with both Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk struggling mightily, if Aaron Banks (knee tendinitis) can’t return to the lineup, LaFleur said that the team could “potentially” look at other options at the position. For whatever it’s worth, the other active linemen available to the Packers on their gameday roster yesterday were Anthony Belton, Jager Burton and John Williams. LaFleur stated that no major injuries came out of Week 1’s action, and confirmed that cornerback Brandon Cisse left the game due to cramps. Cisse’s replacement, Carrington Valentine, was picked on at the end of the game for multiple scores by the Vikings, as they ended the game on a 29-point run.

title: The Packers’ defense got hung out to dry in Week 1
summary: Giving up 39 points in an NFL is a lot. It’s not the number you want to see from your defense at any point in a season, and certainly not in week one, and certainly not against a backup quarterback. But despite that being the number of points that the Green Bay Packers allowed to […]
full_text: Oct 19, 2025; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; NFL referee Shawn Hochuli (83) acknowledges the crowd during the third quarter of the game between the Cleveland Browns and the Miami Dolphins at Huntington Bank Field. Mandatory Credit: Scott Galvin-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Giving up 39 points in an NFL is a lot. It’s not the number you want to see from your defense at any point in a season, and certainly not in week one, and certainly not against a backup quarterback. But despite that being the number of points that the Green Bay Packers allowed to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, that number does not reflect the reality of how the defense actually played. No, this defense got thrown into horrendous situations, particularly throughout the second half, suffering from both awful field position and terrible penalty calls. The latter was particularly an issue on the Vikings’ go-ahead drive in the fourth quarter, but the former was the case the entire second half. Let’s look at each of the Vikings’ scoring drives in this game to illustrate just how badly the defense was let down. First Quarter, Drive #3: FG The Packers scored 10 points on their first two series, with the defense doing an excellent job. They forced a turnover on the second play of the game, then allowed a single first down before forcing a punt on the second. The third drive started at the Vikings’ 30 after a kickoff, and it was on this drive that the defense got its first penalty — an unnecessary roughness call on Javon Bullard for the hit that knocked out Kyler Murray, which came on what would have been a 3rd-down stop. With a fresh set of downs at midfield and Carson Wentz in the game, the Vikings gained just two more first downs, as the Packers held Minnesota to a field goal. Drive totals: 12 plays, 50 net yards (15 via penalty), 3 first downs (1 via penalty), 6:05 TOP Second Quarter, Drive #6: TD The Packers allowed just one first down on the next two series, forcing punts both times, while the offense got a field goal following Bo Melton’s big kickoff return. A Daniel Whelan punt set up the Vikings at their own 15-yard line with a bit more than 5 minutes left in the first half. The drive began with a sack of Wentz by Keisean Nixon and Jonathan Ford, followed by Brenton Cox jumping offsides. A short gain set up a 3rd-and-8, which Wentz converted to Justin Jefferson over the middle as Evan Williams hits him hard in the back as he goes to the ground, drawing another unnecessary roughness call (that’s two, for those counting). Wentz converted another 3rd down near midfield, this time to T.J. Hockenson, before Lukas Van Ness jumped offside and he found Jefferson with a bomb on a free play for a 39-yard touchdown. Drive totals: 7 plays, 65 yards (20 via penalty), 4 first downs, 3:23 TOP Third Quarter, Drive #9: TD Here’s where things start to unravel. Following a Trey Smack field goal to extend the Packers’ lead to 22-10, the kickoff coverage team loses Myles Price, who scampers 59 yards on his return and sets up the Vikings at the Packers’ 28-yard line. Aaron Jones narrowly converts a 3rd-and-1 on the ground and the defense gets a couple of nice plays to set up a 3rd-and-8. But Zaire Franklin gets lost in coverage and Wentz finds Hockenson open up the middle for a 16-yard score. Drive totals: 6 plays, 28 yards, 2 first downs, 3:01 TOP Fourth Quarter, Drive #10: TD This drive is where Packers fans go off the rails, and rightfully so. The defense had three third down stops — one coming on a sack and another with an interception in the end zone — all wiped away by highly questionable penalties from Hochuli and company. Of course, it all starts after Matt LaFleur took a field goal off the board to go for a 4th-and-1 opportunity instead, looking to give the Packers a two-possession lead. Jordan Love’s QB sneak failed and Minnesota took over at their own 17. They picked up an early first down with a 13-yard gain to Josh Oliver, but the drive appeared to be over on the second set of downs. Edgerrin Cooper picks up a sack unblocked on second down then bursts through again for another (split with Devonte Wyatt) on third down, only to see the Vikings bailed out by a holding call on Bullard. That’s third-down save number one. Three plays later, Wentz throws incomplete to Hockenson on 3rd-and-3 near midfield. But wait! Another flag! This time it’s on rookie Chris McClellan for his hit on Wentz as he threw the ball, with Hochuli alleging that McClellan drove the QB into the ground with his body weight. Except that isn’t what happened — McClellan did an excellent job of bracing himself against the turf rather than letting his weight land on Wentz, which was clearly identified on the broadcast and by CBS officiating analyst Gene Steratore. The next play, well, that’s a miss by the defense. Jordan Mason goes 28 yards on a stretch to the left, setting the Vikings up in the red zone. They’d almost certainly have kept the offense on the field on 4th-and-3 near midfield, so maybe that happens regardless. But the third save comes on 3rd-and-5 from the 6, when Evan Williams picks off Wentz in the end zone, only to see a flag thrown on Xavier McKinney for an awful, ticky-tack holding penalty. Aaron Jones then runs wide to the left into the end zone, giving the Vikings a lead they would not relinquish. Drive totals: 9 plays, 83 yards (28 via penalty), 6 first downs (3 via penalty), 6:34 TOP Fourth Quarter, Drive #11: TD Why didn’t they relinquish the lead? Because the Packers’ offense — particularly the line — handed the ball right back to Minnesota. A sack-fumble by Andrew Van Ginkel and his ensuing recovery gave the Vikings the football at the one-yard line. One play, one yard, one touchdown, and suddenly the Packers are down by 10. Making matters worse, the Packers were forced to play with Carrington Valentine on the field in goal line due to Brandon Cisse leaving the game with cramps. Surely they’d have rather kept Cisse on the field in that situation, but it’s just one more negative card dealt to them in an unfortunate spot. Drive totals: 1 play, 1 yard, 1 first down, 0:04 TOP Fourth Quarter, Drive #12: TD The final score came after more of the same. With Jordan Love being constantly harassed, a rushed, tipped pass landed in the hands of cornerback James Pierre and Minnesota took over at the 14-yard line. This time it was Jefferson taking the ball out wide and getting to the pylon, again beating Valentine’s tackle attempt and putting a bow on the scoring. Drive totals: 3 plays, 14 yards, 1 first down, 0:18 TOP Here are the totals for Minnesota’s six scoring drives in this game: 35 plays 261 net yards (198 yards by the offense, 63 yards via penalty) 12 first downs (4 via penalty) 1 field goal 5 touchdowns Exactly twice in this entire game did the Vikings’ offense gain more than 35 yards when penalty yardage is excluded. Three of the four touchdown drives in the second half were on drives that started inside the Packers’ 30. And from the point when the Packers failed to convert on 4th down to the time when Minnesota finished the scoring, the Green Bay offense ran five plays for a net loss of 15 yards. In that span, Minnesota scored three touchdowns, gaining just 70 yards of offense (plus 28 yards on penalties). If there’s a blueprint for losing to a backup quarterback, it’s what the Packers did in the second half: commit a bunch of penalties (or, rather, get flagged for a bunch of penalties, which isn’t necessarily the same thing), let your quarterback get hit constantly and turn the ball over, and keep giving the opposing team a short field. 39 points is a big, scary number. But sometimes — and in this case, it is certainly the case — big numbers can lie if they don’t have context.
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: No one can escape blame for the Packers’ offensive line failure
summary: The Packers’ loss to the Vikings came down to an easily foreseeable problem: Brian Flores was going to blitz like a madman, and the Packers’ offensive line was going to struggle to stop him. Better lines than the Packers have failed to slow Flores’ logical insanity, and don’t get me wrong: when I call him […]
full_text: Football: A close up of Green Bay Packers Donovan Jennings (67) vs Washington Commanders at Lambeau Field.Green Bay, WI 9/19/2025CREDIT: Erick W. Rasco (Photo by Erick W. Rasco/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (Set Number: X164773 TK1) The Packers’ loss to the Vikings came down to an easily foreseeable problem: Brian Flores was going to blitz like a madman, and the Packers’ offensive line was going to struggle to stop him. Better lines than the Packers have failed to slow Flores’ logical insanity, and don’t get me wrong: when I call him a madman, it’s with reverential respect. He’s doing things nobody else is doing and getting away with it. That deserves to be studied and respected. But the problem is the Packers knew this was coming and were systematically unprepared to counter it. I don’t use that description lightly, but I really do think this was a systemic failure, top to bottom. It’s not just that the Packers had a weak offensive line or were caught by surprise by Flores, but it’s that they knew this was how the game was going to be played and did virtually nothing to avoid it. Flores’ approach is, by now, well understood, so I think we can lay that particular point aside for now. They knew it was coming and failed to stop it, simple as. But the way they tried (ha) to stop it, at least from a personnel perspective, merits further attention. Justis said it’s impossible to overstate how bad the Packers’ offensive line was on Sunday, but I’m going to try. It starts with Donovan Jennings, a former undrafted free agent now in his third year with the Packers. Originally signed in 2024, Jennings had played a grand total of six offensive snaps for the Packers before starting on Sunday, though that number would probably be higher had he not ended the 2025 season on injured reserve after a throat injury just before the Packers’ Week 18 game against the Vikings. Matt LaFleur said his decision to start Jennings came down to “time on task.” Jennings, apparently, has played enough at left guard in practice and in the preseason that LaFleur felt comfortable starting him against the most aggressive defensive coordinator in football. “He’s done a nice job, so I feel like he earned that opportunity,” LaFleur said. To his point, Jennings may have been the most-prepared left guard, but that’s not saying much. We can’t count practice reps, but according to Pro Football Focus, Jennings had played 162 snaps at left guard across the 2024-26 preseasons and the 2025 regular season. With Aaron Banks out (more on him in a bit!), the only other options at left guard were Anthony Belton (two snaps at left guard in 2025) and 2026 draft pick Jager Burton (82 snaps at left guard this preseason), and it’s true: Jennings had more time on task than either one of those guys. But we’re not talking about a vast gulf here, and given how he performed, I think it’s worth calling LaFleur’s reasoning into question. Of course, this isn’t the first time the Packers have made a decision to go with a more practiced player over a better option. LaFleur and company made a near-identical situation in 2022, when they started Royce Newman at guard repeatedly despite having the much more promising Zach Bako-Bewele (then known as Zach Tom) waiting in the wings. To my knowledge, LaFleur didn’t specifically outline his reasoning the same way at that time, but it seems comparable enough to essentially be the same; he valued experience over talent, regardless of the fact that the better player was going to take over sooner rather than later. I feel comfortable saying that Donovan Jennings was never going to be the Packers’ future at left guard, but Burton (or Belton, for that matter) might still be. The future has to start at some point, and I’d always rather get to it more quickly. But making those calls (and related ones) falls on the coaching staff, and there’s reason to be suspect there, too. Let’s start again with Jennings. He was the crown jewel of the Packers’ 2024 UDFA class , but apparently hasn’t made major strides since then. True, Brian Flores has made fools of better linemen, but development is going to be a big part of any UDFA’s career journey, and Jennings, apparently, hasn’t done much in the way of development. Who’s to blame for that? It starts with offensive line coach Luke Butkus, who has been in that role since 2022. As a draft and develop team, the Packers’ coaching staff is on the hook for the performance of players they’ve been tasked with developing, and every player who started for the Packers on Sunday, Jennings included, falls into Butkus’ tenure as offensive line coach. That’s some pretty paltry development, across the board, though he should get some credit for Zach Bako-Bewele and Jordan Morgan (such as he is) if we’re going to blame him for Jennings. Above the player level you have tactics, and Jennings and the rest of the offensive line were done no favors by the Packers’ approach on Sunday. Our Justis Mosqueda went into this at some length on the Frozen Tundra Frequencies’ Repack podcast (and you should check it out), but the short version is that the Packers tried to counter Flores’ blitz packages by doing full-line slides to the right and turning someone loose on Jordan Love’s blindside. That led to a bunch of hits on Love and, overall, a pretty bad afternoon for the offense. Those tactical calls run the gamut of responsibility, falling on Butkus, offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich, and head coach Matt LaFleur. Take your pick who you’d like to blame the most, or just blame all three equally to the extent you see fit; it adds up to the same conclusion: the Packers’ coaching staff made some bad calls with their bad players on Sunday. For my money, most of that blame lands on Matt LaFleur. He hired Luke Butkus and promoted him after promoting Adam Stenavich and is the Packers’ offensive playcaller. Who else could be more responsible? Everything leads back to him. Well, not precisely everything. The Packers were in this position in the first place because of their personnel. It’s one thing to use your players badly, but it’s another (albeit related) problem to have only bad or untested options, and that’s the situation the Packers found themselves in on Sunday. The Packers signed Aaron Banks to a massive deal in the spring of 2025, but he’s been injured as often as not and bad during the “not” portions. I don’t know if he’d have been a meaningful upgrade on Sunday. The Packers’ other non-Jennings options were, as previously mentioned, Anthony Belton and Jager Burton. Belton has been disappointing and positionally homeless (thanks to the coaching staff constantly yanking him around since he arrived, much as they did with Jordan Morgan), so he probably wouldn’t have been a slam dunk upgrade over Jennings, either. And Burton, even if he should be the future, may not have been an upgrade either. But this is exactly the problem: you signed a bad lineman and have no good options to replace him when he goes down. Brian Gutekunst can’t escape blame for Sunday’s debacle, either. In summary, what a cavalcade of suck. What a black hole of offensive line ineptitude. What a disaster. The Packers offensive line failed at every level. The players were bad, generally. One player was bad, specifically. The coaches failed to develop that player. The coaches also failed to prepare to even give that player (and all four of the other ones) a chance to succeed. And all this was precipitated by a series of failures to put good linemen on the roster. Systemic failure is the only term that begins to capture what happened, and if the Packers can’t get their system sorted out, this game isn’t going to be an outlier for the rest of the 2026 season.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: You cannot overstate how bad the Packers’ offensive line was on Sunday
summary: I just had the misfortune of watching the Green Bay Packers’ offense on All-22, the third (and final) time I’ve watched the Minnesota Vikings game so far. To make this short: The Packers’ offensive line looked like a second-rate high school team, passing stunts off to no one, turning guys loose when they had to […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images I just had the misfortune of watching the Green Bay Packers’ offense on All-22, the third (and final) time I’ve watched the Minnesota Vikings game so far. To make this short: The Packers’ offensive line looked like a second-rate high school team, passing stunts off to no one, turning guys loose when they had to and getting edged in pass protection left and right. These guards are going to get Jordan killed pic.twitter.com/YmHgGUDNnk — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 14, 2026 Jordan Love deserves a medal of honor for this game. He will not last 17 games if they continue to play like this. Every single offensive lineman disappointed, with the guards disappointing the most and Jordan Morgan disappointing the least. Pass-rush win rate leaders through Sunday's action (min. 20 pass-rush snaps) pic.twitter.com/7s27wEq0ak — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) September 14, 2026 For the most part, the tackles held up decently, aside from their matchups against Dallas Turner. Turner, who had not done great in his first two years in the NFL after being drafted in the first round, had the best game of his career on Sunday. Maybe this is a breakout year for him. Maybe the Packers’ offensive line is just bad. Either way, everyone expected better out of Green Bay’s front, who, despite their shortcomings over the years, were arguably the best team in the league in terms of giving their players extra help, preventing one player from taking over a game and developing a pass protection plan. In this game, Love was hit 15 times, officially, and more than that unofficially. Every NFL defensive play caller ranked by blitz rate in Week 1: Brian Flores: 82.1% Dan Quinn: 50.9% Aaron Glenn: 44.9% Jesse Minter: 43.4% Kelvin Sheppard: 43.0% Todd Bowles: 42.9% Lou Anarumo: 39.1% Mike Macdonald: 35.8% Vic Fangio: 35.8% Christian Parker: 35.3% Zak Kuhr:… — Ryan Paganetti (@RyanPaganetti) September 14, 2026 Yes, Brian Flores blitzed like crazy, even for Flores’ standards. I would have, too, considering how the line played. Even when the Packers were max protecting and running bootlegs, it didn’t look like the team knew the rules they were supposed to be playing, resulting in players being turned loose. According to NFL Pro, Love dropped back 46 times on Sunday, the second-most of any quarterback in Week 1 — only behind the Saints’ Tyler Shough. As a reminder, New Orleans played in an OVERTIME GAME yesterday. NFL Pro has the Packers down for 176 routes run in the game, meaning that Green Bay had 54 extra blockers over Love’s 46 dropbacks in the game, 1.2 per play. At some point, it doesn’t matter if you have extra blockers if the offensive line is performing poorly and guys are getting loose anyway. Both the Lions and Vikings were top 3 in Week 1 in rush/coverage disguise rate, based on pre-snap alignment. pic.twitter.com/3nkiAKsrEC — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 Does Flores drop guys who look like they’re blitzing and blitz guys who look like they’re dropping? Yes! You know who else does that? The New York Jets, the Packers’ next opponent, and the Detroit Lions, who they’ll play twice in divisional play this year. They need to get this issue figured out. Brian Flores is insane pic.twitter.com/HnfEPV3Dvi — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) September 14, 2026 What the Vikings did was a complete and total pantsing of the Packers’ pass protection unit on Sunday. If it doesn’t get better (maybe Aaron Banks’ return will help — hell, there are no bad ideas right now), it’s going to be a long season.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers Film Room: Christian Watson doubles-up
summary: We’ll be dissecting the film on the overall Green Bay Packers offense & passing game later (we already did a little of it with numbers), but, for now, I just wanted to take a few minutes and talk about the game Christian Watson had. With only the Monday Night game left to play, Watson currently […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’ll be dissecting the film on the overall Green Bay Packers offense & passing game later (we already did a little of it with numbers ), but, for now, I just wanted to take a few minutes and talk about the game Christian Watson had. With only the Monday Night game left to play, Watson currently has the 3rd highest EPA of the week at 13.98 (behind Chris Olave’s 15.42 and Zay Flowers’ 14.06). Per SumerSports , he primarily aligned as the outside receiver (75% of his snaps were outside), and 100% of his targets came when he was the outside receiver. He had an ADOT (Average Depth of Target) of 15.9 yards and had 73 yards of YAC (Yards After Catch). He is currently tied with Zay Flowers for the lead in YACOE (Yards After Catch Over Expectation) with +49 (per NFL Pro ). If you want to talk just regular stats, he caught 6 of his 8 targets for 147 yards (18.4 YPA) and 2 TDs. With those numbers, Jordan Love posted a QB Rating of 156.3 when targeting Watson. Let’s take a look at his two TD receptions. Play 1: 2nd & 10, 7:54 remaining in the 1st quarter The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR), starting in a 2×2 shotgun spread look. Tucker Kraft [85] is initially wide on the right, but he slow-motions pre-snap and ends up under the left tackle, leaving Christian Watson [9] as the lone skill player on the right side of the field. The Vikings have 7 bodies at the line and are showing a completely open middle of the field. With Brian Flores calling the defense, you can’t be sure if he’s blitzing everyone at the line or dropping some back into coverage. At the snap, Watson is running a deep in-cutter. On the other side of the field, Jayden Reed [11] is running a flat route while Matthew Golden [0] is running a big post route over the top. That works effectively to clear out some space on the left. Theo Jackson [26] – one of the Vikings’ safeties – starts this play on the edge, opposite of Watson. Blake Cashman [51] is the linebacker who is originally walked-up over the center. At the snap, both of them drop back to the middle. Cashman is more of a straight drop, while Jackson is buzzing back at an angle. Love takes a quick glance at Jackson off the edge and sees the drop. He then moves his eyes back to the middle and sees Cashman. He holds Cashman in place long enough to pry the window open. Love hits Watson just in front of the buzzing Jackson, and Watson does the rest, erasing angles all the way to the end zone. Play 2: 2nd & 2, 00:18 remaining in the 2nd quarter With 18 seconds left in the first half, the Packers trot out 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) at the 2 yard line. They’re in an under center, YY Wing formation (both TEs in-line on the same side). Watson is in a condensed split on the right, while Golden is split wide to the left. Watson motions pre-snap into an insert position. In this YY Wing formation, that puts him under the line between the two TEs. This is something the Packers do a lot as part of their run game, and Watson’s strengths as a blocker put him in that position quite a bit. It’s a way to give the offense an extra blocker at the point of attack. As we’ll see here, it’s also a useful tool in the passing game. The Packers play action to the Wing side, then Love continues with a sprint-out to the right. The Vikings are biting on the play action, so the defender over Watson is expecting to meet him in the hole for a block. Instead, Watson slips right by him and finds a ton of open space. Love flips it out for the easy TD. I love this playcall. I’m always a huge fan of releasing the insert blocker through the line, especially when you can sell the play action. Albums listened to: Karina Rykman – Joyride ; Beach House – Depression Cherry

title: Packers Discussion: 1st impressions of Jonathan Gannon’s defense
summary: I’m sure that we’re going to talk about the offensive line a lot this week, so I just want to give this space for people to fire off their thoughts on another major subject: the first game that Jonathan Gannon called on the defensive side of the ball. For the most part, I thought the […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is shown during the third quarter of their game Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026 at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Minnesota Vikings beat the Green Bay Packers 39-22. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co I’m sure that we’re going to talk about the offensive line a lot this week, so I just want to give this space for people to fire off their thoughts on another major subject: the first game that Jonathan Gannon called on the defensive side of the ball. For the most part, I thought the defense did fine on Sunday. The defense gave up 3.1 yards per attempt in the run game and 4.9 yards per dropback. It’s amazing how the Minnesota Vikings were able to get 39 points with those numbers. They scored 29 points straight with only one drive over 28 yards, because the offense not only was getting off the field quickly but also giving the defense short fields to defend. What really hurt Green Bay at the end was that Carrington Valentine was playing snaps at cornerback, as he was run at directly for a touchdown and gave up another score to Justin Jefferson on a catch-and-run opportunity. In general, the Packers pretty much played their base 3-4 defense and nickel defenses, as the Penny defense was sort of shelved. I thought Gannon put Lukas Van Ness and Edgerrin Cooper in really good positions to succeed, leading to some of their best games as pros. Keisean Nixon had a good game, too. Zaire Franklin didn’t get exposed in coverage, outside of the touchdown where he was the runner in Tampa 2 (a changeup play that Green Bay just got caught in). title: Texans vs. Bills Week 1 analysis: Turnover differential, final plays killed Houston’s chances
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 1: The Missed Turnovers: Last season, Houston ranked 3rd in forced turnovers. They left the game […]
full_text: (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 1: The Missed Turnovers : Last season, Houston ranked 3rd in forced turnovers. They left the game with zero. Yet, the stat sheet doesn’t always tell the tale. Houston missed at least three INTs and two fumble recoveries. Much has been said about Lassiter’s missed INT in the end zone. Jalen Pitre also had a golden opportunity to shut down a Bills’ drive with a near goal-line pick on a play that followed a Lassiter DPI giving the Bills the ball at the HOU 1. On a second quarter drive, Stingley somehow missed on a “ [KITTEN] it” throw from Josh Allen to Dalton Kincaid. Later that drive, if Blankenship was a quarter of a second earlier in his jump, Houston gets that INT. In the fourth quarter, after Houston had taken a 31-30 lead, on the first play of the drive, Allen fumbled the snap, but he managed to jump on it. Then there was the first play of the next drive after Houston went three-and-out (More later). Turnovers can be a fickle mistress from year to year. To start this season, she betrayed the Texans. The Final Plays : For most of the game, the offense carried Houston. After a first drive fumble, Stroud regained his composure, and the offense line did their part to keep the game moving. Yet, on the second to last drive for the Texans, problems returned. While hindered by a curious (at best) play call for a second down toss sweep to the right, when the team had most of its success running to the offensive left, the line could not offer the push needed to get at least one 1st down. On the final drive, they got Houston to the BUF 9. However, G Ed Ingram got badly beaten, forcing a 9-yard sack. At 20 seconds, Houston was forced to either get to the end zone from the 18 or get out of bounds. The next pass was an incompletion, leaving Houston with maybe two more shots. Unfortunately, the right side of the line failed again, as T Trent Brown got beaten, allowing the strip-sack fumble of Stroud. While one could argue the final two sacks were not on him, Stroud can’t shake the turnover narrative. In the post-game comments, all the right things got said. Yet will the outside noise become reality for the line and Stroud? The Critical Play: 4th Quarter, 3:13, BUF ball, 1st and 10 @ BUF 4; RB James Cook rushes for 12 yards to the BUF 16, Derek Stingley Forced Fumble, recovered by BUF at the BUF 19 This game did not lack for game-altering plays. Yet, this missed fumble recovery looms large. Consider the opening play of that final Bills’ drive. After Kroeger and the coverage units pinned the Bills at the 4, Buffalo went with a run play. Cook busted through the Texans defense to get out past the 16-yard line. Then comes Stingley, who knocks the ball out of Cook’s right arm with a well-timed punch. Should Houston recover there, they would have the ball inside the Bills’ 20. Worst case, the Bills use all of their TOs, Houston kicks the FG to go up 34-30, and the Bills, with only the possible 2-minute warning, have to go to the end zone with no timeouts. Possibly the Bills still get the TD, but the percentages would favor Houston a bit more, and perhaps with the momentum of forcing a turnover and punt in the previous two possessions, that might have been enough. FUN WITH NUMBERS: 8/76: Average number of penalties/average penalty yards for Texans in season-openers under Ryans: The first game of the season tends to be a bit sloppy, and the refs got plenty of arm exercises in this one. 7 flags for a whooping 106 yards for the Texans, 10 penalties for 85 yards against the Bills. For Houston, 61 of those yards came on two back-breaking flags (46-yard DPI on Lassiter setting up a Bills TD and a 15-yard Roughing the Passer on Mario Edwards keeping another Bills drive alive). In the three season-opening losses, the Texans average 9 flags for 91 yards. At this point, it is a feature of the Ryans regime that flags will be an issue to start off the season. GAME BALLS: RB David Montgomery : 20 carries for 60 yards and 3 receptions for 19 yards might not seem like much, but throw in 2 rushing TDs, along with a receiving TD, and he showed that Houston might have the back they need. It also allowed Woody Marks to be that change-up back, a role that will suit him better (9 rushes for 42 yards). It wasn’t enough in this game, but especially later in the season, getting nearly 30 total rushes at nearly 4 yards a clip with the RBs will be a good thing. P Kai Kroeger and the Houston Punt Coverage Units: Kroeger had 4 punts, averaging 52.0 yards/kick and landing two inside the 5. The coverage units limited the Bills to two returns for 10 total yards. Those two punts had the perfect height/spin to allow the coverage units to get down the field and pin the Bills deep in their territory. In theory, a great set up for that Texans’ defense. In reality…not so much. TE Dalton Kincaid: Yes, an opposing player is on the list. Then again, he fried any Texans’ defender he came against, from All-Pro Stingley to Blakenship. Coming back after being injured the past two seasons, against what may still be among the best secondaries in the league, and leaving with 5 receptions for 130 yards, including two 35+ yard receptions…yeah, give him credit for that one. SHOULD BE FORCED TO WRITE A DOCTORAL DISSERATION ON HOUSTON’S COVERAGE SCHEMES WHILE LISTENING TO MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY, TED CRUZ AND CAL MCNAIR ATTEMPT TO SING OPERA-STYLE “THE EYES OF TEXAS” S Reed Blankenship: That gamble on the INT backfired spectacularly, as DJ Moore got one of the easiest TD’s he’ll ever have. He didn’t exactly the best day in coverage against the Bills receivers, including getting torched by TE Dalton Kincaid on the final drive. His stats (7 total tackles (4 solo)) are the definition of empty. Arguably, the entire secondary could reside here, but Blankenship leads the pack. DC Matt Burke: The Most Interesting Defensive Coordinator in the World…did not have a good game at all. Sure, Josh Allen can make many a good defense look mortal, but Burke did not seem to have the right answers for slowing down the Bills’ offense. Perhaps most damning, he did not think to have a spy on Allen on a play that resulted in a 21-yard TD run when no defender touched the QB known for rushing. The second half went a bit better, but even those adjustments weren’t enough. Burke usually calls great defense since he took over the defensive play-calling. Not this day. NFL/TV Network Executives: The game of the weekend, and it was relegated to Sunday early afternoon? Sure, there are lots of factors to consider with primetime and marquee matchup times. It got national attention at its timeslot, but this seemed like a real marquee matchup, and one that did live up to the hype that a national/stand-alone game should promise. The Ohio State 4th Quarter Game Plan: Think Houston had a bad 4th Quarter? They didn’t have the worst one in the state of Texas this past weekend. That distinction must go to the Buckeyes of Ohio State. Up 23-3 in the 4th, they proceeded to get out scored 21-0 to end the game. If you are a Longhorn fan (or really can’t stand Ohio State), congratulations, you may continue your crowing. If not, well, I don’t think the insufferability of the previously mentioned groups will go away anytime soon. For the 3rd time in 4 seasons under DeMeco Ryans, the Texans start 0-1. Every time they started 0-1, they at least started 0-2. They will look to avoid that fate when they host the Cincinnati Bengals back at Reliant Stadium for 12:00 CDT kickoff.

title: Texans Place LB Henry To’oTo’o on IR
summary: Following the Houston Texans’ 36-31 loss to the Buffalo Bills, many eyes turned towards the health status of starting LB Henry To’oTo’o. He suffered an injury tackling Bills TE Dawson Knox, and left the game. Now, KPRC2’s Aaron Wilson is reporting that the Texans are placing Henry To’oTo’o on IR: Earlier today, head coach DeMeco […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Henry To'oTo'o #39 of the Houston Texans looks on during an NFC Divisional Playoff game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following the Houston Texans’ 36-31 loss to the Buffalo Bills, many eyes turned towards the health status of starting LB Henry To’oTo’o. He suffered an injury tackling Bills TE Dawson Knox, and left the game. Now, KPRC2’s Aaron Wilson is reporting that the Texans are placing Henry To’oTo’o on IR: https://t.co/in4Am1DgGG — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) September 15, 2026 Houston Texans LB Henry To’oTo’o will miss a significant amount of time with a shoulder injury according to head coach DeMeco Ryans. #Texans #Sarge pic.twitter.com/qhlzEyMoTE — BIG SARGE MEDIA LLC (@BigSargeSportz) September 14, 2026 Earlier today, head coach DeMeco Ryans was quoted as saying To’oTo’o had suffered a shoulder injury and would be out “some time.” He stated that they had not decided at that time if they would place To’oTo’o on IR, but ultimately did so hours later. To’oTo’o will now miss a minimum of four games; the earliest he could return would be Week 6 for Houston’s match with the Jackonsville Jaguars in London, England on October 18th. #Texans Henry To'oTo'o right into blue tent pic.twitter.com/kU4TDXIy2w — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) September 13, 2026 This comes as difficult news for a team that continues to lose players to significant injures. The rash started with third-string QB Graham Mertz tearing his ACL in the first preseason game, then extended to a similar season-ending injury for WR Jayden Higgins, and now, there are a total of five players on offense (Mertz, Higgins, Dell, Smith, Hagen) and seven players on defense (Horton, McDonald, Byrd, Gaye, Ingram) that are on the Texans’ injured reserve. In To’oTo’o’s place, backup LBs Jake Hansen, Jake Hummel (who is considered week-to-week with a groin injury) , and rookies Wade Woodaz and Aiden Fisher will work to fill in his shoes. Hansen has been an exceptional special teams and reserve linebacker for Houston for the last few years, and Woodaz had some big plays in the preseason, but the LB depth is overall fairly inexperienced at this point. Not necessarily bad, but certainly a downgrade from To’oTo’o. Jake Hansen is the only healthy linebacker besides Azeez Al-Shaair with over 200 regular season snaps, so there will be some growing pains with the new players at the weak side position Teach tape by To'oTo'o. — rivers mccown (@riversmccown.bsky.social) 2025-10-26T18:26:02.972Z To’oTo’o, 25, a fifth-round pick in Houston’s vaunted 2023 Draft, had recently signed a two-year, $16 million contract extension, keeping him in Houston through the 2028 season. Originally expected to be a backup LB to former Texan starter (and current Atlanta Falcon) Christian Harris, To’oTo’o would eventually take the starting job at weakside-linebacker his rookie year, and he’s held on to that job since. To’oTo’o has basically been a rock beside MLB Al-Shaair since 2024, and often became the thunder to his lightning. To’oTo’o had the speed and length to mirror running backs from sideline to sideline, and as he grew into his role with the Texans, began to make more plays against the pass and in the backfield. His magnum opus came against the Patriots in the divisional round of the playoffs last year, where he was truly exceptional in coverage. His statistics in 2025 were: 17 Games (14 Starts) 95 Tackles, 9 Tackles For Loss, 4 QB Hits, 2.5 Sacks, 4 Pass Deflections, 1 Fumble Recovery 930 Snaps, 65.1 PFF Grade (66.4 RDEF, 36.5 TACK, 80.6 PRSH, 59.5 COV) Thankfully for Houston, their LB depth has the talent base to replace this production, but that will require the younger players to get up to speed a bit sooner rather than later. It’s another test for a Texans defense that might still be trying to find its footing after giving up 36 points in the opener, but it’s a test head coach DeMeco Ryans and defensive coordinator Matt Burke have prepared the team for. I will dearly, dearly miss Henry To’oTo’o as one of my very favorite players from that great 2023 draft class, but I look forward to seeing how the next generation of Texans take his place until his return later in the season. What do you think of this news? Will the Texans dearly miss Henry To’oTo’o, or will the combination of Hansen/Hummel/Woodaz/Fisher work out just fine? Next week, the Texans will host the 1-0 Cincinnati Bengals, who have a quarterback and running back that will look to test these new pieces on Houston’s defensive lineup. How do you think the Texans will respond to Cincinnati? Let us know down in the comments below! Go Texans!

title: Houston Texans Week 2 Opening Odds
summary: Okay, yesterday sucked. There’s no two ways about it. But the good thing about sports is there’s always another game, always another chance to make good and get the W that the Texans should’ve gotten yesterday but—we’re not talking about that right now. Instead, we’re on to Cincinnati and another home game against the Bengals. […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: David Montgomery #32 of the Houston Texans celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the first half against the Buffalo Bills of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Okay, yesterday sucked. There’s no two ways about it. But the good thing about sports is there’s always another game, always another chance to make good and get the W that the Texans should’ve gotten yesterday but—we’re not talking about that right now. Instead, we’re on to Cincinnati and another home game against the Bengals. According to the nerds in Vegas, it’s going to be another close matchup; at least according to FanDuel Sports Book it is. Here’s what the nerds think of our odds to start off week 2: If you are unfamiliar with gambling odds and this looks like some ancient untranslated tome, allow me to offer some assistance. The first boxes show what is known as the “spread.” The spread is basically imaginary points that would affect the course of a game if they were real. Imagine at the start of the game, a points fairy arrived and blessed one of the teams with some bonus points right away. In the example above, the Bengals would start this game with three points and the Texans would start with three points less. If you were to bet on the Texans, and why wouldn’t you, the Texans would have to defeat the Bengals by more than three points to collect winnings. If they lost or won by one or two points, you would lose your bet. If the Texans won by three points exactly, it would be a push (draw) and you’d get your money back. The second column is the money line. This is a straight up “I’m picking the Bengals or the Texans to win.” The numbers represent the amount you need to bet in order to win that amount. If you bet on the Bengals, you would have to bet $100 to win $130 (because they have a positive money line). If you bet on the Texans, you would have to bet $154 to win $100 (because they have a negative money line). The final column is the over/under. In this, you would bet on whether the total combined points in the game will be over or under an arbitrary number made up by the nerds to split betting evenly. In this case, the over/under is 46.5 points. Which means if you bet the over, you would need the Texans and Bengals to score at least 47 points to win. If you bet the under, you need the teams to score 46 or fewer points. If the O/U were a non-decimal number, a push (draw) would be possible. Clear as mud? Excellent. Here’s the breakdown this week: Point Spread Cincinnati Bengals +3 Houston Texans -3 Money Line Cincinnati Bengals +130 (bet $100 to win $130) Houston Texans – 154 (bet $154 to win $100) Over/Under : 46.5 Please do NOT take financial advice from a football blog. Please play responsibly.
