full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 07: Chandler Brayboy #15 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs with the ball during Training Camp at the Miller Electric Center on August 07, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by James Gilbert/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots made changes to the practice squad as sights set on the 2026 home opener. The organization added wide receiver Chandler Brayboy and outside linebacker Xavier Holmes to the 17-man group amid a series of moves announced Monday afternoon. Brayboy, 25, was in for a workout that included quarterback Connor Bazelak and fellow wideouts Tahj Washington, Bryce Oliver and Isaiah Hodgins. The 6-foot-1, 199-pound Elon alum entered the NFL with the Jacksonville Jaguars as an undrafted free agent in 2025. He spent the duration of his rookie regular season on the practice squad and was waived at the 53-man roster deadline in August. A former FCS All-American, CAA Special Teams Player of the Year and Phoenix team captain, Brayboy’s collegiate career spanned 55 games and 46 starts dating back to 2019. He accumulated 2,660 receiving yards, 245 rushing yards, 1,568 kickoff return yards and 22 all-purpose touchdowns. Holmes, 24, attended rookie minicamp as an undrafted tryout in May on the way to signing his first NFL contract with the Patriots. The 6-foot-2, 252-pound outside linebacker was among the initial wave of roster cuts following the club’s preseason finale in August. Holmes checked into 25 games for Maine before transferring to James Madison for his fifth year of NCAA eligibility. Across 14 appearances as a redshirt senior for the Dukes in 2025, he totaled 30 tackles and six sacks to go with one fumble recovery, one interception and one blocked kick. To make room for Monday’s signings, the Patriots released running back Hassan Haskins and safety Elliott Davison from the practice squad. Haskins, 26, signed with New England on the eve of the preseason opener after visiting for a workout . The 6-foot-2, 228-pound veteran running back was released at the end of August and circled back on the practice squad at its formation. Originally entering the NFL in the fourth round of the 2022 draft at No. 131 overall, Haskins made previous stops with the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers. Through 44 career games, the past first-team All-Big Ten honoree out of Michigan stands with 76 carries for 229 yards, 18 catches for 119 yards, three touchdowns and one start. He has seen 371 snaps on offense and 683 snaps on special teams. Davison, 24, joined the practice squad in Foxborough shortly after the calendar turned to September. The 6-foot, 200-pound safety entered the NFL in 2025 as an undrafted free agent out of UTSA. He spent his rookie regular season on the New Orleans Saints’ practice squad was retained on a futures contract in January. After playing 141 snaps between defense and special teams during his second preseason in the NFC South, the Roadrunners product went through waivers unclaimed at the league’s 53-man roster deadline. Head coach Mike Vrabel’s 0-1 side of the aisle will host the 1-0 Pittsburgh Steelers next Sunday. Kickoff at Gillette Stadium is set for 1 p.m. ET.

Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Following a weekend off, the New England Patriots were back on the practice fields on Monday for a bonus day of work ahead of Week 2. For the first time since Aug. 24, when he suffered an ankle injury, running back TreVeyon Henderson returned to the practice field. He was joined by offensive lineman Ben Brown, who has been out since suffering a knee injury in the preseason opener. “[They’ll] probably try to do some stuff today,“ head coach Mike Vrabel explained. ”We’ll see where they are.“ In the absence list, the Patriots defense was missing captain Robert Spillane. The 30-year old, who was managed at times last season, was present in the locker room and spoke to reporters beforehand. Also missing was third-string quarterback Behren Morton and fellow rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover for unknown reasons. New England also is expected to announce some turnover on the practice squad, as new wide receiver Chandler Brayboy was present following the injury to A.J. Brown. Outside linebacker Xavier Holmes, who spent the offseason with the team before suffering an injury an being part of roster cuts, was also on the field. The Patriots donned full pads on the practice fields as the focus on Monday fell back on fundamentals after their Week 1 loss. “I mean, we’re a big fundamental emphasis here today,” Vrabel said. “Technique has got to improve, all these little things that can help you win football games. title: Mike Vrabel defends Patriots’ offensive game plan against Seahawks
summary: After struggling in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots offense was hopeful to turn things around in its rematch with the Seattle Seahawks defense in Week 1. While the game as a whole was much more competitive, the end result was still disappointing. The Patriots finished with just 10 points on the day, turned […]
full_text: After struggling in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots offense was hopeful to turn things around in its rematch with the Seattle Seahawks defense in Week 1. While the game as a whole was much more competitive, the end result was still disappointing . The Patriots finished with just 10 points on the day, turned the ball over three times, and were plagued by some of the same issues that already haunted them back on Super Sunday. The game was there for the taking, but Drake Maye’s third interception of the day sealed it in the home team’s favor, which came away with a 13-10 victory over the reigning AFC champions. In the aftermath of the loss and New England’s disappointing outing, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels found himself the subject of criticism for what was seen as a fairly conservative game plan. However, head coach Mike Vrabel defended the plan on Monday. “I don’t look at things as conservative. That’s what we felt like was best against this defense,” Vrabel said during an appearance on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show . “We didn’t hit some things and you have to be able to run the football against split safety defense. That’s no secret. You don’t play split safety defense to stop the run; they play it to not give up big plays. We tried to hit some shots down the field. We threw it to the running backs a couple times for 12 or 15 yards when they were all off there, and on the interception should have thrown it to the back again for a third time. You just can’t get bored doing things right. If it’s not there it’s not there.” Through three quarters, the Patriots had performed decently against one of the NFL’s best defenses. They were up 10-3 and managed to move the ball even after losing star wide receiver A.J. Brown to what was later diagnosed as a high-ankle sprain . New England took its first snap of the fourth quarter — a 1-yard Corey Kiner run — in Seattle territory and with a chance of adding to its lead. From that point on, however, things went downhill. Drake Maye threw an interception on the very next play while attempting to hit Romeo Doubs deep on the play Vrabel was referencing; this turnover was a turning point in the contest and opened the floodgates. The Seahawks scored the game-tying touchdown five plays later, while Maye threw another pick on the next possession. Seattle added three more points off of that giveaway, which was then followed by the Patriots driving deep into their opponent’s territory only to be denied on another, game-ending INT. Could a different game plan have changed things and let the Patriots offense perform at the same level as others around the NFL in Week 1? Not in Vrabel’s estimation. “Every game is different, every defense is different,” he said. “We all sit down, we game-plan. Josh game-plans with his staff; each guy has an area. I’ll sit in with those. I think to look and say, ‘Well, this guy, this team put up number…’ — we didn’t win the game.”

title: Saints’ slow starts could become a problem if they continue
summary: The New Orleans Saints showed exactly why there is plenty to be excited about moving forward after Sunday’s 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Unfortunately, they also showed a potential issue that could become much harder to overcome if it continues. For the 12th time under Kellen Moore, the Saints failed to score in the […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-SEPTEMBER 13: Head coach Kellen Moore of the New Orleans Saints reacts to a call during the second half of an NFL football game between the New Orleans Saints and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 13, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints showed exactly why there is plenty to be excited about moving forward after Sunday’s 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Unfortunately, they also showed a potential issue that could become much harder to overcome if it continues. For the 12th time under Kellen Moore, the Saints failed to score in the opening quarter, and this time, the slow start helped put them in a massive hole. Erasing a 21-point deficit is definitely encouraging and shows the kind of resilience that you’d like to see from a young Saints team. But the fact that New Orleans needed to play from behind in the first place is something worth watching as the season progresses. The Saints cannot expect to repeatedly dig themselves out of holes and remain competitive throughout the season. Once New Orleans settled in, the production was there. And the starters not playing in the preseason has a lot to do with why it took so long to find a rhythm. But if this becomes a recurring trend, it could change the entire trajectory of the season. Sunday’s loss should not erase the optimism surrounding this team. If anything, the comeback showed how much fight this team has. But if New Orleans wants to take the next step this season, getting out of the gates faster has to become a priority. With the Baltimore Ravens up next, the Saints may not have the luxury of falling behind early and still having enough time to mount another comeback. Do you think it’s an overreaction to believe the Saints’ slow starts will become a problem, or was Sunday simply a case of early-season rust?

title: Week 1 Film Review: Highlights from the All 22
summary: After experiencing the Saints vs. Lions, I could not wait until the game film was uploaded to be able to see the ins and outs of the team so that true evaluations on the performance could be made. As I went to bed Sunday night, I had no idea what was in store for me […]
full_text: Saints Spot Concept on 2-Point Play After experiencing the Saints vs. Lions, I could not wait until the game film was uploaded to be able to see the ins and outs of the team so that true evaluations on the performance could be made. As I went to bed Sunday night, I had no idea what was in store for me — 7 hours of nightmare in the form of Mike Pereira slowly moving his hand back and forth while patronizingly explaining the definition of a forward pass. Takeaways from the Film Vernon Broughton has Arrived Though he plays a position that hardly shows up in the stat book and can go overlooked by the naked eye during the live broadcast, Vernon Broughton had a very good showing in his first regular-season action since Week 2 of last year. This was most noticeable when he lined up against Penei Sewell (one of the top linemen in the league), where Broughton was able to win multiple reps against the three-time first-team All-Pro. Although the sample size is small, if the Texas product can continue this trajectory, he will be viewed as a Trey Hendrickson-level steal by the Saints in the third round of last year’s draft. Stutsman vs Werner Both linebackers logged quality plays opposite Kaden Ellis this Sunday as they were faced with a tough challenge vs. the Lions. After watching the film, it was clear that each has their own strengths, but it seems like Stutsman is making the case to compete for the starting role throughout the year. Werner played like a savvy veteran and used his instincts to make multiple plays, including a nice TFL on Jahmyr Gibbs and an exceptional pass breakup down the middle of the field. Stutsman, on the other hand, was out of place on some plays but was able to recover due to his superior athletic ability. This is a great sign for the Saints, as the competition between the two seems to have them both playing good football against a very talented Lions offense. 2-Point Play The refs’ worst mistake in the game was missing the pass interference call in the end zone on Bryce Lance for the game-winning 2-point conversion. When watching the play live, I knew people would wonder how Olave wasn’t targeted, and I’m happy to weigh in. The Saints ran a modified version of the “Spot” concept (shown above), which is a great play call in this area. The read is simple, and after the initial motion by Olave to the interior of the 3-receiver bunch, Tyler Shough knew he was getting man coverage. The throw vs. man on this concept is THE CORNER ROUTE (the flat by Olave is intended to pull the flat defender away from the corner route, which it did). He found it slightly late, as the timing was thrown off by a good jam at the line — credit the Lions’ defense here. What was absurd to me is that the Lions defender had at least one hand covering Lance’s face while making contact with his body the entire time the ball was in the air. Am I blaming the refs for a loss? No. I am wondering how NFL officiating can have a review overturn an obvious fumble (which changed the outcome) while the refs are clearly afraid to “decide the game” by changing the outcome with a flag. End of the Day While the Saints had a sluggish start to the game, especially Tyler Shough, it was undeniable that they displayed a level of fight and belief in their quarterback that hasn’t graced the Black and Gold sideline since Drew Brees was captaining the offense. The film review gave me belief that this is a very talented roster with a smart coaching staff that will have plenty of success throughout the year.

title: Chris Olave looks ready to take another step after monster season opener
summary: New Orleans Saints wide receiver Chris Olave entered the 2026 season with plenty of expectations after earning second-team All-Pro honors last season. After Sunday’s season opener against the Detroit Lions, it is difficult to imagine the Saints asking for much more from their star wideout. Olave was one of the biggest reasons New Orleans was […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints drops a pass during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images New Orleans Saints wide receiver Chris Olave entered the 2026 season with plenty of expectations after earning second-team All-Pro honors last season. After Sunday’s season opener against the Detroit Lions, it is difficult to imagine the Saints asking for much more from their star wideout. Olave was one of the biggest reasons New Orleans was able to erase the 21-point deficit and nearly complete the incredible comeback, finishing with a career-high 182 receiving yards on 10 receptions. He was targeted 13 times and consistently gave Tyler Shough a reliable option as the Saints’ offense finally found its rhythm down the stretch. For a Saints offense that struggled to get anything going early, Olave eventually became the spark it desperately needed. The chemistry between him and Shough was especially encouraging, but it wasn’t surprising given what we’ve seen from the two this offseason. Shough finished with a career-high 410 passing yards, and a large part of that production came from his willingness to continue looking Olave’s way when the Saints needed a big play. The two connected for several significant gains throughout the afternoon, including a 47-yard completion that helped New Orleans continue its comeback attempt. Olave’s performance was also impressive considering the circumstances. The Saints were shut out in the first half and eventually fell behind 21-0 before their offense finally came alive. Rather than disappearing when the game became difficult, Olave became increasingly important as New Orleans mounted its comeback. The next step will be seeing whether Olave can stay healthy enough to turn this into a consistent season-long trend. If Sunday was any indication, Olave could be in for a massive season. Now, he will look to carry his momentum into Week 2’s matchup with the Baltimore Ravens.

summary: The New Orleans Saints will start the 2026 season with a loss. While starting the season 0-1 is never good, New Orleans showed a lot of fight in the loss, fighting back from being down 21 points to having a chance to win in it overtime with a two-point attempt. The Saints are now tied […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints will start the 2026 season with a loss. While starting the season 0-1 is never good, New Orleans showed a lot of fight in the loss, fighting back from being down 21 points to having a chance to win in it overtime with a two-point attempt. The Saints are now tied with the entire NFC South with a 0-1 record and will take on the Baltimore Ravens on the road next week. Up: WR Chris Olave Without a doubt, wide receiver Chris Olave was going to land on this week’s ups and downs list. After a drop while fighting through contract issues, we all looked at this game with a different look. The Saints and Olave didn’t look prepared, and his pivotal drop emphasized it. But the Olave and Tyler Shough connection heated up quickly, and the $124 million wideout finished the day with 10 receptions and a career-high 182 receiving yards. The fifth-year receiver was bound for a big day, with the Lions being down Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, and he took every opportunity that was presented. While it’s been just one week of football, Olave is the current league leader in receiving yards. With his growing connection with Shough, Olave has a chance to finish the year as a top-three wide receiver. Up: QB Tyler Shough Some people will be upset that Tyler Shough is making an appearance as a positive after Sunday’s game, and can you blame them? Shough started the day completing 10-of-23 pass attempts for 85 yards and 2 interceptions. That is worse than a terrible start, and it appeared that all Saints fans’ biggest fears have come true. But it’s what happened after that second interception in the second half that completely changed how we view Shough. After his terrible start, Shough completed 25-of-33 pass attempts for 325 yards and 3 touchdowns. A switch was flipped, and the second-year quarterback went from uncomfortable and incapable to a confident passer who was making unbelievable throws. It’s still hard to justify making Shough a positive for this game. If he plays even half as well as he did in the second half, the Saints would’ve walked out victors. But the resilience he showed, along with the rest of the team, is something to highlight and makes me feel better about the team going forward. Up: P Ryan Wright Punter Ryan Wright looks exactly as the Saints hoped after signing him to a large four-year, $14 million deal. The veteran punter had five attempts on Sunday, averaging 47.6 yards per punt and landing the Lions in their own 20-yard line twice. Wright had a long of 57 yards. It’s an advantage to have a top punter, and the former Minnesota Viking showed that in the loss, forcing the once-struggling Detroit Offense to go 70+ yards plenty of times. Down: Rushing offense vs. rushing defense The Saints were completely outclassed in the run game. Jahmyr Gibbs dominated the Saints’ run defense, ending the day with 156 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Gibbs averaged 5.4 yards per carry. On the flip side, the Saints’ entire team finished the day with just 91 rushing yards, led by Travis Etienne, who ran the ball just 9 times for 46 yards. New Orleans spent a lot of money in the offseason to ensure their rushing offense, and we were yet to see it in their Week 1 loss. The Saints rushing struggles led to Shough having to throw 56 passes in the first game in his sophomore season. Throwing 50 times a game for a chance to win is simply not sustainable, and the Saints need to establish the run, especially after the big signings of Etienne and David Edwards. Down: Saints’ slow start Have I said the Saints’ start was horrible yet? You can’t win a game starting like that. Well, maybe you can. The Saints somehow almost did. But realistically, New Orleans needs to be better out the gate and it has been a problem since Moore’s first season as head coach. Shough admitted during the post-game press conference the Lions defense was sending plenty of different unscouted looks. Understandably, this unpreparedness resulted in early struggles. This isn’t the problem. The problem here is how long it took for Moore to identify these looks and counter them. It wasn’t until the middle of the third quarter where the offense finally looked alive. The Saints need to start faster, and make adjustments even quicker.
author: Kyle Besson

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints loss to the Lions
summary: The Good: Resilience The Saints nearly matched the largest comeback in team history after falling behind 21-0 in the 3rd quarter. Instead of folding after a terrible half of football. the offense responded in crunch time. The Saints clawed their way back to force overtime and were a two point conversion away from stealing a […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints throws a pass during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Good: Resilience The Saints nearly matched the largest comeback in team history after falling behind 21-0 in the 3rd quarter. Instead of folding after a terrible half of football. the offense responded in crunch time. The Saints clawed their way back to force overtime and were a two point conversion away from stealing a win on the road against a team with Super Bowl aspirations. They easily could have gone the way of the Cleveland Browns on Sunday and stayed on the mat and lost by 20, but they didn’t. Chris Olave fought through pain to put up a career high 182 yards and Devaughn Vele looked like the solid WR2 we hoped he would be when the team acquired him last year. Tyler Shough responded after the half to finish with 410 yards and 3 TDs. The Saints ultimately came up short, but if the first half was just shaking off some rust that they weren’t able to shake off in the preseason due to the starters not playing then we should expect more of what we saw in the second half in Detroit. The Bad: Officiating Simply put, the officials stole 7 points from the Saints in this game. Don’t let anyone tell you different but Jared Goff fumbled the football and Jonas Sanker took it back for a touchdown, but the refs once again stole a game from the Saints. Why this keeps happening to them I do not know, but the NFL has had an officiating problem for many years that isn’t just exclusive to the Saints and it seems they have no interest in fixing. The incompetence of the officials is costing teams games and people their jobs, and the NFL has no accountability or oversight for their own officials who are supposed to be impartially judging these games with incredibly high stakes. This isn’t a problem that only the Saints suffer from, as I am sure they have been the beneficiaries of a bad call here and there in the past, but the fact is with how advanced the replay system is now, there shouldn’t be this many obviously bad calls anymore. The Saints would have won this game if it was officiated correctly, but there is no use dwelling on it as there is nothing they can do about it but expect more of the same going forward and work to make it not matter. The Ugly: The first half (and the first three minutes of the 3rd quarter) The Saints looked absolutely awful to start the game. Their first eight drives ended in five punts and three turnovers which resulted in them falling in a 21-0 hole. Despite the valiant comeback attempt, it is hard to win games in the NFL after falling behind by 21 points in the second half. If they had been able to manage just a field goal in the first half they would have won, but they couldn’t do that. Let’s hope this was just a fluke and that what we saw on their last five drives of the game is what we will see going forward.

title: Game Recap: Saints visit Lions in season opener
summary: The New Orleans Saints were looking to pull off a road upset against the Detroit Lions on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter The hosts got the ball to begin the game and went three-and-out. But the Saints didn’t fare much better on their opening series, with a 9-yard pass […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Devaughn Vele #14 of the New Orleans Saints attempts to make a catch against Rock Ya-Sin #23 of the Detroit Lions during the fourth quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints were looking to pull off a road upset against the Detroit Lions on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter The hosts got the ball to begin the game and went three-and-out. But the Saints didn’t fare much better on their opening series, with a 9-yard pass from Tyler Shough to Devaughn Vele marking the only first-down gain of the drive. Jared Goff and the Lions offense proceeded to get going on their second possession. A 19-yard connection with Sam LaPorta preceded a pair of big bursting runs from Jahmyr Gibbs to put Detroit in the red zone. From there, the Lions capitalised, with a 1-yard score from Gibbs capping off an 89-yard touchdown drive. Second Quarter The teams then exchanged a number of punts as the game moved into the second quarter. Shough did find Chris Olave on a few big throws, though the Saints never moved into scoring position. Detroit would then turn it over through a Gibbs fumble after a successful Saints challenge, but the visitors returned the favor when Shough threw an interception a few plays later. The Lions went three-and-out again, pinning New Orleans deep in their own half. Shough was able to move the drive past midfield with a 19-yard throw to Bryce Lance, but a sack a few plays later from Aidan Hutchinson forced a Saints punt just before the half. Third Quarter Trailing 7-0, Shough threw another interception on the first play of the second half. Detroit took advantage of the short field as Gibbs continued to punish the Saints defense, breaking off for an 18-yard run before eventually running in another 1-yard score to push the lead to 14-0. Shough proceeded to fumble early on the ensuing possession to give the Lions yet another short field. Goff connected with Amon-Ra St Brown for a 19-yard touchdown pass to give Detroit a 21-0 advantage. Then, at last, the Saints offense burst into life. A 47-yard pass to Olave and a 9-yard throw to Noah Fant put the black and gold on the edge of the red zone. A few plays later, including a third-down scramble from Shough for a first down, Kendre Miller ran in an 8-yard touchdown to get the visitors on the board. The Saints defense responded with a perfect series of their own, forcing a three-and-out. Shough picked up where he left off, completing his first three throws of the ensuing drive for 31 yards. A defensive pass interference call put the Saints down at the 1-yard line, before Shough found Vele for his first touchdown pass of the season to cut into the lead again. Fourth Quarter Now leading just 21-14, Goff and the Lions were forced into another quick punt. The Saints offense continued their momentum, as Travis Etienne ran for 14 yards to begin another scoring series. Shough’s 31-yard connection with Vele put the visitors in the red zone, though this time they were held to a field goal attempt. Daniel Carlson’s 28-yard chip shot put the score at 21-17. Having nearly blown their lead entirely, the Lions at last found some life. A facemask penalty against Tyree Wilson meant they began their drive at midfield. Gibbs continued to have success running the football, but the Saints defense did manage to hold Detroit to a field goal. Jake Bates’ 23-yard kick put the lead back to seven, at 24-17. Needing a touchdown to tie the game, the Saints quickly found themselves on 4th-and-12 with the game on the line. Shough delivered, finding Lance for 15 yards. He connected with Vele on the next play for another first down, and then connected with Olave on another bomb for a 42-yard gain. Juwan Johnson caught the 9-yard touchdown pass a play later, and the extra point tied the game at 24-24. With just over a minute remaining, Detroit would go three-and-out, giving New Orleans a slim chance at winning the game in regulation after an Etienne run and an 18-yard catch from Johnson gave Shough time to spike the ball for a long field goal. But Carlson’s 62-yard effort went wide right as the clock expired. Overtime The Saints deferred to Detroit, who put together a 70-yard touchdown drive highlighted by a 22-yard pass from Goff to Jameson Williams to set up 1st-and-goal. St Brown caught the touchdown pass to put the Lions up 31-24. Needing a touchdown of their own, Shough threw for 20 yards to Olave on another fourth-down conversion as the Saints moved past midfield. He found Fant for 10 yards amidst short runs from Miller and Etienne, before finding Johnson for 27 yards to set up 1st-and-goal. It was Fant again who caught the 8-yard touchdown pass to put New Orleans down by just a point. Kellen Moore elected to go for two and the win, as opposed to tying the game and giving Detroit a chance to score again. But the Lions defense prevailed, as Shough’s pass intended for Lance had almost no chance. Despite a resilient comeback effort from the black and gold, the Lions emerged victorious, 31-30. If it’s any consolation, all three NFC South rivals dropped their opening game on Sunday. Next up for the Saints is a visit to the Baltimore Ravens on September 20.
author: Sam Mackenzie

title: What are the odds? Saints open as 8.5-point underdogs for Week 2 at the Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints will continue their 2026 season on the road Sunday when they take on the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2. What initially looked like a likely loss on the Saints’ schedule has suddenly become a much more fascinating matchup after Week 1. After falling behind 21-0 in Detroit, New Orleans battled back […]
full_text: Sep 1, 2016; New Orleans, LA, USA; Baltimore Ravens quarterback Josh Johnson (2) runs the ball during the fourth quarter against the New Orleans Saints at the Mercedes-Benz Superdome. The Ravens won 23-14. Mandatory Credit: Matt Bush-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints will continue their 2026 season on the road Sunday when they take on the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2. What initially looked like a likely loss on the Saints’ schedule has suddenly become a much more fascinating matchup after Week 1. After falling behind 21-0 in Detroit, New Orleans battled back to force overtime before ultimately losing 31-30 to the Lions. Despite three turnovers, quarterback Tyler Shough delivered an impressive performance, throwing for 410 yards and three touchdowns, while wide receiver Chris Olave hauled in 10 passes for 182 yards. Baltimore, meanwhile, opened its season with an impressive 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. Derrick Henry rushed for 144 yards and three touchdowns, Lamar Jackson threw for 324 yards, and the Ravens piled up 506 yards of total offense. Zay Flowers racked up 150 receiving yards before leaving the game with a hamstring injury, making his status something to monitor throughout this week. That presents another challenge for a Saints defense that struggled early against Detroit before settling in as the game progressed. Slowing down Jackson is difficult enough, but New Orleans will also have to find a way to contain Henry and prevent Baltimore from controlling the game on the ground. For the Saints, however, Week 1 showed that this offense may be capable of keeping them in games many expected them to lose. Shough showed poise in leading the comeback, Olave looked every bit like a No. 1 receiver, and New Orleans refused to fold after falling behind by three touchdowns. Now comes another difficult road test. The Saints may be 0-1, but if what they showed in Detroit was any indication, Sunday’s matchup in Baltimore could be a lot more interesting than it looked when the schedule was first released. According to FanDuel, the Saints are currently 8.5-point underdogs against the Ravens, with an over/under of 48.5 points. However, those odds could move as kickoff approaches. title: NY Giants QB Jaxson Dart was dialed in against the Cowboys
summary: The New York Giants punched the Dallas Cowboys in the mouth en route to a 28-20 Week 1 victory. A smash-mouth, varied rushing attack set the tone for New York, featuring heavy formations and plenty of under-center looks. But the efficient play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart was the catalyst behind the Giants’ rare victory […]
full_text: The New York Giants punched the Dallas Cowboys in the mouth en route to a 28-20 Week 1 victory. A smash-mouth, varied rushing attack set the tone for New York, featuring heavy formations and plenty of under-center looks. But the efficient play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart was the catalyst behind the Giants’ rare victory over Dallas. Dart finished 23 of 29 ( 79% completion rate ) for 230 passing yards and three passing touchdowns, with 54 yards rushingon 11 carries. New York finished 9/11 on third down, and Dart found answers to Christian Parker’s defense, which, in fairness, had several breakdowns in coverage/assingments. Not only did Dart pass the eye-test, but the numbers back his performance up as well: Jaxson Dart with the best QB performance in Week 1. • EPA/Play: +0.73 (1st) • WPA/Play: +2.2% (1st) Every 5 plays, Dart added 3.5 expected points and 11% win probability for the Giants. pic.twitter.com/01OTeikQyu — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 Courtesy of Doug Analytics, Dart’s +0.73 EPA/Play ( Expected Points Added ) ranked first, as well as his WPA/Play ( Win Probability Added ). As Doug states, Dart added 3.5 expected points on every five plays the Giants took — an elite performance by the second-year signal caller. Here’s what NFL Next Gen had to say about Dart’s performance, along with his throwing chart: The Giants punted the football one time against Dallas, and they mounted four touchdown drives, as well as four drives of 10-plus plays. Dart wasn’t exactly slinging the ball all over the yard — he didn’t have to — but he led the offense, made the right checks, was in command for much of the game ( he didn’t account for Caleb Downs on the EMPTY blitz ), and made some high-level throws that allowed the Giants to maintain their time-consuming drives. High-level throws via GIPHY The Giants faced this third-and-4 in the red zone. Stalling out and kicking a field goal was the normal outcome in these situations — last time the Giants opened against Dallas, it was a blocked field goal that Andrew Thomas hurt his hamstring on — but I digress. The Giants align in 11 personnel, shot-gun, 3×1 set with a mesh concept over the middle of the field. Dallas ran a cover-four-match play and Isaiah Likely (9) ran the MOSH ( man over ) Odell Beckham Jr.’s (13) MUSH ( man under ). Daron Bland (26) seemed to be in MEG on the backside No. 1 ( Beckham ), and as the veteran receiver ran the MUSH, linebacker Dee Winters (53) pushed the MOSH ( Likely ) toward Bland and safety Malik Hooker (24). Likely sat inside of Hooker, who was late to receive the push, and Dart did a fantastic job putting the football toward Likely’s inside shoulder — away from Hooker. The middle of the field was cleared out by the drag route from Beckham. I appreciate how the mesh concept was Dart’s second read after he saw match principles when viewing his first read toward Malachi Fields (88) and Darnell Mooney (17). The latter was the No. 2 receiver ( innermost ), and he ran to the flat with Fields running a corner off his vertical stem. With the safety over top, Dallas matched three over two, and Dart came off the look and saw the vacated space in the middle of the field and Hooker’s depth. Precise ball placement and a calm read by Dart led to another third-down conversion on the Giants’ first drive. via GIPHY Up 7-0, just outside mid-field, Dart quickly processed the zone coverage and found Malik Nabers for 7 yards on second-and-9. Nabers ran the hook, and Fields ran the wheel as the No. 2 receiver. Dart had to wait for the curl/flat to expand with Cam Skattebo’s (44) flare route. This put the Giants into a third-and-2 that they failed to convert, which led to their only punt of the game. There was plenty of discussion about Dart’s ability to operate quick game concepts efficiently throughout the off-season; sure, this was from the shotgun, and perhaps not perfect, but it did give New York the opportunity to convert on the following play. via GIPHY Jaxson Dart was such a cool customer on 3rd downs. Giants were faced with 3rd&10 here on their second TD drive. A blown pass protection assignment leads to an immediately free A gap pressure. Dart stands tall in the pocket and delivers a seed on the money outside the numbers 👀 pic.twitter.com/Ej4bQjRctC — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) September 14, 2026 Dart extended a drive with this 19yard throw to Likely. Dallas was in Cover-1 and the Giants ran a DAGGER concept to the field. Dart quickly diagnosed man-coverage and attacked the corner route to Likely on the backside. Shavon Revel (28) faced the unfortunate task of guard Likely in space; the tight end manipulated Revel and exploded outside for the first down. Dart was phenomenal under pressure on the play, as the Giants’ offensive line had a rare mishap. Unfortunately, Tyrone Tracy Jr. would fumble plays later. Two-minute drill Dart executed an impressive two-minute drill after Jevon Holland’s interception. Jon Runyan committed a false-start, which put the Giants into this third-and-9: via GIPHY via GIPHY Dart successfully diagnosed the defense during his shotgun drop, prompting him to switch to the backside one (Nabers) and target vulnerabilities in the now-recognized Cover-2 defense. Dart put touch over the top of the flat defender and in front of the bailing-deep- half player. He was mentally and physically dialed in on this play when the lights were brightest in a crucial two-minute drill. He followed this third-and-9 conversion with this far-hash completion to Darnell Mooney (17): via GIPHY Dallas aligned in a Cover-3 strong-side buzz over Likely’s position against a 2×2 set. The deep third defender to the field lost leverage inside to Darnell Mooney’s vertical stem; Mooney exploded toward the sideline when the defender was on the numbers and the curl/flat was enticed to step forward due to the presence of Devin Singletary (26) in the flat. Dart planted and drove the football into Mooney; credit to Mooney for being a professional wide receiver and having soft hands and feet that are spatially aware. Isaiah Likely was 8.8 yards away from the nearest defender when the ball arrived on this touchdown 🫣 DALvsNYG on NBC/Peacock Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rIenIu8EGo — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) September 14, 2026 Dart finished the two-minute drill by finding a wide-open Isaiah Likely in the back of the end zone. The Cowboys had a blown coverage and Dart quickly recognized that two defenders reacted to Mooney’s whip route underneath. The No. 2 receiver on the previous play was Likely, who caught a whip route underneath. Second half via GIPHY via GIPHY The Giants opened the second half with a 12-play, 74-yard drive. On second-and-9, they picked up 16 yards on a catch that was heavily aided by play action. New York had already established the run, and Dallas failed to adjust, allowing the under-center play-action look to pull the linebackers toward the line of scrimmage. That created space for Dart to layer a touch pass over the top to Malik Nabers. And then there was the Devin Singletary sequence: The Singletary sequence wouldn't have happened on previous #Giants teams. However, a blown screen is all too familiar. JMS misses his block, but space was there. Nagy attacked soft leverage w/ Nabers on the next play and then used the attention paid to Nabers to find Singletary… pic.twitter.com/8kjTSBCQb3 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 The Giants’ coaching staff, Dart, and the entire Giants team just kept exploiting the vulnerable flats, while Dallas stayed at depth and kept multiple pairs of eyes on Nabers. Dart’s rushing Dart rushed for 54 yards on 11 carries. Dart showed vision that was coupled with timely play calls and designs from the Giants’ coaching staff. Dart on the move!!! 💨 📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/6DwDC4ZUdk — New York Giants (@Giants) September 14, 2026 via GIPHY Final thoughts Dart shined in the bright lights and is now technically 2-0 against…

title: NFL power rankings, Week 2: NY Giants take massive jump
summary: Sunday night’s impressive victory over the Dallas Cowboys has resulted in the New York Giants taking a massive leap in Week 2 NFL power rankings. The Giants have moved from No. 23 in our aggregated rankings from around the Internet to No. 16, the league’s midpoint. ESPN | No. 18 Week 1 result: Beat the Cowboys 28-20Non-QB […]
full_text: Sunday night’s impressive victory over the Dallas Cowboys has resulted in the New York Giants taking a massive leap in Week 2 NFL power rankings. The Giants have moved from No. 23 in our aggregated rankings from around the Internet to No. 16, the league’s midpoint. ESPN | No. 18 Week 1 result: Beat the Cowboys 28-20 Non-QB newcomer debut: TE Isaiah Likely Likely was quarterback Jaxson Dart’s go-to receiver, catching two third-down passes on the game-ending drive to go along with two touchdowns earlier. Overall, Likely caught all eight targets for 78 yards. The chemistry with Dart throughout training camp carried over to the season, to the point where it’s easy to see Likely having a huge campaign despite never reaching 500 receiving yards in any of his four years with the Ravens. The performance was no surprise to coach John Harbaugh. “I mean, we paid him a lot,” Harbaugh said with a laugh. “That’s what we paid him for, and he did it.” FOX Sports | No. 17 It’s a well-deserved leap in the rankings after John Harbaugh’s debut showed he has a tough, well-rounded and healthy team. When WR Malik Nabers is off his pitch count, this versatile offense is going to cause problems for everyone. Pro Football Network | No. 23 The John Harbaugh era of New York Giants football kicked off in triumphant fashion. They defeated the Cowboys at home, coming away from Sunday night with a key divisional victory. Emotions were high with the Giants’ pregame ceremony honoring those affected by Sept. 11, and New York went home happy. Jaxson Dart got it done through the air and on the ground, throwing for 230 and three passing touchdowns while rushing for 57 yards. The likes of Isaiah Likely and Cam Skattebo were key in the Giants’ victory, and the team’s run defense limited Dallas’ offense to just 3.8 yards per carry. USA Today | No. 14 Don’t want to overrate them this early, but Sunday night’s victory over the Cowboys was no fluke. This was efficient, smashmouth, Harbaugh football, and the rest of the NFC East is officially on notice. Yahoo Sports | No. 14 No team had a better offensive EPA per play through Sunday’s Week 1 games than the Giants. Not even the Bears, who scored 59 points. What stood out was the impact new tight end Isaiah Likely had. He led the Giants with eight catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns. If the Giants’ offense stays mostly healthy, perhaps this can be a surprise playoff team. The Athletic | No. 18 What we learned: They might be for real High expectations around the hiring of John Harbaugh were tempered by what seemed to be just an OK roster. But the Harbaugh era started smashingly, Jaxson Dart looked legit and the defense more than held its own against a good (or so we thought) Dallas offense. Bleacher Report | No. 21 So maybe hiring John Harbaugh was a pretty good idea. Offensively Sunday night, New York was ruthlessly efficient. Jaxson Dart was poised and accurate. Cam Skattebo didn’t have huge numbers, but he got the tough yards when he needed to. Tight end Isaiah Likely was a revelation in his first game with the team. New York was 9-of-11 on third down. That’s nuts. The defense remains a work in progress, but it made just enough plays against one of the NFL’s best offenses a year ago to win the day—and a second straight contest with the Cowboys at Met Life Stadium. It’s still too early to say the Giants are good—the Dallas defense has been awful dating back to 2025. But they were in Week 1, and we’ll find out soon enough how sustainable the improvement is.

title: Fantasy Football 2026: Waiver wire, Week 2 edition
summary: Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 2. Working the waiver wire can be just as important as nailing your draft – especially if you get hit with a lot of injuries or unexpected underperformance. We don’t have a great crop of free agents to look at this week, but there are definitely […]
full_text: Shough shines again | Getty Images Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 2. Working the waiver wire can be just as important as nailing your draft – especially if you get hit with a lot of injuries or unexpected underperformance. We don’t have a great crop of free agents to look at this week, but there are definitely pickups to think about. The Process : Each week, I try to identify the top Waiver Wire targets and evaluate the short- and long-term prospects of those players. I also do my best to reveal which players who are coming off a big week are fool’s gold. Finally, I look at streamers who might help you in a pinch (this is usually more important during Bye weeks). Note that I’m writing this column BEFORE the Week 1 Monday night game (DEN @ KC). Some players discussed won’t be available in your league. I try to list players who are available in more than 50% of leagues. But what does that even mean? A 10-team league with six bench spots will have a much larger Free Agent pool than a 14-team league with eight. Most leagues fall somewhere in between. This isn’t “one size fits all.” By way of example, I won’t list Jalen Coker or Deebo Samuel, Sr. this week, among others who probably aren’t available in any of your leagues. Two quick words about Week 2 waivers: (1) If you’re in a league that uses FAAB bids to process waivers, remember that your dollars are worth more right now than they will be later, since you’re using them to buy players for the entire season, potentially; and (2) People overreact to Week 1 performance. Keep an eye on who gets dropped this week, and especially rookies who did very little in Week 1. You might be able to scoop up someone else’s discarded treasure. Remember, it’s a long season that’s barely underway. WEEK 2 BYES: NONE Quarterback: Tyler Shough was a Top-10 fantasy QB over the final third of last season, and in Week 1 he kept that going, throwing for 410 yards and three TDs (and two INTs) in a thrilling second half shootout with the formidable Lions. The New Orleans defense is leaky, Kellen Moore’s offense is up-tempo, and more free-for-alls could be in store. Shough isn’t rostered in the majority of 1-QB leagues, but should be. I’m always hesitant to trust Bryce Young , and the Bears kept scoring for three straight hours so Carolina was chasing points throughout. Still, he’s got some decent weapons, he can run, and the Panthers might find themselves in a bunch of high-scoring games. He had four total TDs on Sunday and threw for 361 yards. Just know that it’s always a roller coaster with him. Sam Darnold and Kyler Murray both got hurt in Week 1, and it’s unclear how much time they’ll miss. Carson Wentz threw for three TDs in relief of Murray, and given the weapons at his disposal, he could be a sneaky play if you need a QB2 in a Superflex. The Vikings’ next three opponents: Bucs, Dolphins, and Saints. Hmm… Drew Lock offers less upside, but he can sling it and isn’t the worst option out there if you need a replacement for Murray or Darnold in a 2-QB league. Running Back: There isn’t a ton to recommend at running back this week. Kaelon Black is THE hot name this week, and deservedly so. The question is whether his usage in Week 1 was an anomaly or indicative of an effort to not overwork Christian McCaffrey again. Black and McCaffrey saw 15 touches apiece in the Australia game, with Black getting more carries. He also showed a nice burst. McCaffrey’s backup is always worth rostering – you’re one injury away from having a potential league-winner in Kyle Shanahan’s offense. It appears Black has stand-alone value as well. He’s a priority add. There aren’t many other backs to recommend. But if you need some bench depth and potential lottery tickets, you can consider Emari Demercado , who is now the #2 in a very thin Dallas backfield, or Braelon Allen or Mike Washington, Jr., who both saw a decent number of touches in a backup role. Wide Receiver Here’s where it gets a little more fun, as there are several receivers worth considering if you need some help (and you might if you’ve rostered A.J. Brown, Ladd McConkey, or Zay Flower s). DeVaughn Vele was on my sleepers list for Week 1 and as the WR2 in Kellen Moore’s offense while Jordyn Tyson is out, he’s got some nice upside. We saw that on Sunday. He put up a 7-79-1 stat line on nine targets, and showed excellent hands on several catches. It’s worth noting that he and Shough built a rapport at the end of last season, so his Week 1 role and output doesn’t feel flukey. He’s a WR3/Flex with upside. Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs are worth considering while A.J. Brown is out. Doubs looked awful on Wednesday night (including a key drop), but they paid him a lot of money and I expect him to get his chances. Hollins was open whenever Drake Maye needed him to be. Rookies Caleb Douglas (5-94-0 on 7 targets), Denzel Boston (2-59-1 on 4 targets) and Antonio Williams (4-64-1 on 4 targets) all contributed in Week 1, and given the receiver rooms they’re in, and the defenses their teams have, there’s reason to believe each can each carve out a decent role this season. They’re stashes for me, for now. Another rookie to consider stashing if you have space is Malachi Fields . A few others to consider: Dontayvion Wicks , DeMarcus Robinson , Kalif Raymond , and Rashod Bateman (no catches in Week 1, but the Ravens’ receiver room is running out of healthy bodies). Tight End: Four players to consider if you need help: Mike Gesicki, T.J. Hockenson, Brenton Strange, and Pat Freiermuth . All are proven commodities as pass-catchers, and are in good situations to give you the periodic touchdown that you’re looking for if you plug them in. Michael Mayer should be an OK but unspectacular fill-in for Brock Bowers if he misses more time. Good luck with your waiver claims!
author: David Hartman

title: Giants-Cowboys: 5 plays that were key to victory
summary: The New York Giants defeated the Dallas Cowboys, 28–20, under the bright lights of Sunday Night Football. New York dominated on offense, outgaining Dallas 394–244 and controlling the clock for 36:40 compared to the Cowboys’ 23:20. More importantly, this was a statement win in which the Giants’ offense dictated terms to the Dallas defense, producing […]
full_text: Devin Singletary celebrates a touchdown against the Cowboys. | Getty Images The New York Giants defeated the Dallas Cowboys, 28–20, under the bright lights of Sunday Night Football. New York dominated on offense, outgaining Dallas 394–244 and controlling the clock for 36:40 compared to the Cowboys’ 23:20. More importantly, this was a statement win in which the Giants’ offense dictated terms to the Dallas defense, producing four touchdown drives and four separate drives of at least 10 plays. Matt Nagy and Greg Roman deserve tremendous credit for the offensive game plan and execution. The Giants consistently varied their rushing concepts, pairing a diverse run scheme with well-timed pre-snap motion that manipulated Dallas’ defensive structure and created leverage advantages at the point of attack. By forcing the Cowboys to adjust alignments and responsibilities before the snap, New York repeatedly put Dallas in positions where it was out-leveraged and couldn’t consistently fit the run game. New York was heavy with their personnel, and Jaxson Dart executed several critical situations well throughout the game. The defense failed to sack Dak Prescott, but they held their own in the victory. Overall, the Giants kicked off the John Harbaugh era with an important divisional win against a quarterback who rarely loses to the Giants. It was an excellent effort, and here are five plays — or sequence of plays — that were important to the Giants’ victory. Play 1: What a way to finish an opening drive Ricard motion to lead w/ Isaiah Likely following on a SG counter run that Dallas failed to see. Wonderfully executed by the Giants. The Greg Roman effect in full force on the #Giants opening drive. pic.twitter.com/39wcHvUi4m — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 Firstly, let’s start with this – the Giants set a TONE to conclude their first offensive drive of the season – a ten-play, 83-yard drive that showcased the rushing attack designed by Greg Roman. Matt Nagy did an excellent job calling different running schemes with pre-snap motion that gave the Giants a spatial advantage to one side: ISO, QB read, counter, and weak-side runs were all featured on the Giants’ first drive that ended in this counter three-yard touchdown scamper by Cam Skattebo (44) behind the blocks of Patrick Ricard (45) and Isaiah Likely (9). Play 2: First drive of second half Jet-motion play action roll-out for Dart, who finds Likely sitting after stepping toward the LOS, acting as if he's blocking down. Likely's second TD of the game. Giants go up two scores. pic.twitter.com/dPi8CtdiNg — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 The Giants finished the first half strongly with a touchdown and then started the second half strong with a twelve-play drive that ate up eight minutes of the clock and resulted in an Isaiah Likely touchdown. The Giants continued their physical nature, using heavy personnel from under center – the Giants ran the football seven times on the drive, and it helped set up the play-action passing attack well. To Dallas’ credit, though, they mounted their own 12-play drive that ended in a touchdown, which added drama as the third quarter wound down. Play 3: Tyrone Tracy Jr.’s short leash Tyrone Tracy Jr. Gets Rocked By Jalen Thompson, Fumbles… Balls Loose. Cowboys Quickly Pounce On It, Tough Start For Tracy. Yikes. pic.twitter.com/mD7RJGb0n6 — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) September 14, 2026 Tyrone Tracy Jr. had a rough pre-season for the Giants, and he compounded it by fumbling the football on his second touch of the game. Matt Nagy used multiple backs through the first half, and Tracy gave the football back to Dallas while the Giants were driving in the two-minute drill. It was an excellent effort by Quinnen Williams, and an unfortunate situation for a back who was already on thin ice. Tracy Jr. was bailed out, though, by a Jevon Holland interception of Dak Prescott. We didn’t see Tracy for the rest of the game. Play(s) 4: End of the half scenario Jevon Holland gave the Giants’ offense another chance before halftime: Jevon Holland with the INT in the 2-minute drill! Pressure by Kayvon Thibodeaux: duck to duck assist. pic.twitter.com/BX53rP2Nrk — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 The Holland interception gave Jaxson Dart the football at the Giants’ 45-yard line. A Jon Runyan false-start penalty put the Giants in a third-and-nine situation that was converted with an excellent touch pass over the top of a curl-flat defender; the pass was completed for 13 yards to Malik Nabers. Dart proceeded to go 3 of 3, resulting in a 15-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely, giving the Giants a 14-7 lead that they would maintain into halftime. Jaxson Dart finished the first half in an excellent fashion after the Holland INT. Dart went 4/4 with this third down conversation, as well as the touchdown to Likely off the blown Dallas' coverage. pic.twitter.com/xIaKXPZAfX — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 Dallas blew the high-low corner/whip combination to the boundary side of the field, and Likely was wide open for the score. Play 5: Giants’ offense continues to succeed! Devin Singletary touched the football four consecutive times, leading to this fourth quarter touchdown. This play concluded a 13 play drive. This has been an impressive performance by the #Giants and their staff. pic.twitter.com/y7GmKYDUy6 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 The Giants went up two scores midway through the fourth quarter with this 9-yard touchdown reception by Devin Singletary. Matt Nagy saw a vulnerability in Dallas’ flat and kept attacking the Cowboys; Singletary touched the ball on four consecutive plays, leading to the two-score lead that was too much for Dallas to overcome. I appreciate how Nagy and Greg Roman kept taking what the defense gave them, and consistently matriculated the football down the field for the Giants.
author: Nick Falato

title: NY Giants news: John Harbaugh, roster moves,  grades, game reviews, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants get to face off against the Los Angeles Rams in primetime. How the Giants ‘broke’ Cowboys in the fourth quarter: ‘They were ready to go home’ | New York Post At the end of the day, Big Blue wasn’t “tired” […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants get to face off against the Los Angeles Rams in primetime. How the Giants ‘broke’ Cowboys in the fourth quarter: ‘They were ready to go home’ | New York Post At the end of the day, Big Blue wasn’t “tired” as right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. Dallas sure was. “At the end of the fourth quarter, they had to huddle up. When you see a team huddle up, that’s when you know you are breaking them,” Eluemunor said following the Giants’ 28-20 win over the Cowboys on “Sunday Night Football” at MetLife Stadium. “I can’t tell you how many times they rotated their D-line. They just broke in the fourth quarter. We could’ve played another two or three quarters. They were ready to go home.” NFL Week 1: Takeaways, questions, fantasy spin for Sunday games | ESPN.com Should the Giants be taken seriously in the NFC East? This was a statement game for the John Harbaugh Giants. They looked like the better team in beating a Cowboys squad that had prevailed in 16 of its previous 18 meetings with the Giants. New York’s offense looked dangerous with a power running game (165 yards) led by Cam Skattebo (18 carries, 81 yards), and quarterback Jaxson Dart was in command throughout. The defense also looked greatly improved. With neither the Eagles nor Commanders looking dominant in Week1, the Giants could be a real threat in the NFC East. For the first time in years, it’s not an outlandish thought. NFL Week 1 grades for all 32 teams | CBSSports.com New York Giants: A-. For the first time in more than 10 years, the Giants might actually have a head coach who can get them to the promised land. This was only one game, but John Harbaugh has already turned this team around. The Giants looked more prepared than Dallas and they were definitely more physical: Harbaugh’s team bullied the Cowboys in the trenches. Led by Cam Skattebo, the Giants’ offense totaled 165 yards on the ground, and it was even better through the air with Jaxson Dart throwing for 230 yards and three touchdowns. A new era of football has arrived in New York and Giants fans should be feeling really good about the future of this team. John Harbaugh used his father to motivate the Giants. It was his best call of the week | The Athletic John Harbaugh asked his father to speak to the New York Giants on the night before his grand debut. Jack Harbaugh explained that during a 1967 fight in the Houston Astrodome, Ali battered heavyweight champ Ernie Terrell, who had repeatedly referred to Ali by his birth name, Cassius Clay. “What’s my name?” Ali had shouted at Terrell in the ring. “So I talked to the players about respect,” Jack Harbaugh said. “You can’t ask for it, you can’t pray for it, and you can’t expect it. You’ve got to reach out and you’ve got to demand it. … When you line up over a guy, you’ve got to look him in his eye and say, ‘What’s my name? You’re going to respect me before this is all over’.” In first game with Giants, John Harbaugh delivers statement win: ‘We’re on our way’ | SNY.tv It was a Sunday night statement for a franchise embarrassed and embattled for the better part of a decade. The Giants are here. And with those two as the pillars of their organization, they won’t be going anywhere. “We’re on our way,” Harbaugh said. The Giants’ locker room was subdued by victory standards — a testament to the culture Harbaugh is trying to instill. Players were happy and joking, more talkative than usual, but it was not some rowdy frat party. There was a reason for that, Brian Burns said. This was only one win. “Act like you’ve been there before,” he added. Orlvosky: The tape proves Giants aren’t a fluke "That was the fastest that Jaxson Dart has played with his eyes in his young career.. He saw it well and the ball came out well.. I was very impressed by the way that he played" @danorlovsky7 #PMSLive https://t.co/tmt6iqKlM7 pic.twitter.com/Ex6ZuUKUuV — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) September 14, 2026 How John Harbaugh sets the standard, Jaxson Dart the ceiling for Giants | The Record Jaxson Dart was everything all of his critics said he would never be Sunday night, and the quarterback of the New York Giants shattered that narrative during a defining victory over the Dallas Cowboys. He can’t play in the pocket, they cried. Not a talented enough passer. Injury prone. Celebrity QB. What anyone paying attention to these Giants has known for a while now is that Dart establishes the ceiling. He is to John Harbaugh what Eli Manning was for Tom Coughlin, what Phil Simms was for Bill Parcells. QB Report Cards for 2026 NFL Week 1 | Bleacher Report Jaxson Dart, New York Giants: Grade: A+. Dart’s performance during Sunday Night Football against the rival Dallas Cowboys was nearly flawless, which portends bigger and better things for the quarterback and his team. “For him to have all this on his plate and to execute the way he did, to me, was just tremendous and very impressive,” Harbaugh told reporters. “It was a great performance by Jaxson.” Dart added, “I felt very comfortable. I thought that we just did a really good job of staying in progress throughout the game. I thought (offensive coordinator Matt Nagy) called an awesome game, and I thought the guys just played really, really hard. So it made my job a lot easier, and guys all over the place made a ton of plays, so I’m excited about that.” From Big Blue View ‘Things I think’ about Giants-Cowboys: ‘Unbelievable environment’ best sign of all Giants-Cowboys ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ review: Giants pay off physical summer Giants at Rams Week 2 opening odds: New York opens as big underdogs John Harbaugh ‘couldn’t pass up’ chance to tackle Giants’ WR Malik Nabers Malik Nabers on his comeback: ‘Yeah, it’s time’ Giants waive wide receiver, add running back to practice squad Giants-Cowboys instant grades following New York’s Week 1 victory PFF grades for the NY Giants’ 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys 4 things we learned from the Giants’ 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys This week’s opponent Sean McVay: TBD if Aaron Donald plays vs. Giants in Week 2 | Pro Football Talk Rams’ McVay: Won’t have timeline on Garrett until after surgery | ESPN.com If Rams coach Sean McVay’s postgame comments seemed dramatic, there could be a reason | The Athletic The Giants stole 49ers’ playbook and that is bad news for Rams | Turf Show Times BBV mailbag Have a Giants-related question? full_text: Phil Mafah | Getty Images The New York Giants have waived wide receiver/special teamer Dalen Cambre , who was just added to the team’s 53-man roster on Saturday, per the league’s transactions wire. Cambre, a second-year player, figures to return to the practice squad if he clears waivers. The Giants are signing running back Phil Mafah to their practice squad . Mafah, 23, was a seventh-round pick by the Dallas Cowboys in 2025. He appeared in one game for Dallas last season with five carries for 18 yards, and two receptions for 11 yards. Mafah was waived by the Cowboys at the end of August in the cutdown to the 53-man roster limit. Mafah, 6-foot-1, 232 pounds, was part of a workout conducted by the Giants on Monday. Others in the workout were: DE Dominic Bailey RB Ulysses Bentley LB Jack Dingle DT Jalen Hunt RB D’Ernest Johnson DT Haggai Chisom Ndubuisi LB T.J. Quinn DT Jay Toia RB Blake Watson
