title: NFL Power Rankings: Washington Commanders are better after 2-point loss?
summary: The Washington Commanders lost their season opener to the Philadelphia Eagles, and everyone is trying to find the positives…except for most power rankers. The Commanders were 5.5-point road underdogs, but lost by 24-22 after failing to convert on a game-tying two-point conversion. The defense was improved from last season, and it should have been with […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders celebrates after a touchdown against the Philadelphia Eagles during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Washington Commanders lost their season opener to the Philadelphia Eagles, and everyone is trying to find the positives…except for most power rankers. The Commanders were 5.5-point road underdogs, but lost by 24-22 after failing to convert on a game-tying two-point conversion. The defense was improved from last season, and it should have been with new starters in over half the positions. Jayden Daniels and the offense need work, but did enough in the 4th quarter to keep the game closer than Philly wanted. Week 1 is a weird one with less preseason games leading to rusty players and a lot of mental mistakes. The national media was very down on Washington heading into the season, and that hasn’t changed much after a tough division loss. The ceiling and the floor both raised after a “good” loss, but their average ranking rose less than a spot. The Commanders head to Dallas on Sunday for a division game against the Cowboys who were dominated by the New York Giants in primetime. Washington ranks as high as #18 with high praise for this year’s free agency and draft classes. The other side of the spectrum has them ranked as low as #31, and some dark times in Washington. Winning the Super Bowl odds : +7,000 To Make the Playoffs: Make +265, Miss -330 Jayden Daniels MVP Odds: +3,000 Jayden Daniels Comeback Player of the Year Odds: +1,000 Washington Commanders Win Total O/U: Over 7.5(+105), Under 7.5(-125) High: 16 Low: 27 Average: 23.1 #16 Pro Football Network (Infante) The Washington Commanders deserve credit for how they fought back against the Eagles, scoring 13 points in the fourth quarter and getting into position to tie the game up after a touchdown late in regulation. However, a failed two-point conversion saw the Commanders fall 24-22, kicking off their new season with a divisional loss. Jayden Daniels only averaged 4.8 yards per attempt, and before the fourth quarter, he was largely ineffective for Washington’s offense. The Commanders got good pass-rushing production out of their new-look front seven, but their run defense was a major weakness; they allowed 5.4 yards per carry in the ground game against the Eagles’ dynamic backfield duo of Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley. #18 NFL Trade Rumors (Woodie) All in all, it was an encouraging start for the Commanders. They didn’t get the win, but I thought Washington’s defense acquitted itself well. Even if there are lingering questions about the offensive line, we know what this offense can do. It’s the defense that was a bigger concern. While it was far from perfect, Washington’s defense kept them in the game at times. We’ll see if they can keep that up. Last week: 21 Essentially Sports (Hubbard) The Washington Commanders are in for a dogfight in Philadelphia. Even with the loss, it’s still an encouraging loss for Washington. The offense will settle in under David Blough throughout the week, but the defense was more impressive. The unit held the Eagles to 318 total yards and limited Saquon Barkley to 83 rushing yards. Last week: 19 #20 Team Rankings Last week: 21 #21 USA Today (Davis) Despite all the summer handwringing about the offensive line, QB Jayden Daniels was only sacked once and hit twice Sunday. Clean up their mental errors, and the Commanders likely escape Philly with a W. Last week: 25 #22 Yahoo Sports (Schwab) Everything was labored with Jayden Daniels and the Commanders’ offense . The line didn’t protect well but Daniels often held the ball too long, perhaps because his receivers weren’t getting open. He averaged 3.41 seconds per throw, the slowest among all QBs through Sunday’s games, per Next Gen Stats. ( H/T to reporter Tashan Reed for pointing that out .) The Eagles have a good defense and that led to some of the issues. But the opener wasn’t a good omen, especially for new coordinator David Blough . At least he has Daniels in his corner. The QB defended the shovel pass play that the Eagles stuffed on a 2-point conversion attempt, preventing a tie in the final minute of regulation. “It was the right call,” Daniels told reporters postgame . “Anything Blough calls, man. I’m with him. Regardless, however everybody else might want to view it, man, I’m with Blough 100%.” Last week: 22 AZ Central (Cluff) Jayden Daniels went 18-for-34 for 164 yards and two touchdowns in his return for the Commanders and also had Washington in position for a nice comeback late in the game. Last week: 20 Stadium Rant (North) The Commanders would’ve liked to see a little more from the offense against Philadelphia. They struggled to consistently move the ball in the first half and couldn’t capitalize on a tired Eagles defense in the fourth quarter. #23 ESPN Non-QB newcomer debut: LB Sonny Styles Styles finished with one sack, in which he trucked running back Saquon Barkley en route to Jalen Hurts , as well as two tackles for a loss and a QB hit. Styles got caught out of position on a 43-yard touchdown pass to tight end Dallas Goedert — but that was because Styles and two teammates pointed at Goedert at the snap, expecting a false start call. Styles also took over playcalling duties when Frankie Luvu injured his groin. The No. 7 pick wasn’t perfect, but it was a good debut. Last week: 20 Sharp Football Analysis (Summerlin) Despite a mixed offensive performance, the Commanders were just a failed two-point try away from tying the game with the Eagles and potentially forcing overtime. That’s promising, but the offense will need to be more consistent, and the defense will need to give up fewer big plays moving forward. Last week: 23 Fansided (La Canfora) They showed up and they played hard. But Jayden Daniels did not look comfortable in that offense at all until they had to get desperate late. Might need more option looks and designed runs. I think it’s going to be a long season, but they gave the Eagles a game. Last week: 26 Deadspin (Weiler) OL struggles made life hard for Jayden Daniels, who still nearly led a comeback. #24 Sports Illustrated (Orr) It’s not a consolation prize, but to be one boneheaded Stefon Diggs decision away from taking your division rivals to extra innings is no small task, especially with a totally revamped defense and new coordinators on both sides. Still, Jayden Daniels looked pedestrian and the Commanders had a lower offensive success rate in the first weekend than the Titans. Last week: 18 Sporting News (Iyer) Jayden Daniels was struggling for much of the day in Philadelphia but got revved up late by trusting the running game and new weapons Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams. That late rally that fell short will give Commanders hope that Daniels is getting back on track. Dan Quinn, however, should keep feeling the heat after a frustrating two-point loss. Last week: 21 The Score Bad vibes will ruin the team . The Commanders don’t look anything like the electric team that reached the NFC title game during Jayden Daniels’ rookie season. The third-year passer was mocked in the offseason for his odd dispute with LSU over the No. 5 jersey. Dan Quinn is a popular pick for the first coach to be fired this season. And Stefon Diggs committed a costly penalty in his team debut. On and off the field, the energy around the 2026 Commanders doesn’t feel right. Last week: 23 #25 NFL.com (Shook) I heard the complaints from you, Commanders fans, about where I had placed Washington in my rankings last week and your team had your back on Sunday. Dan Quinn’s squad came up short but battled for four quarters with the reigning NFC East champion Eagles. The Commanders were a two-point conversion away from potentially forcing overtime in a game many expected them to lose by double-digits. I give credit…

title: Washington Commanders Whiteboard: Notes and observations from Week 1
summary: Before the advent of media devices, football coaches at all levels used simple whiteboards to outline plays, map out player positions and explain schemes in real time. Nowadays digital playbooks and tablets have taken over, but coaches still use whiteboards on occasion to impart information quickly and effectively. The following are some quick notes and […]
full_text: Before the advent of media devices, football coaches at all levels used simple whiteboards to outline plays, map out player positions and explain schemes in real time. Nowadays digital playbooks and tablets have taken over, but coaches still use whiteboards on occasion to impart information quickly and effectively. The following are some quick notes and observations from the Washington Commanders’ heartbreaking 22-24 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field. The Commanders’ defense has been upgraded There was plenty of speculation this offseason about what exactly Daronte Jones’ defense would look like and if Adam Peters’ offseason additions would make a difference. The early returns weren’t perfect, but the defense looks to have taken a massive step forward from what we have seen from Dan Quinn’s first two years at the helm. Jones’ defense is fast and aggressive. The Commanders defensive coordinator didn’t look like a rookie in in his first game at the controls. Jones did a nice job of rotating Daron Payne, Javon Kinlaw, and Charles Omenihu along the defensive line. As expected, Daronte called plenty of blitzes in front of zone coverage and, for the most part, the pressures were effective when they were dialed up. The front seven played fast and disciplined, and aside from one long run, they bottled up Eagles running back Saquon Barkley for most of the game. Washington Commanders’ defense Week 1 per @SumerSports : •Zone: 84.8% •Man: 15.2% •Blitz Rate: 39.39% (16.27% higher than NFL avg) •Pressure Rate: 48.48% (9.93% higher than NFL avg) •TFL Rate: 24% (15% higher than NFL avg) Ya that’ll play Daronte Jones. #Commanders — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) September 14, 2026 #Eagles run game is going to need massive improvement. Per @NextGenStats , 78 of Saquon Barkley's 83 yards came after contact, and he was hit at or behind the LOS on 7 of 15 carries. He forced five missed tackles. pic.twitter.com/50fvYxrtBI — Devin Jackson (@RealD_Jackson) September 14, 2026 The performance was far from perfect though, as the defense allowed several explosive plays that altered the course of the game. That number includes Dontayvion Wicks’ 64-yard reception and two Dallas Goedert touchdowns. A 22-yard rush by Jalen Hurts on 3rd-and-18 was particularly damaging. 3rd and 18? No problem for Jalen Hurts 💨 WASvsPHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/JZ3ltUv3v5 — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Payne and Ominehu both fell down on the play, and at this point Payne was noticeably gassed and takes some time to get back on his feet. Hurts recognized the opening and took off, but when Jordan Magee goes to close on him, the linebacker appeared to injure his hamstring. The net result is a 22-yard scramble and conversion that led to the second Goedert touchdown shortly afterwards. Still, there were lots of positives for the Commanders defense. Amik Robertson largely went unnoticed, which typically means a cornerback had a good game and marquee free-agent signing Odafe Oweh got home for a sack to go along with two tackles for a loss and one quarterback hit. No turnovers for a defense that emphasizes their importance is glaring, but the Commanders’ defense looks like it can keep the team competitive as long as the offense holds up its end of the bargain. David Blough will continue to grow as an offensive coordinator Unlike his counterpart, David Blough certainly looked the part of a first-time offensive coordinator. After a positive first series, the Commanders’ offense only accumulated 126 yards of total offense and converted 2-of-8 third-down attempts in the first half. As expected, the offense had a number of false start penalties, but Blough’s play-calling and tempo were also stagnant for most of the first three quarters. There is reason for optimism, though, as Blough shifted Daniels to a shotgun look in the fourth quarter, sped up the tempo and capitalized on Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams’ ability to get open in the intermediate portion of the field. This demonstrates that Blough is not only willing, but also able to adjust his play-calling on the fly, something we haven’t always seen from the Commanders’ offensive coordinators in the past. Jayden Daniels goes 9/11 100yds and 2TDs in the 4th quarter. Noticeably he spent less time calling plays from his wrist band in the 4th quarter and the offense was kore uptempo. #Commanders #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/QnslHz3iVH — Mando 🐍 (@TheMandoReport) September 14, 2026 The play call on the 2-point conversion certainly deserves criticism, but for those that believe Blough should have left the game in Jayden Daniels’ hands, in some ways he did. There were multiple options available to the Commanders’ quarterback on the play, and Daniels made the correct read as the defensive end commits up the field, going with the primary option in tight end John Bates on the shovel pass. The play had Sam Cosmi out in front to block and could have been a conversion, but Nick Allegretti failed to seal Moro Ojomo, as the defensive tackle made a beautiful spin move to avoid his block. Why didn’t Jayden Daniels hit the open flat on the 2 pointer? (Explained in the clip) pic.twitter.com/C4yIAdorul — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) September 14, 2026 For a quarterback learning a new system and a suspect interior offensive line, it was the wrong call, but Blough will develop his situational play-calling and acumen as he grows into his role. The question is if Dan Quinn and the Washington Commanders have the luxury of waiting for it to happen. Plenty of new faces, many of the same problems Blough certainly isn’t the only one that deserves to take blame for the Commanders’ loss. While both coordinators and a good portion of the roster may have changed, the perpetual problems that plague Washington’s football team remain the same. Eagles DC Vic Fangio was able to create pressure by only rushing four linemen, which allowed the defense to bracket the wide receivers. They failed to create separation down the field and often times Daniels had nowhere to go with the ball. That resulted in some late pressures, although Daniels did a nice job throwing it away when the play was not there. Commanders QB Jayden Daniels was pressured on 19 of 38 dropbacks in Week 1 against the Eagles (50.0% pressure rate), tying his career high (Week 9, 2025 vs. Seahawks) per Next Gen Stats. — Andrew Erickson™ (@AndrewErickson_) September 14, 2026 Terry McLaurin was targeted four times for two receptions and 14 receiving yards, while Stefon Diggs dropped two passes, the same number he dropped over the entire season last year. title: What Dorance Armstrong could add to Washington Commanders pass rush
summary: The Commanders pass rush got a little harder to handle on Monday, with Dorance Armstrong reinstated after serving a one-game suspension.   Armstrong missed Sunday’s 24-22 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles for violating the NFL’s personal conduct policy – read more about the violation here – but will be back in the mix moving forward. […]
full_text: The Commanders pass rush got a little harder to handle on Monday, with Dorance Armstrong reinstated after serving a one-game suspension. Armstrong missed Sunday’s 24-22 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles for violating the NFL’s personal conduct policy – read more about the violation here – but will be back in the mix moving forward. There’s no corresponding roster move required, the Commanders already had an open roster slot after releasing offensive tackle D.J. Humphries last week. Getting Armstrong back is a good thing for a Commanders defensive front that showed signs of real quality without him. Washington had three sacks and five quarterback hits against Philadelphia, using high blitz rate and an active front to create chaos in the backfield. Adding Armstrong to the mix should serve to help the Commanders in both versatility and depth. He has been a starter or a heavy rotational presence most of his career. He had 16 sacks combined for Dallas over the 2022-23 seasons, with five in 2024, his first year in Washington. He had 5.5 last season and an absolutely scorching 19.5% quarterback pressure rate before a torn ACL ended that campaign early. Armstrong was able to practice during the preseason, though it remains uncertain if he’ll be ready in time to play his former team when Washington plays at Dallas in Week 2. He’ll be an asset to be sure, but exactly how might he fit into Daronte Jones’ new scheme? It’s markedly different that what he was in during previous seasons. I texted Mark Tyler that question. Here’s a summary of what our HH analyst said: Armstrong is more of a pure defensive end than a 3-4 outside linebacker who can drop into coverage. He could be an edge rusher with his hand in the dirt coming from out wide, or he could kick inside on sub packages with Odafe Oweh or K’Lavon Chaisson outside of him. In other words, he gives the Commanders options. That last prospect sounds intriguing and illustrates how Jones could use Armstrong creatively. He’ll be a key depth piece, providing quality even with Oweh or Chaisson catching a break. Both of those guys played roughly 80% of the defensive snaps against the Eagles, and rookie Joshua Josephs fared well in limited action. Washington has a quality collection of pass rushers now, which should allow the defense to get after the quarterback or make life difficult in the run game. What are your expectations for Armstrong now that he’s back in mix? Let us know in the comments below.

There are a lot of good things fans can take away from this game, however, there are no moral victories and a loss is a loss — especially within the division. Quinn and company will have a week to clean some things up before traveling to Dallas to take on a Cowboys squad who lost to the Giants Sunday evening. title: Commanders News: A lot of good, a lot of bad in Week 1 loss to Eagles
summary: The Daily Slop – 15 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: The Daily Slop – 15 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles The Athletic (paywall) Commanders’ loss to Eagles revealed a new-look defense with an edge Facing Philadelphia’s vaunted offensive line and its multiple playmakers, Washington held the Eagles to only 10 first downs, half as many as the Commanders’ offense. That was the lowest total in the league through the first 15 games of Week 1. The physicality coach Dan Quinn has preached since he arrived in Washington two seasons ago was evident throughout, with 13 total “havoc” plays — takeaways, tackles for loss, sacks and pass breakups — the Commanders’ fourth-most in a game since the start of the ’24 season. View Link Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles, who wore the green dot in the second half when Frankie Luvu was sidelined with a groin injury, showed his mettle in the third quarter when he trucked Eagles running back Saquon Barkley on the way to his first career sack. On the next drive, he stuffed Barkley for a three-yard loss on a run. Just as promising as the production was much of Washington’s process: It sent five-man pressures on 12 of the Eagles’ 33 dropbacks and generated pressure on two-thirds of them. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Eagles outlast Commanders, but lots of issues for both teams’ new-look offenses Washington, in its first game with 31-year-old David Blough as offensive coordinator, struggled to generate consistent offense until its final two possessions. Meanwhile, Philadelphia had issues of its own sustaining drives in the second half under 34-year-old first-time coordinator Sean Mannion. Leading 14-9 at halftime, Philadelphia went three-and-out on each of its first three drives in the second half — setting the stage for Washington’s near comeback. Eagles fans will not be happy after having to sit through yet another system going mostly stale in the second half. Mannion’s offense stagnated after entering the second half with a 14-9 lead. The Eagles went three-and-out on their first three drives. They opened each drive under center while fielding two tight ends. Barkley was stuffed on the first run for a 1-yard loss. On the third drive, the Eagles fielded the same look on second-and-7, and Commanders linebacker Sonny Styles shot through a gap on a blitz to bring Barkley down for a 3-yard loss. Hurts was sacked on the subsequent third-and-10, and the Eagles punted again. The style of play mirrored that of the 2025 season. Former offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo oversaw an offense that too often leaned on the strength of the Eagles’ defense. The 2025 Eagles had a minus-30 point differential while playing with a lead in the second half. They had a minus-3 point differential in the second half against the Commanders. Commanders fans should put their heads on their pillows believing their defense isn’t going to be the utter disaster it has been for two seasons. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles recorded the first sack of his career and absolutely blew up Barkley in the process. Safety Nick Cross, linebacker Frankie Luvu, cornerback Rasul Douglas and others delivered heavy hits. And the Commanders sacked Hurts three times — from Styles, Luvu and new $100-million man Odafe Oweh. View Link But even with the flashes, there is plenty to clean up — most notably, the absolute gash plays that killed the Commanders all day. At halftime, the Eagles had 182 yards of offense — 64 on a Hurts-to-Wicks completion and 42 on a Barkley run. That’s 58 percent of their output on two plays, and that doesn’t count the 17-yard touchdown pass on third-and-goal to Goedert. That continued in the second half. On third-and-18, Hurts was allowed to scamper for 22 yards. And the play that ended up being the difference in the game: Goedert’s 43-yard touchdown — on which he got wide open. That’s 171 of the Eagles’ 318 total yards on just four plays. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig (paywall) If only the Commanders had another shot at two Jayden Daniels, hemmed in much of the game by one of the league’s top defenses and hampered by pre-snap penalties, threw touchdown passes to Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams. On Washington’s final 12-play, 63-yard drive, Williams snatched Daniels’ throw a nanosecond before it hit the ground for a 1-yard touchdown with one minute remaining. Momentum, Washington. Now came the chance to tie the game. The two-point play call from first-time offensive coordinator David Blough had Daniels attempting a shovel pass to tight end John Bates. Daniels and head coach Dan Quinn liked the call from the Eagles’ 2-yard line. But as the play began, Quinn’s eyes told him danger lurked. For more from Ben Standig, click here Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . ESPN NFL Week 1: Takeaways, questions, fantasy spin for Sunday games Commanders Did quarterback Jayden Daniels show enough to inspire a bounce-back season? Daniels looked sharp this summer in new coordinator David Blough’s offense. But for most of Sunday’s game — his first since Week 14 last season — the offense struggled against one of the NFL’s best defenses. Daniels hesitated too many times because he didn’t have an open target or wasn’t confident in what he saw. That’s concerning, as one of his best traits is being decisive. In the first half, he completed 6 of 16 passes for 43 yards. Daniels still finished strong, leading two scoring drives to nearly tie the score. But if Washington is going to avoid a bad start, Blough and Daniels need to find a better rhythm early. Most surprising performance: Wide receiver Terry McLaurin did not catch a pass until less than five minutes remained in the contest. He finished with just two catches and four targets. It’s not what Blough had in mind when he took over, saying he wanted to get McLaurin 10 targets per game. But the Eagles often doubled him, rolled coverage his way or simply blanketed him. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Mistakes doomed the Commanders — but Jayden Daniels finished standing upright For most of the first three quarters, the Commanders offense, and Blough, its first-year offensive coordinator , got very little done, wasting multiple opportunities given to it by Washington’s defense, which stacked three-and-outs much of the night and forced seven Eagles punts. (To be sure: The defense gave up a handful of killer big plays, too.) Washington’s offense produced a field goal on its first possession, then didn’t move the ball again until its next-to-last possession of the first half. Eagles linebacker Zack Baun was just … everywhere. They have to be better. But. Sunday marked the first time Daniels started and finished a game for Washington since Oct. 13, against the Chicago Bears. Think of that: It’s almost been a year since Jayden Daniels actually played four full quarters for the Commanders. That is a significant hurdle for him to overcome, after his disastrous 2025, which included separate hamstring, knee and elbow injuries that limited him to seven games. He is the North Star for owner Josh Harris’ team, capable of doing great things when on the field. With Daniels, Washington has a chance. View Link Daniels, in his third season, looked like a quarterback who understood his importance. He didn’t take off at the first sign of pressure. He tried to climb the pocket and throw downfield, and when that wasn’t available, he threw the ball away. He ran Blough’s plays well, and spread the ball around. The Eagles played cloud coverage with safety help on Terry McLaurin most of the day, so Daniels went to Williams,…

title: Podcast: The Commanders Left a Win on the Table Against the Eagles
summary: The Washington Commanders season opener came down to a 2-point conversion against the Philadelphia Eagles. What’s most frustrating about the loss in Philadelphia is seeing how a lack of execution in key moments throughout the game ultimately cost Washington points. Washington has no one to blame but themselves. The Commanders’ offense didn’t come alive until […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders signals for a two point conversion attempt while a touchdown is under review against the Philadelphia Eagles in the fourth quarter of a game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Washington Commanders season opener came down to a 2-point conversion against the Philadelphia Eagles. What’s most frustrating about the loss in Philadelphia is seeing how a lack of execution in key moments throughout the game ultimately cost Washington points. Washington has no one to blame but themselves. The Commanders’ offense didn’t come alive until the fourth quarter, but for the first three quarters against the Eagles, the unit couldn’t get favorable second and third downs to stay ahead of the chains. Jayden Daniels completed nine passes on 23 attempts for 64 yards through the first three quarters; the only chance that the Commanders had at success offensively was with running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Bill finished the game with 63 yards on 16 attempts, but was the catalyst behind the run game, wearing down the Eagles’ defense as the game went on. Between the pressure Jayden Daniels faced on his dropbacks and the wide receivers not getting open quickly enough for him (and drops), Washington has to find an immediate fix for its pass-game issues. On the Trap or Dive post-game recap, Dre and I dissect the Commanders mistakes that led to their 24-22 loss to the Eagles. The defense undoubtedly kept Washington in the game by containing Saquon Barkley and consistently getting home on Jalen Hurts, preventing him from attacking the secondary. Between Washington’s two first-time coordinators, Daronte Jones had the most impressive debut, and his scheme highlighted the front seven’s potential to take over games. However, even with a strong debut, Washington lost the explosive-play battle, couldn’t create a turnover, and the Eagles scored three touchdowns by capitalizing on just a handful of defensive mistakes. title: 2027 NFL draft order projections for Round 1, top pick, more
summary: ESPN's Football Power Index projects the 2027 NFL draft order for Round 1, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.
full_text:
The 2027 NFL draft is still months away, but with the 2026 season underway, we're starting to track pick order in Round 1. Which teams are in position to add elite prospects in the top 10 next April? What about the top five ... or even at No. 1?

 What follows is not the current draft order based on records. It is a projection of what ESPN's Football Power Index thinks the order ultimately will be by the end of the season. Each week during the season, the FPI projects the draft order by simulating the remainder of the season 10,000 times. Game probabilities are based primarily on the model's team ratings and game locations. The draft order is determined by the records the model projects for each team after 17 games, as well as each team's average draft position across the simulations.

 So where do things stand? Here are the full sortable projections, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.

title: 2026 NFL Power Rankings: How all 32 teams stack up for Week 2
summary: How do all 32 NFL teams stack up ahead of Week 2? Plus, we picked out the top newcomers from each roster.
full_text:
The opening week of the 2026 NFL season is now complete after the Chiefs defeated the Broncos 31-10 on "Monday Night Football." We saw a lot of scoring, as 49.4 points per game tied 2012 for the most in Week 1 since the AFL/NFL merger in 1970, per ESPN Research. But that still led to some close finishes, including an overtime win by the Lions over the Saints and the Bills' dramatic five-point victory over the Texans.

 How do these teams fit in our updated Power Rankings ahead of Week 2? To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another, ranking them from No. 1 to 32.

 In addition to our 1-32 ranking, NFL Nation reporters named a non-QB newcomer -- defined as a rookie, offseason acquisition or coaching hire -- who shined in Week 1. From Texans running back David Montgomery scoring three touchdowns to third-round defensive tackle Domonique Orange 's big stop for the Vikings, we picked 32 players and coaches who impressed in their debuts.  1. Buffalo Bills (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Texans 36-31

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR DJ Moore 

 Moore's five catches for 100 yards were somewhat aided when Houston safety Reed Blankenship went for an interception and missed badly, giving Moore an easy path to a 43-yard touchdown. However, Moore also did a lot of things that didn't end up in his standard receiving totals. He drew a 46-yard pass interference penalty and later an illegal contact flag. He also slapped away what appeared to be a very likely interception for Houston safety  Calen Bullock . It was everything the Bills could have asked for when they traded for Moore  in March. -- Aaron Schatz 

 

 
 

 

 2. Seattle Seahawks (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Patriots 13-10 
 Preseason ranking: 2 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: S Rodney Thomas II 

 Rookie running back Jadarian Price had a solid debut, but Thomas gets the nod for helping Seattle's defense hold New England to 10 points. Starting for an injured Ty Okada , Thomas had a pass breakup that resulted in an interception and an open-field tackle on consecutive drives. The plays got Seattle the ball back for drives that ended with a field goal and the tying touchdown. Thomas, a former starter with the Colts, signed a one-year, $1.4 million deal with the Seahawks and began on the practice squad. -- Brady Henderson 

 

 
 

 3. Baltimore Ravens (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Colts 41-23 
 Preseason ranking: 8 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle

 In his first game as Baltimore's offensive playcaller, Doyle kept the Colts on their heels by putting quarterback Lamar Jackson under center and using play-action. The result? For the first time in the Ravens' 31-year history, they had a 300-yard passer (Jackson), a 150-yard receiver ( Zay Flowers ) and a 100-yard rusher ( Derrick Henry ) in the same game. There will be plenty of opportunities for Doyle's unit to put up more points. Over the next seven games, Baltimore faces five teams -- the Saints, Cowboys, Browns, Bengals and Bills -- who allowed 27-plus points in Week 1. "Man, first NFL game, [he] came out of the gates on fire," Ravens head coach Jesse Minter said of Doyle. -- Jamison Hensley 

 

 
 

 4. Los Angeles Rams (0-1) 
 Week 1 result: Lost to the 49ers 27-7 
 Preseason ranking: 1 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: CB Trent McDuffie 

 The Rams traded four draft picks for the All-Pro cornerback in March as part of their effort to rehaul their CB room. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, McDuffie allowed only two receptions for 22 yards on four targets in Week 1, including two passes defensed. One of the passes defensed came in the first quarter, when McDuffie broke up a pass intended for Niners tight end George Kittle . McDuffie intercepted the ball but was just out of bounds. -- Sarah Barshop 

 

 
 

 5. San Francisco 49ers (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Rams 27-7 
 Preseason ranking: 9 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Mike Evans 

 Defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa was also impactful in his Niners debut, but it's hard to argue with Evans' production. He finished with six receptions for 49 yards and a touchdown, and each of those catches somehow went for either a first down or a score. That gave him the most receiving first downs by any player in a team debut since the Rams' Puka Nacua had six in 2023. Evans signed a three-year deal with the 49ers in free agency.  -- Nick Wagoner 

 

 
 

 6. Philadelphia Eagles (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Commanders 24-22 
 Preseason ranking: 5 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Dontayvion Wicks 

 Wicks had two catches for 73 yards and a touchdown against the Commanders. His 64-yard catch-and-run in the first half marked the longest reception of his career, providing a much-needed spark to the Eagles' new-look offense. Wicks, acquired via trade from the Packers in April, has assumed the role of WR2 behind DeVonta Smith . QB  Jalen Hurts and Wicks built a rapport over the spring and summer, and it translated to Week 1. -- Tim McManus 

 

 
 

 7. Chicago Bears (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Panthers 59-37 
 Preseason ranking: 12 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Kalif Raymond 

 The veteran wideout led the Bears with eight catches on nine targets for 84 yards. Five of his receptions came on third down, demonstrating the trust quarterback Caleb Williams quickly built with Raymond after  he signed  a one-year deal in March. Perhaps the moment most emblematic of his buy-in for what coach Ben Johnson asks of his offensive players is the block Raymond had during running back Kyle Monangai 's 61-yard touchdown in the third quarter. -- Courtney Cronin 

 

 

 
 

 8. Kansas City Chiefs (1-0) 
 Week 1 result: Beat the Broncos 31-10 
 Preseason ranking: 13 

 Non-QB newcomer debut:  RB Kenneth Walker III 

 For one game at least, Walker was everything the Chiefs could've hoped for, bringing more explosive highlights to their rushing attack. Walker produced a career-high 173 rushing yards, with his best moment being a breakaway 60-yard touchdown on fourth-and-inches early in the third quarter. His best trait against the Broncos was his elusiveness, as he forced 14 missed tackles, the most by any Chiefs player in a game since 2018. Walker caught a short touchdown pass, too. -- Nate Taylor 

 

 
 

 9. Denver Broncos (0-1) 
 Week 1 result: Lost to the Chiefs 31-10 
 Preseason ranking: 4 

 Non-QB newcomer debut:  RB Jonah Coleman 

 You know it was a bad opener -- and the three-touchdown loss to the Chiefs was brutal -- when Coleman's 27-yard kickoff return made him the best non-quarterback newcomer. It was that kind of night for a team that returned more players from last season than any other in the league. Jaylen Waddle had one catch for 2 yards, safety Tycen Anderson had one tackle and Coleman was the only rookie in uniform for the game.  -- Jeff Legwold

 Week 1 result: Lost to the Seahawks 13-10 
 Preseason ranking: 6 

 Non-QB newcomer debut: Edge rusher  Dre'Mont Jones 

 Signed to a three-year, $36.5 million deal in free agency, the eight-year veteran totaled four QB hits, one sack and two tackles. He was generally a solid presence setting the edge in the running game, as well. The Patriots targeted Jones over retaining K'Lavon Chaisson , who led the team with 7.5 sacks last season. Runner-up choice: sixth-round rookie linebacker Namdi Obiazor (TCU), who led the team with three special teams tackles, including one on the opening kickoff. -- Mike Reiss

title: Touchdowns galore, awards market moves and a great Sunday for NFL bettors
summary: A high-scoring Week 1 with a variety of players scoring TDs made for a bettor-friendly Sunday.
full_text:
The Bears ' 59-37 victory over the Carolina Panthers in Sunday's early slate kept the momentum of Chicago's offseason hype train going and was representative of a great first Sunday of NFL action for bettors. 

 For starters, the Bears were one of the most popular teams to win and cover the spread (-3) on Sunday, which they did with ease in the second half. DraftKings classified the Bears as the second-most-backed team by bets and handle going into Sunday's action, while BetMGM said Chicago minus-3 was the most-bet spread of the early slate by tickets, with the sportsbook's senior trading manager Christian Cipollini classifying it as "a good outcome for bettors."

 

 Then there was the avalanche of touchdowns. Five Bears got in the end zone on Sunday, with QB Caleb Williams and RB D'Andre Swift each getting in multiple times. With the Panthers contributing plenty of scoring on their own, the game flew over its total of 47.5 with 2:35 left in the second quarter. The final score's 96 total points were the most for a Week 1 game in NFL history.

 The game set the pace for an explosive opening Sunday that saw six teams score 24 or more points in the first half of their games -- also the most in Week 1 in NFL history, according to ESPN research. With players such as  Jahmyr Gibbs , Amon-Ra St. Brown , Derrick Henry , Jonathan Taylor and Josh Allen finding the end zone multiple times, that made for a tremendous day for a betting public that makes a habit of rooting for scoring from superstars.

 "The first NFL Sunday of the season was a champagne-popping day for bettors, while the book was left cleaning up the corks," Caesars Sportsbook football lead Joey Feazel told ESPN. "Seven of the eight morning favorites won outright, six games flew over the total -- many reaching that mark by halftime -- and eight of the top 10 most popular touchdown scorers found the end zone. 

 "Favorites, overs and touchdown scorers combined to create a bettor-friendly trifecta on opening Sunday."

 Chicago's big win built on the goodwill the team had accrued with bettors throughout the offseason via the futures market -- both for the team as a whole and its star quarterback.

 The Bears were a hot commodity in a variety of futures markets before the season, chief among them being the Super Bowl. Just before the campaign kicking off, DraftKings reported 7.5% of its Super Bowl handle backing Chicago -- the third most behind the Los Angeles Rams (20.2%) and Buffalo Bills (9.8%) -- while BetMGM said the Bears had garnered the most NFC championship tickets at 14.4%. Feazel called Chicago "a moderate position" in the Super Bowl market Sunday. 

 

 "Chicago's offense looks great," Circa Sports NFL oddsmaker Jamey Pileggi told ESPN. "Bad defense is going to hold them back from being real contenders."

 At DraftKings, Chicago made only a small move from 24-1 to 21-1 to win the title, but the big odds move came for Williams in the MVP market, where he went from 12-1 to +700, tying him for second with Lamar Jackson behind Allen in the lead at +500. 

 Several sportsbooks considered Williams a liability in the awards market coming into the season, and he accumulated around 10% of the tickets at both BetMGM and Caesars. Joe Burrow (+950) has been the public's favorite throughout the offseason, but if Williams can continue to put up performances like Sunday's, he could continue to gain traction with bettors.

 "Given his Week 1 performance and the amount of early support we've already seen, we would expect Caleb Williams to remain one of the more heavily backed players in the MVP market moving forward," Feazel said.

 Odds & Ends 

 
 The Arizona Cardinals closed as 8.5-point underdogs to the Los Angeles Chargers before upsetting them outright on the road. It was the largest Week 1 upset since 2018 ( Tampa Bay Buccaneers +10 over the New Orleans Saints ). 
 The Chargers were the most-picked team in ESPN Survivor contests (21.4%), the second-most in Circa Survivor (30.3%) and the second-most in Splash Sports' $1,000 entry survivor contest (21.5%). 
 The Cardinals are the first team with a preseason win total of 3.5 or lower to win their Week 1 game since at least 1990, according to ESPN Research. 
 After losing and failing to cover plus-3.5 on Sunday, the Buccaneers are now 0-10 against the spread in their past 10 games, tying the longest ATS losing streak in the Super Bowl era. 
 On the flip side, the Jacksonville Jaguars have covered nine consecutive regular-season games, the longest ATS winning streak since the Green Bay Packers in 2021 and the longest in Jaguars history.  
 
 ESPN's David Purdum contributed to this report.

title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces seven active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald , who un-retired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7 all-time. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach top-five all-time territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks were 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research, heading into the seaosn. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the all-time list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all of the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: NFL Week 1: Takeaways, questions, fantasy spin for Sunday games
summary: Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering the biggest questions coming out of each Sunday game. Here's what we learned from Week 1.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL season  is already off to an exciting start.

 In the early window Sunday, the Bears and Panthers combined for 96 points, the most in a season opener in NFL history, per ESPN Research. The host Jaguars easily handled the Browns in quarterback  Deshaun Watson 's first regular-season game since October 2024. The Bills looked sharp offensively in Joe Brady's head coaching debut against the Texans, and the Lions needed overtime to get past the Saints.

 In the late window, the Cardinals and Raiders won in the respective debuts of first-year coaches Mike LaFleur and Klint Kubiak. The Commanders fell despite a comeback against division foe Philadelphia. And after losing quarterback Kyler Murray to a concussion early, the Vikings scored 29 unanswered to defeat the Packers. The Giants finished things off by beating the Cowboys on Sunday night, marking the first time since 2009 both New York teams opened with a victory.

 Our NFL Nation reporters reacted to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game and detailing everything else you need to know for teams that played Sunday. Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup. Let's get to it.

 
 Jump to: 
 DAL-NYG |  GB-MIN |  WSH-PHI 
 MIA-LV  |  ARI-LAC  |  CHI-CAR 
 BUF-HOU  |  NO-DET  |  BAL-IND 
 ATL-PIT  |  NYJ-TEN  |  TB-CIN 
 CLE-JAX 

 Catch up on weekday games: 
 SF-LAR | NE-SEA 

 
 

 

 N.Y. Giants 28, Dallas 20 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Giants 
 Should the Giants be taken seriously in the NFC East? This was a statement game for the John Harbaugh Giants. They looked like the better team in beating a Cowboys squad that had prevailed in 16 of its previous 18 meetings with the Giants. New York's offense looked dangerous with a power running game (165 yards) led by Cam Skattebo  (18 carries, 81 yards), and quarterback Jaxson Dart was in command throughout. The defense also looked greatly improved. With neither the Eagles nor Commanders looking dominant in Week1, the Giants could be a real threat in the NFC East. For the first time in years, it's not an outlandish thought.

 What to make of the QB performance: Brilliant. Dart was in control throughout, running and throwing with precision. He finished 23-of-29 for 230 passing yards with three touchdown and added 54 rushing yards. The chemistry that Dart showed all summer with new tight end Isaiah Likely translated to the opener. Likely caught eight passes on eight targets for 78 yards with two touchdowns and helped ice the game late with two big third-down receptions. -- Jordan Raanan 

 Next game: at Rams (Monday, Sept. 21, 8:15 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Cowboys 
 Will this serve as a wake-up call for the Cowboys? After a drama-free offseason, the return of a top-tier offense and a revamped defense, expectations were high. Though there are 16 more games to go, the loss to the Giants showed the Cowboys have a lot of work to do. An ill-timed Dak Prescott interception at the end of the first half led to a Giants' TD. There were far too many penalties in the first half (seven, tied for the most in an opener since 2008) and a costly one in the fourth quarter, as Javonte Williams ' taunting penalty led to a missed extra point attempt in a one-score game. The Giants were able to control the line of scrimmage and the clock in the second half to win a game that went according to the Giants' desired script.

 Most surprising performance: Things were supposed to be different for this Cowboys defense. Not necessarily a massive move to the top of the league, but they were disappointing throughout Christian Parker's first game as playcaller. The end-of-half work that saw New York go ahead 14-7 was filled with coverage breakdowns. The second half opened with the Cowboys needing to call timeout because they had only 10 defenders on the field, and they could not come up with any stops in the final two quarters. With eight new starters from last season's opener and another handful of new key contributors, it's clear it will take time for it to come together. -- Todd Archer 

 Next game: vs. Commanders (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET)

 
 Fantasy football takeaway:  Likely paced the Giants with eight catches -- the most by any Giants tight end in nearly three years -- with two going for touchdowns. His 27.8 fantasy points led the position, and are an indicator he'll be involved enough to be a weekly TE1.  -- Cockcroft 

 

 

 Minnesota 39, Green Bay 22 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Vikings 
 What now at quarterback? For the second consecutive season, and for the third campaign in the past four, the Vikings are dealing with an injury to their quarterback. This time, new starter Kyler Murray made it only 11 plays -- and they were 11 shaky plays, at that -- before suffering a concussion at the end of a first-quarter scramble. Backup Carson Wentz , named the No. 2 quarterback last week after he was a bystander in the competition between Murray and J.J. McCarthy this summer, was understandably rusty at the outset but hung in to throw three touchdown passes and avoid a turnover. Wentz will be the starter until Murray is cleared to return.

 Trend to watch: The Vikings blitzed Packers quarterback Jordan Love on nearly every first-half snap (15-of-18, or 83%), and Love burned them repeatedly en route to putting up 19 points. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores adjusted with more variety in the second half, taking down the blitz rate to 63%. It wasn't the only reason the Packers struggled to score thereafter, but it made the blitzes the Vikings did execute more effective. -- Kevin Seifert 

 Next game: at Bears (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 

 
 

 

 Packers 
 Did the Packers learn nothing from last year? So much for all that offseason talk about finishing. Week 1 followed the same script from late last season: Grab the lead, make major mistakes in the second half and let the opponent back in the game. The blunders were many in this matchup: a special teams miscue (allowing a 69-yard kickoff return); a blown coverage (leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson wide open for a touchdown); bad penalties (three of them on the Vikings' go-ahead drive that wiped out a pair of would-have-been third-down stops and nullified an interception); shoddy offensive line play; and a poor coaching decision (opting to take a field goal off the board on a penalty then failing on the ensuing QB sneak).

 What to make of the QB performance:  Love, despite a 387-yard passing game, barely had a chance, especially down the stretch, thanks to a disastrous performance by his offensive line. Being without starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee) wasn't the reason the Vikings recorded 15 QB hits on Love; it was because the Packers couldn't handle the myriad of blitzes. When the Packers needed a fourth-quarter drive to regain the lead, Love was sacked on back-to-back plays, losing a fumble on the second one that was returned to Green Bay's 1-yard line. -- Rob Demovsky 

 Next game: at Jets (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 Fantasy football takeaway:   Christian Watson 's 32.7 fantasy points were the second most among wide receivers in Week 1 through the late window. He caught 6-of-8 targets for 147 yards and two touchdowns for the Pack. With an expanding route tree and big-play speed, Watson can be safely played as a lower-tier WR2 for Week 2. -- Bowen 

 

 

 Philadelphia 24, Washington 22 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Eagles 
 Did the Eagles' new offense pass the test Week 1? There was a boom-or-bust element to it, but the explosive plays carried them to a passing grade and a win over Washington. From WR Dontayvion Wicks ' 64-yard reception (a career high) to QB Jalen Hurts ' 22-yard scramble on third-and-18 to TE Dallas Goedert 's 43-yard score moments later, there was plenty to be encouraged about from offensive coordinator Sean Mannion's debut. Some issues along the offensive front (left…

title: Lamar Jackson looks like old self in Ravens' new offense
summary: In his first season with new OC Declan Doyle, Jackson has embraced changes to how he played football for most of his life.
full_text:
INDIANAPOLIS -- It was third-and-16 in the first quarter Sunday when Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson dropped back and saw two Indianapolis Colts pass rushers quickly closing in. 
 
 For many quarterbacks, it would have been a sack, the loss of 11 yards and the end of the drive. For Jackson, it was an opportunity to show he can create plays that make you question what exactly you just saw. 
 
 Ducking under linebacker Arden Key and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner , Jackson made an unlikely escape and scrambled 16 yards for a first down. In Baltimore's 41-23 season-opening win, Jackson proved he can be his old self in the Ravens' new offense. 
 
 "It was just like, 'What just happened? How did he get it in there and get the first down?'" Ravens defensive end Calais Campbell said. "It is like, 'How many people can actually do that?' Not many -- not many. He might be one of the only ones." 
 
 
 
 It was a play that had everyone shaking their heads except for Jackson himself. 
 
 "I believe I did it a few times throughout my career, but [I'm] just playing football," Jackson said. "I am trying to get out of the situation. [The] offensive line [is] doing a great job at protecting me, [and] sometimes I have to have their back." 
 
 In his first season with new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, Jackson has embraced changes to how he played football for most of his life. 
 
 Instead of primarily working out of the pistol formation, Jackson was under center 53% of the time (34 of 64 snaps), which was the highest percentage of his nine-year NFL career. He also altered his footwork, switching to a left foot-forward stance because Doyle believed it would help the timing of the passing game. 
 
 The result was a throwback game for the two-time MVP. This was Jackson's sixth game where he threw over 300 yards and ran for at least 40 yards -- but it was his first such performance since October 2024. 
 
 
 
 "The best player in the league," Ravens running back Derrick Henry said. "He's been one of the best players in the league for a long time. That's never [been a] doubt in my mind. I know what Lamar's about. You all have seen it. He just keeps showing you." 
 
 One of the buzzwords with Doyle all offseason has been explosiveness, which soon became a theme for the opener. 
 
 On the first play called by Doyle, Jackson rolled left off play-action and connected with wide receiver Zay Flowers for 49 yards to set up Baltimore's first touchdown. On the first play of the fourth quarter, Jackson threw a 53-yard pass to wide receiver Chris Moore to set up the Ravens' fifth and final touchdown of the day. 
 
 Jackson finished 17-of-25 passing (68%) for 324 yards and one touchdown. 
 
 "You can see he is just comfortable back there," Ravens wide receiver  Chris Moore  said. "He is reading his keys. He is going through his progressions, and he is finding the open guy. We already know Lamar has an incredible playmaking ability, so that just happens naturally. But for him to be able to just have that poise in the pocket now, you can see it shine." 
 
 
 Jackson will face an increased challenge throwing the ball downfield. Two of Baltimore's top three wide receivers -- Flowers (hamstring) and Ja'Kobi Lane (wrist) -- were injured Sunday and didn't play in the second half. 
 
 If Flowers is forced to miss some games, it would be a major loss because he is Jackson's most reliable receiver. On passes where Jackson threw the ball 10 yards or longer Sunday, he was 4-of-5 for 96 yards when targeting Flowers and 2-of-5 for 70 yards when targeting others, according to ESPN Research. 
 
 The Ravens' only healthy wide receivers are Rashod Bateman , the No. 2 wide receiver who didn't record a catch Sunday; Moore, who was elevated from the practice squad; LaJohntay Wester , who's primarily a punt returner; and Elijah Sarratt , a rookie fourth-round pick who was a healthy scratch. 
 
 "I have all the confidence in my guys who stepped in," Jackson said. "You never know when the next guy [is] going to be up, so just dial in [and] stay locked in."

title: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 2
summary: Will the Titans score any points against the Eagles? Can Ben Johnson solve Brian Flores' Vikings defense? Get ready for Week 2 with seven takes.
full_text:
Who's ready to put their thinking caps on? Big-time offensive scoring was the story in Week 1 of the NFL season, but Week 2 is now right around the corner. What will it bring?

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from last week to this week with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions -- those come later in the week. They aren't concrete takeaways off the past week of NFL action, either -- those are fired off on Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain things. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games for us to really find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 This week, I'm starting off with my expectations for the schemer heavyweight fight of the century, my theories on the real skeleton key for the Bills' offense and my worry that the first shutout of the season will come this Sunday.

 Here are seven things I think for Week 2.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite 
 Texans' offense will win games 
 Bengals defense is showing promise 
 Kincaid is the Bills' secret sauce 
 Titans will not score in Week 2 
 Lions have an Achilles' heel on defense 
 Lawrence is league MVP this week 
 Five extra inklings 

 

 
 

 I think ... Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite 
 Two heinous crimes were committed Sunday by two of football nerddom's favorite coaches.

 Let's start with Johnson. The Bears scored 59 points against the Panthers, which is like if you scored 50 points, and then decided to score nine more points. Both running backs  D'Andre Swift  and Kyle Monangai  reached 100 yards and scored two touchdowns, and quarterback Caleb Williams added another two scores on scrambles of his own. And for those tracking Williams' accuracy metrics: 72.4% completion percentage with an off-target rate of only 13.8%.

 Everything worked for the Bears' offense, which barely left first gear against the Panthers. The Bears will face far stiffer competition in Week 2 against the Vikings and Flores, who rendered an unbelievable performance against the Packers in Week 1.

 The Vikings blitzed Jordan Love on 73.8% of his dropbacks Sunday -- the highest rate at which any quarterback has been blitzed since the 2023 season. The Packers were in a difficult position entering the game; starting left guard Aaron Banks was hurt, and the camp campaign to build up Anthony Belton at the starting right guard spot was abandoned late in the process. The Packers fielded 2024 fifth-round pick Jacob Monk at right guard and 2024 undrafted free agent  Donovan Jennings at left guard. It was Jennings' first career start and Monk's second.

 In an effort to insulate the young guards, the Packers kept more players in to block than basically any offense over the past few seasons. Love had three or fewer receivers in the route concept on an astonishing 15 dropbacks. Only three quarterbacks have had more such dropbacks over the past five seasons.

 Flores has little interest in occupying those routes with multiple defenders -- he'd rather throw bodies against the wall of your pass protection and find a weak point. Like water against a dam, it didn't really matter how many players the Packers kept in to protect -- if there was a weak point (which there often was), Flores had a rusher in that spot. His distinctive approach to early-down blitzing breaks the rules. It forces opposing offenses to play a different sport than the one for which they're prepared against other opponents.

 But Johnson knows Flores well. He called offense against him as the coordinator of the Lions -- twice in 2023, twice in 2024 -- then picked up another two games in 2025 as the head coach of the Bears. Across six matchups, Johnson's team is 5-1 -- the only loss was last season's opener and Williams' first start in Johnson's offense. Over those six games, Johnson's offense doesn't look like a 59-point monster ... but it's clearly better than the average offense against the marauding Vikings coordinator.

 

 So what does Johnson do that other teams can't replicate? A few things stick out. The first is communication. Flores' defense requires as much pre-snap coordination between 11 players as any in football -- that's why Harrison Smith is back and so valuable. He can be the coach on the field, changing the playcall after the defense sees the formation.

 Johnson rises to meet Flores. His offense is as communication-heavy as any in the league, and his group is empowered to make adjustments based on what it sees. Flores wants to get opposing offenses stuck in a bad protection look or run call; Johnson's groups are elite at getting out of such sticky wickets. Williams' pre-snap command, which has reportedly taken big strides through Year 1 and into Year 2 with Johnson, will be tested here.

 To challenge Flores' reliance on communication, Johnson will randomly snap the football quickly -- no motion, no checking. Immediate snaps. The Bears had 19 quick snaps against the Vikings in Week 11 -- snaps in which less than two seconds elapse between the line getting set and the ball being snapped. It was the most they had in any game last season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Second most? The 17 such snaps in Week 1 ... also against Flores.

 

 The second thing that sticks out is formational. The Lions loved condensed sets under Johnson, and the Bears have continued that approach. Condensed sets are typically a bad idea against blitz-heavy teams. When you spread out the field, it's easier to identify suspicious defensive alignment that reveals who's blitzing from where. Against Flores and the Vikings, there's no point in trying to riddle things out -- the blitzes are too frequent and too varied. You'll think you're right, you'll actually be wrong, and then you'll be dead in the water.

 So Johnson turns into the skid. He gets as condensed as possible against Flores. In 2025, no offense had more condensed formations in any game than the Bears in Week 11 against the Vikings, with an average formational width of only 17.7 yards. Teeny tiny formations allow Johnson to throw the ball on out-breakers into a ton of space, to stress the Vikings' cornerbacks who are typically insulated by trap coverages and quick throws. It also allows Johnson to meet Flores' duplicity and disguise with the beautiful simplicity of the running game. With lighter players such as  Joshua Metellus and Dallas Turner on the edge against double-teams from extra tight ends and condensed wide receivers, the Bears can grind out physical yardage and set up the play-action pass.

 

 Does Flores have an answer to this approach? Yes ... but not on the chalkboard. The Vikings' first three picks in the 2026 draft were trench picks: defensive tackle Caleb Banks in the first round, on/off-ball linebacker hybrid Jake Golday in the second round and another defensive tackle in the third round in space-gobbler Domonique Orange . Any defense that plays in a division with the Bears needs to be serious about its run defense -- doubly true for Flores, who will never get to third-and-long against Chicago unless he has some run-stuffing hog mollies up front to slow down Swift and Monangai.

 

 Johnson won Assistant Coach of the Year in 2024. Second place in voting was Flores. When Flores was a young defensive assistant cutting his teeth in New England, Johnson was doing the same in Miami on offense -- twice a year, they saw each other. These two have circled their matchups like heavyweight fighters for years now, and on Sunday, we get another 90-minute dance in the ring. Bring your popcorn.

 

 

 I think ... the Texans' offense will win some games this year 
 The Texans' defense was a machine last season, and it entered 2026 with all of the Super Bowl hype. Houston just needed an offense that could do enough to win those games in which the defense struggled.

 Sunday was one such game. The Texans…
